Asking about disagreement culture, post-mortems, and tech debt signals you've worked somewhere those things mattered. Two cautions: don't lead an early round purely with perks, salary, and time-off (save those for the recruiter/offer stage), and genuinely listen — a canned question you ask without engaging with the answer is transparent. The best candidates react ("that's interesting — how are you thinking about tackling that?") and let it become a dialogue.

Q15. Salary negotiation basics.

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: Extremely High (at the offer stage)

Short Answer

Research the market first, avoid naming a number before you have to, give a researched range anchored to your value when pushed, negotiate on the total package rather than base alone, and stay collaborative — never combative or dishonest. The offer stage is a negotiation, not a favour, and politely negotiating is expected.

Detailed Answer

Negotiation makes many engineers anxious, but a few principles cover most situations:

  • Do the research before you talk numbers. Use levelling/market data, local benchmarks, and your current comp plus a reasonable step. You negotiate from knowledge, not hope.
  • Let them go first if you can. When asked early for a number, it's fine to deflect: "I'd like to understand the role and level first, but I'm targeting a range in line with the market for a senior React engineer here." If pushed, give a range whose bottom you'd genuinely accept — interviewers anchor low.
  • Anchor to value, and get the offer in hand first. The most leverage you'll ever have is after they've decided they want you and before you've said yes. That's the moment to negotiate, calmly.
  • Negotiate the whole package. Base, equity, bonus, sign-on, level, remote flexibility, learning budget — if base is capped, other levers often aren't.
  • Never lie. Don't invent a competing offer or misstate your current salary; it's easy to get caught and it destroys the trust you just built.

"Based on my research for a frontend engineer at my level in this market, I'm targeting roughly X to Y. I'm flexible depending on the overall package — level, equity, and growth matter to me as much as base — and I'd want to understand the full compensation structure before landing on a number. I'm excited about the role, so I'm confident we can find something that works for both of us."

A useful closing tactic when you get an offer: thank them, express genuine enthusiasm, then ask "is there any flexibility on the base / the level?" A polite, specific ask paired with real enthusiasm almost never backfires, and companies routinely leave room for exactly this.

Senior Engineer Perspective

The single biggest mistake engineers make is not negotiating at all — accepting the first number out of relief or fear. Recruiters expect a counter, and a calm, informed one rarely costs you the offer (if a company rescinds because you politely negotiated, that's a red flag about them). The second mistake is giving a hard single number too early, which either leaves money on the table or prices you out before they know your value. The winning posture is calm, researched, and collaborative: you know your worth, you've done the homework, and you're solving for a package that works for both sides — not fighting for scraps.

02 - JAVASCRIPT FUNDAMENTALS

Target Audience: Frontend / React Engineer (3–6 Years) Goal: Not just answer questions, but survive follow-up grilling from experienced interviewers.

TOP HIGHEST-ROI QUESTIONS IN THIS CHAPTER

  1. What is the difference between var, let, and const — and what is the Temporal Dead Zone?
  2. Explain hoisting for variables and functions.
  3. What is the difference between == and === and when is coercion dangerous?
  4. Primitive vs reference types — how does copying and passing work?
  5. Name the most common type-coercion gotchas.
  6. What is a closure? Give real production use cases.
  7. Explain lexical scope and the scope chain.
  8. How is this determined? Explain all five binding rules.
  9. What do call, apply, and bind do — and how do they differ?
  10. Explain prototypal inheritance and the prototype chain.
  11. What does the new operator actually do, step by step?
  12. How do destructuring, spread, rest, and default parameters work?
  13. Explain optional chaining and nullish coalescing (ES2020).
  14. Shallow copy vs deep copy — and what is structuredClone?
  15. When should you use Map/Set instead of a plain object?
  16. What are pure functions, immutability, and higher-order functions?
  17. Explain map, filter, and reduce — and when reduce is the wrong tool.

SECTION 1 - TYPES & COERCION

Q1. What is the difference between var, let, and const, and what is the Temporal Dead Zone?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

var is function-scoped and hoisted with an initial value of undefined. let and const are block-scoped and, although hoisted, they live in the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) until the line where they are declared — accessing them before that throws a ReferenceError. const additionally forbids reassignment of the binding (not deep immutability).

Detailed Answer

Scoping

var ignores block boundaries — a var declared inside an if or for block leaks to the enclosing function. let/const are confined to the nearest { } block, which is why they fixed the classic loop-closure bug where every callback captured the same var i.

The Temporal Dead Zone

All three are hoisted to the top of their scope, but they behave differently before initialization. var is initialized to undefined during hoisting, so reading it early is merely useless, not fatal. let/const bindings are created but left uninitialized; the span from the top of the block to the declaration line is the TDZ, and any access in that window throws. The TDZ exists deliberately — it turns silent bugs into loud errors and makes const semantically coherent (you can never observe a const before its one and only assignment).

const is not "immutable"

const freezes the binding, not the value. A const object can still have its properties mutated; only reassigning the variable itself is blocked. Use Object.freeze (shallow) if you need value-level immutability.

Featurevarletconst
ScopeFunctionBlockBlock
HoistedYes (= undefined)Yes (TDZ)Yes (TDZ)
ReassignableYesYesNo
Redeclarable in scopeYesNoNo

Code Example

console.log(a); // undefined  (var is hoisted & initialized)
var a = 1;

console.log(b); // ReferenceError: Cannot access 'b' before initialization
let b = 2;      // b was in the TDZ above this line

const obj = { n: 1 };
obj.n = 2;      // OK — mutating a property
// obj = {};    // TypeError — reassigning the const binding

Project Example

In React you almost always declare hooks and derived values with const (const [count, setCount] = useState(0)). It signals intent — this reference will not be reassigned within the render — and prevents accidental shadowing bugs. let shows up for accumulators inside a useMemo body; var should essentially never appear in modern code.

Senior Engineer Perspective

The interviewer wants to hear "TDZ" unprompted and to know that const is about the binding, not the value — juniors often claim const means immutable. A strong follow-up: "Why does typeof undeclaredVar return 'undefined' but typeof on a let in its TDZ throws?" Answer: typeof is the historical exception that safely handles never-declared names, but TDZ variables are declared, so even typeof throws for them.

Q2. Explain hoisting for variables and functions.

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Hoisting is the JS engine's compile phase moving declarations to the top of their scope before execution. Function declarations are hoisted whole (callable before their line). var declarations are hoisted and set to undefined. let/const and function expressions/arrow functions are hoisted but stay uninitialized (TDZ).

Detailed Answer

It helps to think of two phases. In the creation phase the engine scans the scope and registers bindings; in the execution phase it runs the code line by line. Only the declaration is hoisted, never the assignment. So var x = 5 is conceptually split into var x (hoisted) and x = 5 (stays in place).

Function declarations are special: the entire function object is available before its textual position, which is why you can call a helper defined lower in the file. A function expression assigned to a variable follows that variable's rules — a var holding a function is undefined until assigned, and a const arrow function is in the TDZ.

Code Example

greet();            // "hi" — declaration hoisted whole
function greet() { console.log("hi"); }

sayBye();           // TypeError: sayBye is not a function
var sayBye = function () { console.log("bye"); };
// var sayBye is hoisted as undefined; calling undefined() throws

Senior Engineer Perspective

The trap is the difference between ReferenceError (TDZ / undeclared) and TypeError (calling an undefined value). If a candidate says "everything gets moved to the top," push them: does the value move too? The precise answer — declarations are registered, initializations stay put — is the senior signal. In practice, rely on hoisting only for function declarations; write everything else before use.

Q3. What is the difference between == and === and when is coercion dangerous?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

=== (strict equality) compares type and value with no conversion. == (loose equality) coerces the operands to a common type first, which produces surprising results. Rule of thumb: always use ===; the one pragmatic exception is x == null to test for both null and undefined at once.

Detailed Answer

== follows the abstract equality algorithm: if types differ it applies a chain of conversions — null and undefined are loosely equal to each other and nothing else; strings and numbers compare as numbers; booleans are converted to numbers; objects are converted to primitives via valueOf/toString. This is why 0 == "", 0 == false, and "" == false are all true, and why [] == ![] is true — a genuinely confusing surface.

The pragmatic exception is the loose null check. value == null is true for exactly null and undefined, which is a concise nullish guard many codebases (and ESLint configs) explicitly allow.

Code Example

0 == "";        // true  — both coerce to 0
0 == false;     // true
"" == false;    // true
null == undefined; // true
null === undefined; // false

0 === "";       // false — no coercion
NaN === NaN;    // false — use Number.isNaN()

// The accepted exception:
if (value == null) { /* runs for null OR undefined */ }

Senior Engineer Perspective

Expect a whiteboard trap like [] == ![]. Walk it: ![] is false, so it becomes [] == false, then [] == 0, then "" == 0, then 0 == 0 → true. You do not need to memorize the table, but you should demonstrate that you understand coercion happens in steps and that this is exactly why === is the default. Bonus: mention Object.is, which is like === but treats NaN as equal to itself and distinguishes +0 from -0.

Q4. Primitive vs reference types — how do copying and passing work?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

Primitives (string, number, boolean, null, undefined, symbol, bigint) are copied and compared by value. Objects, arrays, and functions are held by reference — assigning or passing them copies the reference (a pointer), not the underlying data, so two variables can mutate the same object. Equality (===) compares primitives by value and objects by identity.

Detailed Answer

JavaScript is always "pass by value" — but for objects the value that is passed is the reference. So a function can mutate the properties of an object you passed in (the caller sees the change), yet reassigning the parameter to a brand-new object does not affect the caller. This distinction trips up many candidates.

This is the single biggest source of React state bugs: mutating an object or array in place does not change its reference, so React's Object.is bailout sees "no change" and skips the re-render. You must produce a new reference.

Code Example

let a = { n: 1 };
let b = a;          // b holds the SAME reference
b.n = 99;
console.log(a.n);   // 99 — same object

function replace(x) { x = { n: 0 }; } // reassigns local param only
replace(a);
console.log(a.n);   // 99 — caller unaffected

{ n: 1 } === { n: 1 }; // false — different identities

// React: WRONG (same reference, no re-render)
state.items.push(newItem); setState(state.items);
// RIGHT (new reference)
setState(prev => [...prev, newItem]);

Senior Engineer Perspective

The interviewer is really testing whether you understand why React needs immutable updates and why comparing objects with === checks identity, not contents. Strong candidates connect the language semantics directly to React.memo, dependency arrays, and Redux reducers. A common follow-up: "Why does useEffect fire on every render when a dependency is an object literal?" — because the literal is a new reference each render.

Q5. Name the most common type-coercion gotchas.

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

The usual suspects: + concatenates when either operand is a string; typeof null is "object"; NaN !== NaN; [] + [] is "" and [] + {} is "[object Object]"; and falsy values (0, "", NaN, null, undefined, false) all coerce to false in boolean context.

Detailed Answer

The key mental model: + is overloaded — if either side is a string (or coerces to one), it concatenates; otherwise it adds numerically. Every other arithmetic operator (-, *, /) forces numeric coercion. That is why "5" - 1 is 4 but "5" + 1 is "51".

In React the falsy-coercion gotcha bites when you conditionally render with &&: {items.length && <List/>} renders a literal 0 on screen when the array is empty, because 0 is falsy and gets returned. Use items.length > 0 && ... or a ternary.

Code Example

1 + "2";        // "12"  (concatenation)
"5" - 1;        // 4     (numeric coercion)
typeof null;    // "object"  (historical bug)
typeof NaN;     // "number"
Number.isNaN(NaN); // true — the correct NaN test

// React footgun — renders "0" when empty:
{count && <Badge value={count} />}
// Fix:
{count > 0 && <Badge value={count} />}

Senior Engineer Perspective

The {0 && ...} JSX bug is a favourite because it connects raw language behaviour to a real React defect. If you volunteer it, you signal that you have shipped React and been burned. Also mention that String(x), Number(x), and Boolean(x) are explicit conversions you should prefer over relying on implicit coercion.

SECTION 2 - SCOPE & CLOSURES

Q6. What is a closure? Give real production use cases.

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

A closure is a function bundled together with references to the variables from the scope where it was defined. Because that scope stays alive as long as the inner function is reachable, the function "remembers" and can keep reading and updating those variables even after the outer function has returned.

Detailed Answer

Closures are the mechanism behind private state, function factories, and event handlers. In React, every hook relies on closures: the callback you pass to useState, useEffect, or an event handler closes over the props and state from the render in which it was created. This is also the source of the "stale closure" bug — an effect or interval captures an old value and never sees updates unless dependencies or a functional updater are used.

Real use cases

  • Private state / encapsulation: variables unreachable from outside, exposed only through returned methods.
  • Counters & ID generators: maintain a private tally across calls.
  • Memoization: a cache held in the enclosing scope, shared across invocations.
  • Currying & partial application: capturing earlier arguments.
  • Debounce / throttle: the timer handle lives in the closure.

Code Example

// Private state + counter
function createCounter() {
  let count = 0;                 // private, not accessible outside
  return {
    inc() { return ++count; },
    get() { return count; },
  };
}
const c = createCounter();
c.inc(); c.inc();
c.get();  // 2  — count survives via closure

// Memoization
function memoize(fn) {
  const cache = new Map();       // captured across calls
  return (arg) => {
    if (cache.has(arg)) return cache.get(arg);
    const result = fn(arg);
    cache.set(arg, result);
    return result;
  };
}

// Debounce
function debounce(fn, ms) {
  let timer;                     // handle lives in the closure
  return (...args) => {
    clearTimeout(timer);
    timer = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), ms);
  };
}

Project Example

A debounced search box in React: const debounced = useMemo(() => debounce(onSearch, 300), [onSearch]). The returned function closes over the timer so successive keystrokes reset it. The classic bug — an interval inside useEffect(() => setInterval(() => setCount(count + 1)), []) always logging 1 — is a stale closure; the fix is the functional updater setCount(c => c + 1).

Senior Engineer Perspective

Anyone can recite the definition. The senior differentiator is naming a concrete production use (memoization, debounce, private state) and connecting closures to React's stale-closure pitfall. Expect the loop question: why does for (var i...) setTimeout(() => log(i)) print the final value repeatedly, and how does let fix it? Because let creates a fresh binding per iteration, so each closure captures its own i.

Q7. Explain lexical scope and the scope chain.

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Lexical (static) scope means a variable's accessibility is determined by where it is written in the source, not by where the function is called. When resolving an identifier, the engine walks outward through the chain of enclosing scopes until it finds the binding or reaches the global scope.

Detailed Answer

Each function creates a new scope nested inside the scope where it was defined. Name lookup goes inner → outer (the scope chain); it never goes into sibling or caller scopes. This is precisely what makes closures predictable — a closure captures the lexical environment of its definition site, so you can reason about which variables it sees just by reading the code.

Contrast with dynamic scope (used by some other languages) where lookup would follow the call stack. JavaScript is lexically scoped for variables, but note that this is the exception — for ordinary functions this is bound dynamically at call time, which is why arrow functions (which capture this lexically) were introduced.

Code Example

const outer = "O";
function parent() {
  const mid = "M";
  function child() {
    const inner = "I";
    console.log(inner, mid, outer); // I M O — walks up the chain
  }
  child();
}
parent();
// child cannot be called from elsewhere and still see mid — scope is
// fixed by where child is DEFINED, not where it is called.

Senior Engineer Perspective

The distinction interviewers probe is "lexical vs dynamic scope" and the fact that variables are lexical while regular-function this is dynamic. If you nail that one sentence, you have separated yourself from candidates who conflate the two. It also sets up the next topic cleanly.

SECTION 3 - THIS & FUNCTIONS

Q8. How is this determined? Explain all five binding rules.

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

this is decided at call time by how a function is invoked, in this priority order: (1) new binding — a fresh object; (2) explicit binding via call/apply/bind; (3) implicit binding — the object left of the dot; (4) default binding — undefined in strict mode, else the global object. Arrow functions ignore all of these and inherit this lexically from their enclosing scope.

Detailed Answer

RuleHow this is setExample
Defaultundefined (strict) / global (sloppy)fn()
ImplicitThe object before the dotobj.fn()
ExplicitThe first arg to call/apply/bindfn.call(ctx)
newThe newly constructed objectnew Fn()
ArrowLexical — captured from definition() => this

The most common bug is losing implicit binding: passing obj.method as a callback strips the object off the left of the dot, so at call time it invokes as a bare function and this becomes undefined. Arrow functions solve this because they have no this of their own — they close over the surrounding scope's this, which is exactly why they are the default for React class-method handlers and array-callback bodies.

Code Example

const user = {
  name: "Ada",
  greet() { return "Hi " + this.name; },
  greetArrow: () => "Hi " + this.name, // this = enclosing (module) scope
};

user.greet();               // "Hi Ada" — implicit binding
const g = user.greet;
g();                        // "Hi undefined" — lost binding (default)
g.call(user);               // "Hi Ada" — explicit binding

// Arrow captures lexical this — fixes callbacks:
class Timer {
  seconds = 0;
  tick = () => { this.seconds++; }; // arrow keeps `this` = instance
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

Interviewers love "predict the output" chains that alternate methods, detached references, and arrows. Say out loud "this depends on the call site, not the definition site — except arrows." Then apply the priority order. A sharp follow-up: what does bind do if you also call the result with new? The new binding wins over the earlier bind for this, though bound leading arguments are preserved.

Q9. What do call, apply, and bind do, and how do they differ?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

All three set this explicitly. call invokes immediately with arguments listed individually; apply invokes immediately with arguments as an array; bind does not invoke — it returns a new function permanently bound to the given this (and optional preset arguments) for later use.

Detailed Answer

Mnemonic: apply takes an array; call takes a comma-separated list; bind gives you back a function. With modern spread syntax, apply is largely replaced by fn.call(ctx, ...args) or just fn(...args), but it still appears in older code and in interview questions. bind also supports partial application — you can pre-fill leading arguments.

Code Example

function intro(greeting, punct) {
  return greeting + ", " + this.name + punct;
}
const p = { name: "Lin" };

intro.call(p, "Hi", "!");         // "Hi, Lin!"
intro.apply(p, ["Hi", "!"]);      // "Hi, Lin!"  (args as array)
const bound = intro.bind(p, "Hi");// returns fn, not called yet
bound("!");                        // "Hi, Lin!"  (partial application)

// apply's classic use, now obsolete with spread:
Math.max.apply(null, [3, 1, 4]);  // 4
Math.max(...[3, 1, 4]);           // 4  (modern equivalent)

Senior Engineer Perspective

Be ready to hand-implement bind — it is a standard exercise and forces you to combine closures, apply, and the new-vs-bind priority. Also mention that in React with hooks you rarely reach for bind (arrows and useCallback handle context), but you must recognize it in legacy class components where handlers were bound in the constructor to fix this.

SECTION 4 - OBJECTS & PROTOTYPES

Q10. Explain prototypal inheritance and the prototype chain.

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Every object has a hidden link ([[Prototype]], exposed as __proto__) to another object. When you read a property that an object lacks, the engine walks up this chain of prototypes until it finds the property or reaches null. This is how objects share behaviour without copying — and it is what class syntax compiles down to.

Detailed Answer

A constructor function has a .prototype object; instances created with new get their [[Prototype]] pointed at it. Methods defined on the prototype are shared by all instances (one copy in memory) rather than duplicated per object. The lookup chain typically runs instance → Constructor.prototype → Object.prototype → null.

ES6 class is syntactic sugar over exactly this — extends sets up the prototype link, and super delegates up the chain. There is no separate "classical" inheritance under the hood. Writes always happen on the own object (they do not travel up), which is why setting a property shadows rather than mutates the prototype.

Code Example

function Animal(name) { this.name = name; }
Animal.prototype.speak = function () {
  return this.name + " makes a sound";
};

function Dog(name) { Animal.call(this, name); }        // inherit fields
Dog.prototype = Object.create(Animal.prototype);       // inherit methods
Dog.prototype.constructor = Dog;
Dog.prototype.speak = function () { return this.name + " barks"; };

const d = new Dog("Rex");
d.speak();                       // "Rex barks" (own prototype wins)
d.hasOwnProperty("name");        // true — found via Object.prototype

// Equivalent modern syntax:
class Animal2 { constructor(n){ this.name = n; } speak(){ return this.name; } }
class Dog2 extends Animal2 { speak(){ return this.name + " barks"; } }

Senior Engineer Perspective

The differentiator is stating that class is sugar over prototypes, not a different model, and knowing the difference between __proto__ (the instance's link) and .prototype (a property on constructor functions). A common follow-up: why put methods on the prototype instead of inside the constructor? Memory — one shared function versus one per instance. In day-to-day React you rarely author prototype chains, but understanding them explains instanceof, Object.create, and polyfills.

Q11. What does the new operator actually do, step by step?

ROI: ★★★☆☆ Frequency: Medium

Short Answer

new Fn(args) does four things: (1) creates a fresh empty object; (2) links its [[Prototype]] to Fn.prototype; (3) calls Fn with this bound to that new object; (4) returns the new object — unless the constructor explicitly returns its own (non-primitive) object, in which case that is returned instead.

Detailed Answer

Understanding these four steps demystifies constructors, explains why forgetting new leaks properties onto the global object (in sloppy mode) or throws (in strict mode), and lets you hand-write a myNew polyfill — a favourite interview exercise. The subtle step is the return rule: returning a primitive is ignored, but returning an object overrides the freshly created instance.

Code Example

function myNew(Constructor, ...args) {
  const obj = Object.create(Constructor.prototype); // steps 1 + 2
  const result = Constructor.apply(obj, args);      // step 3
  return (result !== null && typeof result === "object")
    ? result                                        // step 4 (explicit object)
    : obj;                                          // step 4 (default)
}

function Point(x, y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
const p = myNew(Point, 1, 2);   // Point { x: 1, y: 2 }

Senior Engineer Perspective

Reciting the four steps in order is the whole game here, plus the return-value edge case. If asked "what happens if you call a constructor without new?", answer: this falls back to default binding, so in strict mode you get a TypeError assigning to undefined, and in sloppy mode you silently pollute the global object — which is why new.target guards exist.

Q12. Shallow copy vs deep copy — and what is structuredClone?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

A shallow copy duplicates the top level but shares nested objects by reference ({...obj}, Object.assign, Array.slice). A deep copy recursively clones every level so nothing is shared. The modern built-in for deep cloning is structuredClone(value) (ES2021, in all evergreen browsers and Node 17+), which replaces the old JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(...)) hack.

Detailed Answer

The JSON round-trip technique is limited: it drops undefined, functions, and symbols, turns Date into a string, and throws on circular references. structuredClone handles Date, Map, Set, typed arrays, ArrayBuffer, and circular references — but it cannot clone functions, DOM nodes, or class instances' prototype chain (you get a plain object) and will throw on those.

In React you rarely need a full deep clone; the idiomatic approach is targeted immutable updates — spread only the levels along the path you are changing, which is cheaper and preserves referential equality for untouched branches (helping memo and re-render bailouts).

Code Example

const state = { user: { name: "A" }, tags: ["x"] };

const shallow = { ...state };
shallow.user.name = "B";
state.user.name;            // "B" — nested object was shared!

const deep = structuredClone(state);
deep.user.name = "C";
state.user.name;            // "B" — fully independent

// React idiom: copy only the path you change
setState(prev => ({
  ...prev,
  user: { ...prev.user, name: "New" }, // new refs only on this path
}));

Senior Engineer Perspective

Interviewers want you to (a) know why {...obj} is not enough for nested data, (b) reach for structuredClone over the JSON hack and name the JSON hack's failure modes, and (c) argue that in React you usually want surgical immutable updates, not blanket deep cloning, because preserving references for unchanged subtrees is what makes memoization work.

Q13. When should you use Map/Set instead of a plain object?

ROI: ★★★☆☆ Frequency: Medium

Short Answer

Use a Map when you need keys of any type (objects, not just strings/symbols), guaranteed insertion order, a clean size property, and frequent additions/removals. Use a Set for a collection of unique values with O(1) membership tests. Reach for a plain object for fixed-shape records and when you need JSON serialization.

Detailed Answer

AspectObjectMap
Key typesstring / symbol onlyany value (incl. objects)
Ordermostly insertion, integer keys sortedstrict insertion order
Sizemanual (Object.keys().length).size
Iterationneeds Object.entries etc.directly iterable
Prototype keysrisk of collision (e.g. "toString")no prototype pollution
JSONnativeneeds conversion

Set gives a concise dedupe ([...new Set(arr)]) and fast lookups compared to Array.includes (O(1) vs O(n)). Note that both use SameValueZero equality, so object keys compare by identity, not by content.

Code Example

// Dedupe an array
const unique = [...new Set([1, 1, 2, 3, 3])]; // [1, 2, 3]

// Map with object keys (impossible with plain objects)
const meta = new Map();
const node = { id: 1 };
meta.set(node, { visited: true });
meta.get(node);           // { visited: true }
meta.size;                // 1

// Fast membership in a React filter
const selected = new Set(selectedIds);
const rows = all.filter(r => selected.has(r.id)); // O(1) per check

Senior Engineer Perspective

The senior nuance is prototype pollution and key flexibility: using a user-supplied string as an object key risks colliding with __proto__ or constructor, whereas a Map is immune. Also mention WeakMap/WeakSet for keying private data off objects without preventing garbage collection — useful for caches keyed by DOM nodes or component instances.

SECTION 5 - ES6+ FEATURES & FUNCTIONAL JS

Q14. How do destructuring, spread, rest, and default parameters work?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

Destructuring unpacks values from arrays/objects into variables. Spread (... in a call or literal) expands an iterable/object into individual elements or properties. Rest (... in a parameter list or destructuring target) collects the remaining items into an array/object. Default parameters supply a fallback when an argument is undefined.

Detailed Answer

The same ... token is spread or rest depending on position: on the right of = or inside a call it spreads; on the left as a target or in a parameter list it collects. Object spread creates a shallow copy and is the workhorse of immutable React updates. Destructuring supports renaming, defaults, and nested patterns, which is why React props are almost always destructured in the function signature.

One gotcha: defaults trigger only for undefined, never for null or other falsy values. So function f(x = 5) uses 5 for f() and f(undefined), but keeps null, 0, and "".

Code Example

// Destructuring with rename + default
const { name, role = "guest" } = user;

// Array destructuring — the useState pattern
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

// Rest collects the remainder
const [first, ...others] = [1, 2, 3];      // others = [2, 3]
function sum(...nums) { return nums.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0); }

// Spread — merge / copy (shallow)
const merged = { ...defaults, ...overrides };
const cloned = [...items];

// Common React prop-forwarding idiom
function Button({ variant, ...rest }) {
  return <button className={variant} {...rest} />;
}

// Default only fires for undefined:
function greet(name = "friend") { return "Hi " + name; }
greet(null);       // "Hi null"  — null is NOT replaced

Senior Engineer Perspective

These appear in nearly every React file, so fluency is assumed, not impressive — the differentiator is knowing the edge cases: spread is shallow, defaults fire only on undefined, and rest must be the last parameter. A frequent follow-up: "How would you clone-and-update a nested object immutably?" — nested spread along the changed path, connecting back to Q12.

Q15. Explain optional chaining and nullish coalescing (ES2020).

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Optional chaining ?. short-circuits and returns undefined instead of throwing when a reference in the chain is null or undefined. Nullish coalescing ?? returns its right side only when the left is null or undefined — unlike ||, it does not treat 0, "", or false as missing.

Detailed Answer

Together they eliminate defensive a && a.b && a.b.c ladders and the || default-value bug. The classic || bug: const page = input.page || 1 wrongly overrides a legitimate 0; ?? 1 keeps 0. Optional chaining also works for method calls (obj.fn?.()) and dynamic keys (obj?.[key]). Note ?. short-circuits the whole rest of the chain the moment it hits nullish.

Code Example

const city = user?.address?.city;      // undefined if any link is nullish
const onClick = props.onClick?.();      // calls only if it exists

// ?? vs || — the key difference:
const count = data.count ?? 10;         // keeps 0
const bad   = data.count || 10;         // 0 becomes 10 (bug!)

// Common in React data fetching:
const items = response?.data?.items ?? [];

Senior Engineer Perspective

The expected insight is why ?? exists when we already had || — specifically the falsy-but-valid values 0, "", and false. Bonus: mention you cannot mix ?? with &&/|| without parentheses (a syntax error by design), and that optional chaining stops evaluating the rest of the chain but does not swallow errors thrown deeper in a called function.

Q16. What are pure functions, immutability, and higher-order functions?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

A pure function returns the same output for the same input and has no side effects. Immutability means never mutating existing data — you produce new values instead. A higher-order function takes a function as an argument and/or returns a function. These three ideas underpin React's rendering model, hooks, and state management.

Detailed Answer

React leans hard on these principles. A component's render should be pure — same props/state produce the same UI, no side effects during render (those belong in useEffect or event handlers). Immutable state updates are mandatory because React detects change by reference identity (Object.is); mutating in place defeats memo, useMemo, and reducer purity. Higher-order functions are everywhere: array methods, custom hooks that wrap other hooks, and the (now less common) higher-order component pattern.

Benefits: pure + immutable code is trivially testable, cacheable/memoizable, time-travel-debuggable (Redux DevTools relies on it), and safe under React's concurrent rendering, which may call render multiple times.

Code Example

// Pure — no external state touched, no mutation
const add = (a, b) => a + b;

// Impure — mutates argument (side effect)
const pushImpure = (arr, x) => { arr.push(x); return arr; };
// Pure alternative — returns new array
const pushPure = (arr, x) => [...arr, x];

// Higher-order function: takes and returns functions
const withLogging = (fn) => (...args) => {
  console.log("calling", fn.name, args);
  return fn(...args);
};
const loggedAdd = withLogging(add);

// Immutable Redux-style reducer
function reducer(state, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case "add": return { ...state, count: state.count + 1 };
    default: return state;
  }
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

Tie it explicitly to React: "components should be pure functions of props and state, and state must be updated immutably so React's reference comparison detects changes." Mention that React 18+ Strict Mode intentionally double-invokes renders and effects in development to surface impurity. That connection — language principle → framework guarantee — is what marks a senior answer rather than a textbook recital.

Q17. Explain map, filter, and reduce — and when is reduce the wrong tool?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

map transforms each element into a new array of the same length; filter keeps elements matching a predicate; reduce folds the array into a single accumulated value. All three are pure (they return new values and do not mutate the source). Reduce is powerful but often abused — if map/filter/some/find express the intent more clearly, prefer them.

Detailed Answer

reduce is the right tool when you are genuinely collapsing a collection into one result — a sum, a lookup object, a group-by, or a min/max. It is the wrong tool when you are really just mapping or filtering, because a reduce that builds an array is harder to read than the equivalent map/filter and typically re-creates or spreads the accumulator each step (a hidden O(n²) if you spread inside it). Always pass an explicit initial value to reduce — omitting it uses the first element as the seed and throws on an empty array.

In React these show up constantly for rendering lists (items.map(...)), filtering data before display, and computing derived totals inside useMemo.

Code Example

const nums = [1, 2, 3, 4];

nums.map(n => n * 2);              // [2, 4, 6, 8]
nums.filter(n => n % 2 === 0);     // [2, 4]
nums.reduce((sum, n) => sum + n, 0); // 10  — always seed the accumulator

// Legit reduce: build a lookup / group-by
const byId = users.reduce((acc, u) => {
  acc[u.id] = u;                    // mutate the accumulator = O(n)
  return acc;
}, {});

// Reduce ABUSE — just a filter+map in disguise:
const bad = nums.reduce((acc, n) => (n > 1 ? [...acc, n * 2] : acc), []);
// Clearer AND faster (no per-step spread):
const good = nums.filter(n => n > 1).map(n => n * 2);

Project Example

Rendering a table: orders.filter(o => o.active).map(o => <Row key={o.id} {...o} />). Computing a cart total with useMemo(() => items.reduce((t, i) => t + i.price * i.qty, 0), [items]). Normalizing an API response into a keyed lookup with reduce so components can index by id in O(1).

Senior Engineer Perspective

The maturity signal is knowing when not to use reduce. Interviewers respect a candidate who says "I could reduce this, but a filter-then-map reads better and avoids spreading the accumulator every iteration." Also mention flatMap, and that all these methods skip holes in sparse arrays. If pushed on performance, note that chaining map().filter() creates intermediate arrays — fine for UI-sized lists, but for very large data a single loop or a transducer/generator may be warranted.

03 - ADVANCED JAVASCRIPT & ASYNCHRONY

Target Audience: Frontend / React Engineer (3–6 Years) Goal: Not just answer questions, but survive follow-up grilling from experienced interviewers.

React is a thin abstraction over JavaScript, and every serious React bug you will ever debug — a stale closure in a useEffect, a race between two fetches, a memory leak from a forgotten listener, a re-render storm from an un-debounced input — is really a JavaScript asynchrony bug wearing a React costume. This chapter is where interviewers separate people who "use hooks" from people who understand what the engine is actually doing underneath them. Expect "what does this log?" puzzles, expect to implement debounce and throttle on a whiteboard, and expect to be asked why your awaits are slow.

TOP HIGHEST-ROI QUESTIONS IN THIS CHAPTER

  1. How does the JavaScript event loop work (call stack, task queue, microtasks)?
  2. Macrotasks vs microtasks — what does this snippet log?
  3. What are the three Promise states and how does chaining work?
  4. Promise.all vs allSettled vs race vs any — when do you use each?
  5. How do you handle errors correctly in promise chains and async/await?
  6. async/await mechanics — what is it really doing under the hood?
  7. Sequential vs parallel awaits — why is my async code slow?
  8. How do you convert a callback-based API into a promise?
  9. Implement debounce from scratch.
  10. Implement throttle from scratch.
  11. Explain currying and partial application.
  12. What are generators and iterators and where are they useful?
  13. Implement a memoize higher-order function.
  14. ES Modules vs CommonJS — differences and why they matter for tree-shaking.
  15. How does garbage collection work and what causes memory leaks?
  16. WeakMap and WeakRef — what problem do they solve?
  17. AbortController — how do you cancel a fetch?
  18. requestAnimationFrame vs setTimeout for animation.

SECTION 1 - THE EVENT LOOP

Q1. How does the JavaScript event loop work? Explain the call stack, task queue, and microtask queue.

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

JavaScript runs on a single thread with one call stack. Synchronous code executes frame by frame on that stack. Asynchronous work (timers, network, DOM events) is handed off to the host (the browser or Node), which pushes a callback into a queue when the work completes. The event loop is the loop that, whenever the call stack is empty, drains all pending microtasks (promise reactions, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver) and then takes exactly one macrotask (a timer callback, an I/O callback, a UI event) before repeating.

Detailed Answer

The crucial mental model is: JavaScript itself has no concept of "later." The language spec only knows how to run a job to completion on the call stack. Everything asynchronous is provided by the host environment — Web APIs in the browser, libuv in Node — which owns the timers, the network stack, and the queues. The event loop is the choreography between the engine and the host.

The pieces

  • Call stack — the LIFO stack of function frames currently executing. Only one thing runs at a time. If a function never returns (an infinite loop), the whole page freezes because the loop can never advance.
  • Macrotask queue (a.k.a. task queue) — callbacks from setTimeout, setInterval, I/O, and UI events. One macrotask is processed per loop iteration.
  • Microtask queue — callbacks from resolved/rejected promises (.then/.catch/.finally), await continuations, queueMicrotask, and MutationObserver. The entire microtask queue is drained after every task and before the next task or a render.

One iteration of the loop

  1. Run the current script / one macrotask to completion (until the stack empties).
  2. Drain all microtasks — including any microtasks those microtasks schedule. This can starve rendering if you keep scheduling microtasks.
  3. The browser may perform layout/paint (roughly aligned to requestAnimationFrame at ~60fps).
  4. Pick the next macrotask and repeat.

The single most important consequence for interviews: a promise callback (microtask) always runs before a setTimeout callback (macrotask) that was scheduled in the same tick, even a setTimeout(fn, 0). Microtasks are the fast lane.

Code Example

console.log("1: sync start");

setTimeout(() => console.log("2: setTimeout (macrotask)"), 0);

Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("3: promise (microtask)"));

queueMicrotask(() => console.log("4: queueMicrotask (microtask)"));

console.log("5: sync end");

// Output:
// 1: sync start
// 5: sync end
// 3: promise (microtask)
// 4: queueMicrotask (microtask)
// 2: setTimeout (macrotask)
//
// All synchronous code runs first (1, 5). The stack empties, so the loop
// drains ALL microtasks (3, 4) before touching the macrotask queue (2).

Project Example

In React this explains why state updates inside an event handler are batched and flushed asynchronously, and why useEffect cleanup + re-run ordering feels the way it does. It also explains a classic bug: doing heavy synchronous work (parsing a large JSON blob, sorting 100k rows) inside a click handler freezes the UI, because that work sits on the single call stack and no paint can happen until it returns. The fix is to yield — chunk the work across macrotasks, move it to a Web Worker, or use startTransition.

Senior Engineer Perspective

The interviewer is checking whether you understand that JS concurrency is cooperative, not preemptive — nothing interrupts a running function. Common traps: (1) claiming setTimeout(fn, 0) runs "immediately" — it runs after the current task and after all microtasks; (2) not knowing that await desugars into a microtask, so code after an await is scheduled like a .then; (3) not realising an infinite chain of microtasks can starve rendering and macrotasks entirely. A senior answer names the host environment as the owner of the queues, not "JavaScript."

Q2. "Trace the output." What does this log, and in what order?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

You must classify every line as synchronous, microtask, or macrotask, and remember that the microtask queue is fully drained between each macrotask. The trick is that async function bodies run synchronously up to the first await, and everything after an await is a microtask.

Detailed Answer

Walk through it deterministically. Never guess — build the queues on paper.

Code Example

console.log("A");

setTimeout(() => console.log("B"), 0);

async function run() {
  console.log("C");            // sync — runs when run() is called
  await null;                  // suspends; rest becomes a microtask
  console.log("D");            // microtask
}

run();

Promise.resolve()
  .then(() => console.log("E"))
  .then(() => console.log("F"));

console.log("G");

// Reasoning:
//   Sync pass:  A, C (inside run before await), G
//   run() hits `await null` -> schedules "D" as a microtask
//   Promise chain schedules "E" as a microtask
//   Microtask drain: D, E ... then .then(F) is queued during E, so F runs next
//   Microtask drain continues: F
//   Macrotask: B
//
// FINAL OUTPUT:
// A
// C
// G
// D
// E
// F
// B

Subtle point on D vs E ordering: both are queued as microtasks, but run() is called before the Promise.resolve().then(...) line executes, so await null's continuation ("D") is enqueued first, then "E". Chained .thens do not all queue at once — the second .then callback is only enqueued once the first resolves, which is why "F" comes after "E" but the whole chain still finishes before the macrotask "B".

Senior Engineer Perspective

These puzzles look like trivia but they test a real skill: reasoning about ordering when you have a race between a promise and a timer, which is exactly what causes flaky tests and "sometimes the spinner flashes" bugs. The two mistakes that sink candidates are (a) forgetting that the code before the first await is synchronous, and (b) assuming a whole .then().then() chain is enqueued in one go. State your rule out loud — "drain all microtasks, then one macrotask" — before you trace.

Q3. requestAnimationFrame vs setTimeout — which should you use for animation and why?

ROI: ★★★☆☆ Frequency: Medium

Short Answer

Use requestAnimationFrame (rAF) for anything visual. The browser calls your rAF callback right before the next repaint, synchronised to the display's refresh rate (~60fps, or 120fps on high-refresh screens) and automatically paused when the tab is hidden. setTimeout is unaware of the paint cycle, drifts, keeps firing in background tabs, and produces janky animation.

Detailed Answer

AspectrequestAnimationFramesetTimeout(fn, 16)
TimingJust before next repaint, refresh-syncedBest-effort after ~16ms, not paint-aligned
Background tabPaused (saves CPU/battery)Keeps firing (throttled to ~1s)
Frame budgetCallback gets a high-res timestampNo timing info
Refresh rateAdapts to 60/120/144 HzFixed guess, drifts over time

Because setTimeout delays are a minimum, not a guarantee, repeated timers accumulate drift and land in the wrong part of the frame, causing tearing and dropped frames. rAF hands control back exactly when the browser is ready to paint.

Code Example

// Smooth scroll-to-top using rAF
function animateTo(target, duration = 300) {
  const start = window.scrollY;
  const startTime = performance.now();

  function frame(now) {
    const t = Math.min(1, (now - startTime) / duration);
    const eased = 1 - Math.pow(1 - t, 3);      // ease-out cubic
    window.scrollTo(0, start + (target - start) * eased);
    if (t < 1) requestAnimationFrame(frame);   // keep going until done
  }
  requestAnimationFrame(frame);
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

The nuance: rAF is for visual updates; for precise timing (audio, game logic) you want a fixed timestep decoupled from rendering. Also note that in React you rarely hand-roll rAF loops — you reach for CSS transitions/transforms (GPU-composited, off the main thread) or a library like Framer Motion. Mention that setTimeout is throttled to ~1s in background tabs — candidates who know this understand why their "keep-alive polling" behaves oddly when the tab is hidden.

SECTION 2 - PROMISES

Q4. What are the three states of a Promise, and how does chaining actually work?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

A promise is a placeholder for a future value in one of three states: pending, fulfilled (resolved with a value), or rejected (with a reason). It's settled once it moves to fulfilled or rejected, and that transition is one-way and permanent. Each .then() returns a new promise, which is why chains work — the return value of one callback becomes the resolution value of the next.

Detailed Answer

The behaviour that trips people up is how .then flattens return values:

  • If a .then callback returns a plain value, the next promise fulfils with that value.
  • If it returns another promise, the chain waits for that promise to settle and adopts its result (this is "thenable assimilation" — no nested Promise<Promise>).
  • If it throws, the next promise rejects with the thrown error, skipping subsequent .then callbacks until a .catch.

.catch(fn) is just sugar for .then(undefined, fn), and .finally(fn) runs regardless of outcome and passes the settlement through untouched (its return value is ignored unless it throws or returns a rejected promise).

Code Example

Promise.resolve(1)
  .then(x => x + 1)                 // returns 2  -> next fulfils with 2
  .then(x => Promise.resolve(x * 10)) // returns a promise -> waits, adopts 20
  .then(x => { throw new Error("boom at " + x); }) // rejects
  .then(x => console.log("skipped", x))            // skipped
  .catch(err => console.log("caught:", err.message)) // caught: boom at 20
  .finally(() => console.log("cleanup runs regardless"));

// Output:
// caught: boom at 20
// cleanup runs regardless

Senior Engineer Perspective

Probes: "What does .then return?" (a new promise — this is the whole basis of chaining). "Can a settled promise change state?" (no, it's immutable once settled). A subtle trap is that .finally does not receive the value and does not alter it — juniors sometimes try to transform data in .finally. Also worth mentioning: an unhandled rejection now surfaces as an unhandledrejection event / process warning, so a chain without a terminal .catch is a real bug, not just style.

Q5. Promise.all vs Promise.allSettled vs Promise.race vs Promise.any — when do you use each?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

All four take an iterable of promises and return one promise, but they differ in when they settle and how they treat failures. Use all for "I need everything and want to fail fast," allSettled for "run everything and tell me each outcome," race for "first to settle wins (success or failure)," and any for "first success wins, ignore failures until all fail."

Detailed Answer

MethodFulfils whenRejects whenResult shape
Promise.allALL fulfilANY rejects (fails fast)Array of values
Promise.allSettledALL settleNever rejectsArray of {status, value|reason}
Promise.raceFirst settles (fulfilled)First settles (rejected)Single value/reason
Promise.anyFirst fulfilsALL reject (AggregateError)Single value

Promise.all rejects the instant one input rejects — but note the other promises keep running; they aren't cancelled, you just stop waiting for them. That's why for a "load everything, show partial results" dashboard you want allSettled, which never rejects and gives you a per-item verdict.

race settles on the first to finish regardless of outcome, which makes it ideal for timeouts. any is its optimistic cousin — it resolves on the first success and only rejects (with an AggregateError containing all reasons) if every input fails, perfect for "hit whichever mirror responds first."

Code Example

// Fail-fast fan-out
const [user, orders] = await Promise.all([
  fetchUser(id),
  fetchOrders(id),
]); // rejects if EITHER fails

// Resilient dashboard: never throws, inspect each result
const results = await Promise.allSettled([fetchA(), fetchB(), fetchC()]);
const ok = results.filter(r => r.status === "fulfilled").map(r => r.value);
const failed = results.filter(r => r.status === "rejected");

// Timeout pattern with race
function withTimeout(promise, ms) {
  const timeout = new Promise((_, reject) =>
    setTimeout(() => reject(new Error("timeout")), ms)
  );
  return Promise.race([promise, timeout]);
}

// Fastest successful mirror wins
const fastest = await Promise.any([
  fetch("https://mirror1/data"),
  fetch("https://mirror2/data"),
]);

Senior Engineer Perspective

Follow-ups: "With Promise.all, if one rejects, do the others stop?" (No — promises can't be cancelled from the outside; use AbortController for real cancellation.) "Difference between race and any?" (race settles on first settle including rejection; any settles on first fulfilment.) A senior nuance: Promise.all preserves input order in the result array even though the promises finish in arbitrary order — the array index maps to the input index, not completion order.

Q6. How do you correctly handle errors in promise chains and async/await?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

In promise chains, attach a terminal .catch — a rejection propagates down the chain until something catches it. In async/await, wrap awaited calls in try/catch. The most common bug is a floating promise with no error handler, producing an unhandled rejection; the second most common is swallowing errors by catching too broadly and doing nothing.

Detailed Answer

Rejections behave like exceptions travelling down the chain. A single .catch at the end handles a rejection from any earlier step. But there are traps:

  • Errors inside a .then callback after the .catch aren't caught by that catch — position matters.
  • Not returning the inner promise inside a callback breaks the chain, so its rejection escapes handling ("fire and forget" inside a chain).
  • A try/catch around an async call without await catches nothing — the function returns a pending promise before it can reject.

Code Example

// BUG: try/catch without await catches nothing
async function bad() {
  try {
    fetchData();          // missing await -> rejection escapes this try
  } catch (e) {
    console.log("never reached", e);
  }
}

// CORRECT
async function good() {
  try {
    const data = await fetchData();
    return process(data);
  } catch (e) {
    logger.error("fetchData failed", e);
    throw new AppError("Could not load data", { cause: e }); // rethrow with context
  } finally {
    hideSpinner();
  }
}

// Chain equivalent
fetchData()
  .then(process)
  .catch(e => { logger.error(e); throw e; }); // catch, log, rethrow to caller

Senior Engineer Perspective

Interviewers love the "try/catch without await" trap because it exposes whether you understand that an async function's rejection only materialises at the await point. Strong candidates also mention the { cause } option on Error for preserving the original error, and the difference between recoverable errors (catch, show a toast, retry) and programmer errors (let them bubble to an error boundary / crash reporter). Blanket catch blocks that silently swallow are worse than no catch at all.

Q7. How do you convert a callback-based API into a promise?

ROI: ★★★☆☆ Frequency: Medium

Short Answer

Wrap the call in new Promise((resolve, reject) => ...) and call resolve/reject from inside the callback. For Node-style (err, result) callbacks, use util.promisify; for custom shapes, write the wrapper by hand. Crucially, call the executor exactly once and never mix a callback and a promise for the same operation.

Code Example

// Promisify a Node-style callback: fn(...args, (err, result) => ...)
function promisify(fn) {
  return (...args) =>
    new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
      fn(...args, (err, result) => {
        if (err) reject(err);
        else resolve(result);
      });
    });
}

const readFileAsync = promisify(fs.readFile);
const text = await readFileAsync("./config.json", "utf8");

// Wrap an event-based API (e.g. an image load)
function loadImage(src) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const img = new Image();
    img.onload = () => resolve(img);
    img.onerror = () => reject(new Error("Failed to load " + src));
    img.src = src;
  });
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

Gotchas the interviewer listens for: the Promise executor runs synchronously; resolve/reject after the first call are no-ops (the promise is already settled), so double-settling is a silent bug, not an error. Also, throwing synchronously inside the executor automatically rejects the promise. Bonus points for mentioning that this pattern is a "boundary adapter" — you promisify once at the edge and keep the rest of the codebase promise-native.

SECTION 3 - ASYNC / AWAIT

Q8. What is async/await really doing under the hood?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

async/await is syntactic sugar over promises and (conceptually) generators. An async function always returns a promise. await pauses the function, yielding control back to the event loop, and schedules the code after it as a microtask that resumes when the awaited value settles. It does not block the thread — it suspends just that one function.

Detailed Answer

When you call an async function, it runs synchronously until the first await. At that point it returns a pending promise to the caller and "parks" its remaining body. When the awaited promise settles, the continuation is queued as a microtask, the function resumes with the resolved value (or throws the rejection reason at the await expression, which is why try/catch works), and eventually the returned promise settles.

Two facts flow from this: (1) an async function that returns a value x actually resolves with Promise.resolve(x), so returning a promise doesn't double-wrap; (2) await on a non-promise value still defers to a microtask (await 5 is not free — the rest of the function runs later).

Code Example

async function demo() {
  console.log("1"); // sync
  const v = await Promise.resolve("resolved");
  console.log("2", v); // microtask continuation
  return "done";       // resolves the returned promise with "done"
}

console.log("start");
demo().then(r => console.log("3", r));
console.log("end");

// Output:
// start
// 1
// end
// 2 resolved
// 3 done

Senior Engineer Perspective

Say clearly: "await does not block the thread, it suspends the function and lets the event loop keep running." Juniors describe it as "waiting/blocking," which betrays a wrong model — if it truly blocked, the UI would freeze. Follow-up: "Is return await x different from return x?" Functionally usually identical, but return await keeps the frame on the stack one extra microtask (relevant for stack traces and for try/finally — inside a try, return await ensures rejections are caught locally).

Q9. Sequential vs parallel awaits — why is my async code slow, and how do I fix it?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Because await pauses the function, writing awaits back-to-back runs the operations sequentially — each waits for the previous to finish even when they're independent. If the tasks don't depend on each other, start them all first (or pass them to Promise.all) so they run in parallel, then await the combined result.

Detailed Answer

This is one of the most impactful real-world performance bugs. Three independent 300ms requests awaited in sequence take 900ms; in parallel they take ~300ms. The fix is to kick off the promises (which begins their work immediately) before awaiting. Only serialise when there's a genuine data dependency — e.g. the second call needs the first call's result.

Code Example

// SLOW — sequential: ~900ms total
async function slow(id) {
  const user = await fetchUser(id);       // 300ms
  const posts = await fetchPosts(id);     // waits, then 300ms
  const stats = await fetchStats(id);     // waits, then 300ms
  return { user, posts, stats };
}

// FAST — parallel: ~300ms total (independent calls)
async function fast(id) {
  const [user, posts, stats] = await Promise.all([
    fetchUser(id),
    fetchPosts(id),
    fetchStats(id),
  ]);
  return { user, posts, stats };
}

// Genuine dependency -> sequential is CORRECT
async function dependent(id) {
  const user = await fetchUser(id);
  const org  = await fetchOrg(user.orgId); // needs user.orgId
  return org;
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

A subtle intermediate form worth knowing: you can start the promises without await, do other work, then await them later — const p1 = fetchUser(id); const p2 = fetchPosts(id); const user = await p1; const posts = await p2; — this is also parallel because the requests fire on the assignment lines, not the await lines. The interviewer may push on error handling: with Promise.all a single failure rejects the whole thing; if you want partial success switch to allSettled. This is exactly the trade-off from Q5, applied.

Q10. How do you loop over async work — and what's the trap with forEach?

ROI: ★★★☆☆ Frequency: Medium

Short Answer

Array.prototype.forEach ignores the promise your async callback returns, so it does not wait — your surrounding code runs before the iterations finish. Use a for...of loop with await for sequential processing, or map + Promise.all for parallel processing.

Code Example

// BUG: forEach does not await -> "done" logs before any item finishes
async function broken(items) {
  items.forEach(async (item) => {
    await save(item);
  });
  console.log("done"); // runs immediately, saves still pending
}

// Sequential (one at a time, ordered) — for rate limits or ordering
async function sequential(items) {
  for (const item of items) {
    await save(item);
  }
  console.log("done"); // truly after all saves
}

// Parallel (all at once) — fastest for independent items
async function parallel(items) {
  await Promise.all(items.map(item => save(item)));
  console.log("done");
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

Beyond the forEach trap, seniors talk about concurrency control: firing 10,000 requests in parallel with Promise.all will hammer the server and blow rate limits. The mature answer is a bounded pool (e.g. process N at a time with something like p-limit, or chunk the array). Mention that for streaming/backpressure scenarios, for await...of over an async iterable is the idiomatic tool.

SECTION 4 - ADVANCED PATTERNS

Q11. Implement debounce from scratch. When do you use it?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

Debounce delays invoking a function until it has stopped being called for a given wait period — it "collapses" a burst of calls into one, executed after the burst ends. It's the go-to for search-as-you-type, autosave, and resize handlers, where you only care about the final state after activity settles.

Detailed Answer

The mechanism: every call clears the previous pending timer and sets a new one. Only when wait ms pass with no new calls does the timer fire. So typing "react" fires once, wait ms after the last keystroke, not five times.

Code Example

function debounce(fn, wait) {
  let timer = null;
  function debounced(...args) {
    clearTimeout(timer);              // cancel the pending call
    timer = setTimeout(() => {
      timer = null;
      fn.apply(this, args);           // preserve `this` and latest args
    }, wait);
  }
  debounced.cancel = () => { clearTimeout(timer); timer = null; };
  return debounced;
}

// Usage: only search after the user pauses typing for 300ms
const search = debounce((q) => api.search(q), 300);
input.addEventListener("input", (e) => search(e.target.value));

Senior Engineer Perspective

Interviewers push on: preserving this and arguments (use a regular function + fn.apply, not an arrow that loses this); a cancel method (needed for React cleanup); and a leading/immediate option to fire on the first call instead of the last. In React, a common bug is creating a new debounced function on every render — you must wrap it in useMemo/useRef (or use useDebouncedCallback) or the timer resets each render and never fires.

Q12. Implement throttle. How is it different from debounce?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

Throttle guarantees a function runs at most once per interval no matter how often it's called — it enforces a steady maximum rate. Debounce waits for silence before firing once; throttle fires regularly during activity. Use throttle for scroll position, mousemove, drag, and analytics pings; use debounce for "act after the user stops."

Detailed Answer

DebounceThrottle
FiresOnce, after calls stopAt most once per interval, during calls
Rapid burst of 100 calls / 1s (wait 200ms)1 call total~5 calls, evenly spaced
Best forSearch box, autosave, resize-endScroll, mousemove, drag, rate-limited pings

Code Example

function throttle(fn, interval) {
  let last = 0;
  let timer = null;
  return function (...args) {
    const now = Date.now();
    const remaining = interval - (now - last);
    if (remaining <= 0) {
      // enough time has passed -> run immediately (leading edge)
      last = now;
      fn.apply(this, args);
    } else if (!timer) {
      // schedule a trailing call so the final event isn't dropped
      timer = setTimeout(() => {
        last = Date.now();
        timer = null;
        fn.apply(this, args);
      }, remaining);
    }
  };
}

const onScroll = throttle(() => updateScrollProgress(), 100);
window.addEventListener("scroll", onScroll);

Senior Engineer Perspective

The distinguishing follow-up is the trailing call: a naive throttle that only fires on the leading edge can drop the final event, so the UI ends up one frame stale (e.g. scroll progress that never reaches 100%). The implementation above handles both edges. Also expect: "How would you throttle with rAF instead of a timer?" — for pure visual updates, gating on requestAnimationFrame naturally caps you at the refresh rate and avoids doing work between paints.

Q13. Explain currying and partial application. Implement a curry helper.

ROI: ★★★☆☆ Frequency: Medium

Short Answer

Currying transforms a function of N arguments into N nested unary functions: f(a, b, c) becomes f(a)(b)(c). Partial application is fixing some arguments now and getting a function that takes the rest later. Both are ways to build specialised functions from general ones and to make functions more composable.

Detailed Answer

Partial application (often via Function.prototype.bind or a closure) pre-fills arguments; currying is the stricter form that hands arguments one at a time. They matter in functional pipelines and in React for creating reusable handler factories.

Code Example

// Partial application
const multiply = (a, b) => a * b;
const double = multiply.bind(null, 2); // fix a = 2
double(5); // 10

// A flexible curry that accepts args in groups
function curry(fn) {
  return function curried(...args) {
    if (args.length >= fn.length) return fn.apply(this, args);
    return (...next) => curried.apply(this, args.concat(next));
  };
}

const add = curry((a, b, c) => a + b + c);
add(1)(2)(3);   // 6
add(1, 2)(3);   // 6
add(1)(2, 3);   // 6

// Practical: a handler factory in React
const onFieldChange = (field) => (e) =>
  setForm((f) => ({ ...f, [field]: e.target.value }));
<input onChange={onFieldChange("email")} />

Senior Engineer Perspective

The interviewer wants you to distinguish the two terms crisply (many candidates conflate them) and to relate fn.length (arity) to how the curry helper knows when it has enough arguments. A senior note: over-currying hurts readability and, in React, factory functions like onFieldChange("email") create a new function each render — usually fine, but worth knowing when you're chasing referential-equality re-renders with React.memo.

Q14. What are generators and iterators, and where are they actually useful?

ROI: ★★★☆☆ Frequency: Medium

Short Answer

An iterator is any object with a next() method returning { value, done }; the iterable protocol (a Symbol.iterator method) is what lets for...of and spread work. A generator (function*) is a factory for iterators — yield pauses the function and hands a value out, resuming where it left off on the next next() call. They shine for lazy sequences, custom iteration, and modelling async flows.

Detailed Answer

Generators give you pausable functions with preserved local state — which is precisely the machinery async/await is built on (an async function is essentially a generator that yields promises and is auto-driven). Practically, they're great for infinite/lazy sequences (you compute values on demand, not all upfront), for making your own objects iterable, and they power libraries like Redux-Saga where yielded "effects" describe side effects declaratively.

Code Example

// Lazy infinite sequence — nothing is computed until you pull
function* idGenerator() {
  let id = 1;
  while (true) yield id++;
}
const ids = idGenerator();
ids.next().value; // 1
ids.next().value; // 2

// Make a custom object iterable
const range = {
  from: 1, to: 3,
  *[Symbol.iterator]() {
    for (let i = this.from; i <= this.to; i++) yield i;
  },
};
[...range];            // [1, 2, 3]
for (const n of range) console.log(n); // 1, 2, 3

// Two-way communication: next() can send a value back into the generator
function* chat() {
  const name = yield "What's your name?";
  yield `Hello, ${name}!`;
}
const c = chat();
c.next().value;        // "What's your name?"
c.next("Ada").value;   // "Hello, Ada!"

Senior Engineer Perspective

The connection interviewers fish for: "How does await relate to generators?" — async/await is generators + a promise-driving runtime. Bonus: async function* creates async generators consumed with for await...of, the clean way to model streaming/paginated APIs with backpressure. Be honest that in day-to-day React app code you rarely hand-write generators — but understanding them demystifies async/await and iteration protocols.

Q15. Implement a memoize higher-order function. What are the caveats?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Memoization caches a function's results keyed by its arguments so repeated calls with the same inputs return instantly. It's a classic space-for-time trade-off, valid only for pure functions (same input → same output, no side effects). The hard parts are key generation, cache invalidation, and unbounded memory growth.

Code Example

function memoize(fn, keyFn = (...a) => JSON.stringify(a)) {
  const cache = new Map();
  return function (...args) {
    const key = keyFn(...args);
    if (cache.has(key)) return cache.get(key);
    const result = fn.apply(this, args);
    cache.set(key, result);
    return result;
  };
}

const slowFib = (n) => (n < 2 ? n : slowFibM(n - 1) + slowFibM(n - 2));
const slowFibM = memoize(slowFib); // turns O(2^n) into O(n)
slowFibM(40); // fast

Senior Engineer Perspective

Caveats to raise proactively: (1) JSON.stringify keys fail for functions, undefined, circular refs, and are order-sensitive for object args; (2) an unbounded Map is a memory leak — real caches need an LRU bound or a TTL; (3) memoizing across object identity for single-arg functions is better done with a WeakMap so entries are GC'd when the key object dies. Tie it to React: useMemo, useCallback, and React.memo are memoization, and the same "is this actually pure / do the deps really change?" reasoning applies.

Q16. AbortController — how do you cancel a fetch or any async operation?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

AbortController exposes a signal you pass to fetch (and many other APIs). Calling controller.abort() triggers the signal, causing the fetch to reject with an AbortError. It's the standard way to cancel in-flight requests — essential for cancelling stale requests when a component unmounts or a search term changes.

Detailed Answer

Promises themselves can't be cancelled, so the platform added AbortSignal as an out-of-band cancellation channel. Beyond fetch, you can listen to signal.addEventListener("abort", ...) to make your own async work abortable, and you can pass the same signal to addEventListener to auto-remove listeners on abort. In React 18, the classic use is aborting a fetch in a useEffect cleanup to avoid setting state on an unmounted component and to prevent race conditions between fast-changing requests.

Code Example

useEffect(() => {
  const controller = new AbortController();

  fetch(`/api/search?q=${query}`, { signal: controller.signal })
    .then(res => res.json())
    .then(setResults)
    .catch(err => {
      if (err.name === "AbortError") return; // expected on cancel — ignore
      setError(err);
    });

  // Cleanup: abort the previous request when query changes / unmount
  return () => controller.abort();
}, [query]);

// Abort on a timeout with the built-in helper
const res = await fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000) });

Senior Engineer Perspective

Key points that mark seniority: an aborted fetch rejects with an AbortError you must deliberately swallow, not treat as a failure; aborting stops you waiting and lets the browser cancel the request, but doesn't guarantee the server didn't process it (so it's not a substitute for idempotency); and the real reason to abort in React is the race condition — without it, a slow earlier request can resolve after a faster later one and overwrite fresh results with stale data. Note that AbortSignal.timeout() and AbortSignal.any() are the modern conveniences.

SECTION 5 - MODULES & MEMORY

Q17. ES Modules vs CommonJS — what are the differences and why do they matter for tree-shaking?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

CommonJS (require/module.exports) is synchronous, dynamic, and resolved at runtime — Node's original module system. ES Modules (import/export) are the standard, statically analysable, asynchronously loaded, and support live bindings. Because ESM imports are static, bundlers can determine exactly which exports are used and drop the rest — that's tree-shaking, which CommonJS largely defeats.

Detailed Answer

AspectCommonJSES Modules
Syntaxrequire / module.exportsimport / export
LoadingSynchronous, runtimeAsync, parsed statically
BindingsCopy of value at require timeLive, read-only bindings
Tree-shakeableNo (dynamic)Yes (static analysis)
Top-level awaitNoYes
this at top levelmodule.exportsundefined

Tree-shaking is dead-code elimination based on static import/export analysis. Because ESM tells the bundler at parse time exactly what each module exports and imports, a bundler like Vite/Rollup/webpack can keep only the reachable exports. This is why importing import { debounce } from "lodash-es" can ship just that function, while const _ = require("lodash") tends to pull the whole library. It relies on modules being side-effect-free — hence the "sideEffects": false field in package.json.

Code Example

// CommonJS — dynamic, evaluated at runtime, hard to tree-shake
const { debounce } = require("lodash");
module.exports = { helper };

// ESM — static, live bindings, tree-shakeable
import { debounce } from "lodash-es";
export function helper() { /* ... */ }

// Live binding demo (ESM): importers see updates to the exported variable
// counter.js
export let count = 0;
export const inc = () => count++;
// main.js
import { count, inc } from "./counter.js";
inc();
console.log(count); // 1  — a live view, NOT a stale copy

Senior Engineer Perspective

Deep follow-ups: "Why can't CommonJS be tree-shaken?" (imports are dynamic expressions resolvable only at runtime, so the bundler can't prove an export is unused). "What breaks tree-shaking in ESM?" (side effects at module top level, re-export barrels, and "sideEffects" not set correctly). Also mention live bindings — the fact that ESM imports are live read-only views, not value copies, is a favourite distinguishing question, and it's why you can't reassign an import.

Q18. How does garbage collection work, and what causes memory leaks in a JS/React app?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

JS engines use a mark-and-sweep collector: starting from roots (global object, current call stack), they mark everything reachable and sweep away the rest. You never free() manually. A "leak" is therefore always the same thing — an object stays reachable when you no longer need it. The four classic culprits are lingering timers/listeners, closures capturing large state, detached DOM nodes, and ever-growing caches/global collections.

Detailed Answer

Reachability is the whole model: as long as any chain of references from a root reaches an object, it can't be collected. Leaks happen when you accidentally keep such a chain alive.

  • Forgotten event listeners / subscriptions: addEventListener, WebSocket handlers, store subscriptions, and setInterval that are never removed keep their callbacks — and everything the callbacks close over — alive. In React, always clean these up in the useEffect return function.
  • Closures capturing large data: a long-lived callback that closes over a big array pins that array in memory even if you only needed one field.
  • Detached DOM nodes: you remove a node from the document but a JS variable (or a listener) still references it — the node and its subtree can't be freed.
  • Unbounded caches / module-level Maps: a global Map you keep set-ting into but never evict grows forever.

Code Example

// LEAK: interval + listener never cleaned up; closure keeps `data` alive
function LeakyComponent({ data }) {
  useEffect(() => {
    const id = setInterval(() => process(data), 1000);
    window.addEventListener("resize", onResize);
    // no cleanup -> interval + listener survive unmount
  }, []);
}

// FIXED: cleanup on unmount frees everything
function CleanComponent({ data }) {
  useEffect(() => {
    const id = setInterval(() => process(data), 1000);
    window.addEventListener("resize", onResize);
    return () => {
      clearInterval(id);
      window.removeEventListener("resize", onResize);
    };
  }, [data]);
}

Project Example

A dashboard that mounts/unmounts many chart widgets is the classic offender: each widget subscribes to a resize observer and a data store. If a widget forgets to unsubscribe on unmount, navigating around the app slowly climbs in the DevTools Memory profiler and the app gets sluggish over a long session.
