You catch it by taking heap snapshots before/after repeated mount-unmount cycles and looking for a growing count of "detached" nodes or retained component instances.

Senior Engineer Perspective

Say "reachability" and "mark-and-sweep" explicitly — that's the vocabulary. Then demonstrate the debugging workflow: Chrome DevTools → Memory → heap snapshots and the "detached DOM tree" view, or the Performance/Memory timeline showing a sawtooth that never returns to baseline. The senior insight is that in React nearly every leak traces back to a missing useEffect cleanup or a stale closure — knowing the framework-level fix is what they want, not just the CS-101 definition.

Q19. What are WeakMap, WeakSet, and WeakRef, and what problem do they solve?

ROI: ★★★☆☆ Frequency: Medium

Short Answer

WeakMap/WeakSet hold weak references to their keys/values: if the only thing referencing an object is the WeakMap, that object can still be garbage-collected, and its entry disappears automatically. This makes them the leak-proof choice for associating metadata with objects you don't own the lifecycle of. WeakRef is a lower-level, explicit weak reference to a single object.

Detailed Answer

A normal Map keeps its keys reachable forever, so caching against DOM nodes or component instances in a plain Map leaks. A WeakMap's keys are held weakly, so when the DOM node is removed and nothing else references it, both the node and its WeakMap entry are collected. Constraints: keys must be objects (not primitives), and WeakMaps are not iterable and have no size — precisely because their contents can vanish at any time, so exposing enumeration would be non-deterministic.

WeakRef (and its companion FinalizationRegistry) let you hold an object without preventing its collection; you call ref.deref() to get the object or undefined if it's gone. It's a sharp tool for advanced caches — the spec explicitly warns against relying on GC timing.

Code Example

// Associate private metadata with objects — auto-cleaned when the key dies
const metadata = new WeakMap();

function tag(node, info) {
  metadata.set(node, info); // node held weakly
}
// When `node` is removed from the DOM and dereferenced elsewhere,
// the WeakMap entry is GC'd automatically — no manual cleanup, no leak.

// WeakRef: cache without pinning the object in memory
const cache = new WeakRef(expensiveObject);
const obj = cache.deref(); // the object, or undefined if collected

Senior Engineer Perspective

The contrast question is "why not just use a Map?" — answer: a Map's strong keys prevent GC and leak. The follow-up trap is "iterate a WeakMap" — you can't, and explaining why (non-deterministic contents) shows real understanding. On WeakRef, a senior signals caution: it's rarely needed, GC timing is unspecified so you must not build correctness on it, and reaching for it usually means an ordinary bounded/LRU cache would be simpler and more predictable.

04 - TYPESCRIPT FOR REACT

Target Audience: Frontend / React Engineer (3–6 Years) Goal: Not just answer questions, but survive follow-up grilling from experienced interviewers.

TOP HIGHEST-ROI QUESTIONS IN THIS CHAPTER

  1. interface vs type — when to use which?
  2. Union vs intersection types
  3. unknown vs any vs never
  4. Type narrowing and user-defined type guards
  5. Discriminated unions, literal types and as const
  6. Typing component props and children (ReactNode)
  7. Typing hooks: useState, useRef, useReducer
  8. Typing event handlers (React.ChangeEvent and friends)
  9. Typing custom hooks (tuple returns, const assertions)
  10. Typing React Context correctly
  11. Generics — what problem do they actually solve?
  12. Utility types: Partial, Pick, Omit, Record, Required, Readonly
  13. keyof, mapped types and conditional types
  14. Generic (reusable) components
  15. Typing forwardRef components
  16. Typing a fetch / API layer safely
  17. Declaration files, strict mode and tsconfig essentials
  18. Common TypeScript + React mistakes

SECTION 1 - TS CORE

Q1. What is the difference between interface and type? When do you use each?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

Both describe the shape of a value and are largely interchangeable for objects. interface is open — it supports declaration merging and reads naturally for object/class contracts. type is a general alias — it can name unions, intersections, tuples, primitives and mapped/conditional types, which interfaces cannot. A common team rule: use interface for public object shapes and component props, use type for everything else (unions, function types, utility compositions).

Detailed Answer

What only type can do

A type alias can name any type expression, not just object shapes: unions, tuples, primitives, template literals, and the output of conditional/mapped types. Interfaces are restricted to object and function shapes.

What only interface can do

Interfaces support declaration merging: declaring the same interface name twice merges the members. This is how you augment third-party or global types (e.g. extending Window). Type aliases throw a duplicate-identifier error instead.

Extension

Both compose. Interfaces use extends; types use & (intersection). Interface extends gives slightly better error messages and is cached by the compiler, so for large hot object shapes it can be marginally faster to type-check.

Capabilityinterfacetype
Object / function shapesYesYes
Union / tuple / primitive aliasNoYes
Declaration mergingYesNo
Extend / composeextends&
Mapped / conditional typesNoYes

Code Example

// type can express things interface cannot
type ID = string | number;                 // union
type Point = [number, number];             // tuple
type Handler = (e: MouseEvent) => void;    // function alias

// interface for object/prop shapes + extension
interface ButtonProps {
  label: string;
  onClick: () => void;
}
interface IconButtonProps extends ButtonProps {
  icon: string;
}

// declaration merging — impossible with `type`
interface Window {
  __APP_VERSION__: string;
}
window.__APP_VERSION__ = "1.4.0";

Project Example

In a real app I define component props with interface because IDEs surface them well and other engineers can augment them, but I reach for type when modelling an API response that is a discriminated union (type Result = Success | Failure) or when composing utility types (type FormValues = Partial<User>). Consistency matters more than the choice — pick a convention and lint it.

Senior Engineer Perspective

The interviewer wants to hear that you know the real functional differences (declaration merging, union aliasing) rather than the myth that "interfaces are for objects and types are for primitives" as if it were a hard rule. A classic trap: "Can an interface represent a union?" — no, and if you claim yes you're sunk. Another: performance — extending interfaces is generally faster for the checker than deep intersection chains, which matters in very large codebases but is irrelevant in small ones. Say that nuance out loud.

Q2. Explain union and intersection types. How do they behave differently?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

A union (A | B) means the value is one of the types — you can only access members common to all members until you narrow. An intersection (A & B) means the value satisfies all types at once — it has the combined members. Unions are "either/or"; intersections are "both/and".

Detailed Answer

The counterintuitive part is what happens to object types. With a union of objects, TypeScript only lets you access properties that exist on every branch (the intersection of properties), because it cannot know which branch you hold. To use branch-specific members you must narrow first (see type guards). With an intersection of objects you get the union of properties, since the value must satisfy both shapes simultaneously.

Intersecting incompatible primitives produces never (nothing can be both string and number), which is a subtle source of bugs when composing generics.

Code Example

type A = { id: number; a: string };
type B = { id: number; b: string };

type U = A | B;   // either A or B
type I = A & B;   // both A and B

function useUnion(x: U) {
  x.id;   // OK — common to both
  // x.a; // Error — might be B, which has no `a`
}

function useIntersection(x: I) {
  x.id; x.a; x.b;  // all available
}

// Intersecting incompatible primitives -> never
type Impossible = string & number;  // never

Senior Engineer Perspective

Interviewers probe the object-property surprise because juniors expect a union to expose all properties. The senior insight: a union widens the set of possible values but narrows the guaranteed API, while an intersection does the reverse. This is exactly why props modelled as unions force you to narrow before use — a good feature, not a limitation.

Q3. What is the difference between unknown, any, and never?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

any disables type checking entirely — anything is assignable to it and from it, so it silently spreads and defeats the purpose of TS. unknown is the type-safe counterpart: any value is assignable to it, but you cannot use it until you narrow. never is the empty type — a value that can never occur (a function that always throws, or an exhausted union branch).

Detailed Answer

TypeAssign anything TO it?Use it without narrowing?Meaning
anyYesYes (unsafe)Opt out of checking
unknownYesNo — must narrowSafe top type
neverNo (nothing fits)N/AEmpty / impossible

Rule of thumb: prefer unknown at the boundaries of your program (JSON parsing, third-party callbacks, catch clauses in useUnknownInCatchVariables mode) and narrow inward. Use never to enforce exhaustive handling of unions — assign to a never variable in the default case so adding a new union member becomes a compile error.

Code Example

// unknown forces a check before use
function parse(json: string): unknown {
  return JSON.parse(json);
}
const data = parse("{}");
// data.id;                    // Error
if (typeof data === "object" && data !== null && "id" in data) {
  // now narrowed
}

// never for exhaustiveness
type Shape = { kind: "circle"; r: number } | { kind: "square"; s: number };
function area(shape: Shape): number {
  switch (shape.kind) {
    case "circle": return Math.PI * shape.r ** 2;
    case "square": return shape.s ** 2;
    default: {
      const _exhaustive: never = shape; // errors if a new kind is added
      return _exhaustive;
    }
  }
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

Saying "I use unknown instead of any at trust boundaries and lint any to a warning" instantly signals seniority. The never-in-default exhaustiveness trick is a favourite follow-up because it demonstrates you use the type system to catch future bugs, not just current ones. Watch the trap: in TS 4.4+, catch (e) gives unknown, not any — many candidates still write e.message and get burned.

Q4. What is type narrowing and how do you write a user-defined type guard?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Narrowing is TypeScript refining a broad type to a more specific one within a code branch, using control-flow analysis. Built-in narrowing comes from typeof, instanceof, in, equality checks and truthiness. When those aren't enough you write a type guard: a function whose return type is a type predicate arg is Type.

Detailed Answer

Inside a guarded branch, TypeScript treats the variable as the narrowed type, so branch-specific members become accessible. A user-defined guard returns a boolean but its return annotation is a predicate, which teaches the compiler what a true result implies. This is the safe way to validate unknown data from the network. There is also asserts arg is Type for assertion functions that throw instead of returning a boolean.

Code Example

interface Cat { meow: () => void }
interface Dog { bark: () => void }

// user-defined type guard: return type is a predicate
function isCat(pet: Cat | Dog): pet is Cat {
  return "meow" in pet;
}

function speak(pet: Cat | Dog) {
  if (isCat(pet)) {
    pet.meow();   // narrowed to Cat
  } else {
    pet.bark();   // narrowed to Dog
  }
}

// assertion function variant
function assertString(v: unknown): asserts v is string {
  if (typeof v !== "string") throw new Error("not a string");
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

The danger with hand-written guards is that they are unchecked — the compiler trusts your predicate. If isCat returns true for a dog, TS will happily let you call .meow() and it crashes at runtime. That is why seniors validate with a schema library (Zod, Valibot) that generates both the runtime check and the inferred type from a single source, eliminating drift between the guard and the actual type.

Q5. What is a discriminated union and why is it so useful in React?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

A discriminated (tagged) union is a union of object types that all share a common literal-typed field — the "discriminant". Checking that field narrows the whole object automatically. It's the idiomatic way to model mutually exclusive states like loading | success | error so that impossible combinations are unrepresentable.

Detailed Answer

The magic is the shared literal key. When you switch on it, TypeScript narrows to exactly the matching member, exposing only its valid fields. This kills the classic React bug of having isLoading, data and error as independent booleans/values where nothing stops isLoading === true alongside a populated error. With a discriminated union, data simply doesn't exist on the loading branch, so you cannot read it by mistake.

Code Example

type FetchState<T> =
  | { status: "idle" }
  | { status: "loading" }
  | { status: "success"; data: T }
  | { status: "error"; message: string };

function UserView({ state }: { state: FetchState<User> }) {
  switch (state.status) {
    case "idle":
    case "loading":
      return <Spinner />;
    case "success":
      return <Profile user={state.data} />; // data only exists here
    case "error":
      return <Error text={state.message} />;
  }
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

The senior framing is "make illegal states unrepresentable". Interviewers love asking you to critique a component that juggles three separate flags — the strong answer is to collapse them into one discriminated union. Combine it with the never exhaustiveness check from Q3 and you get a component that fails to compile when a new state is added but not handled. Note the discriminant must be a literal type, not string, for narrowing to work — a common mistake.

Q6. What do as const and literal types do, and when do you need them?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: Medium

Short Answer

A literal type is a single exact value used as a type, e.g. "admin" or 200. By default TypeScript widens literals (const x = "admin" stays "admin", but a property or array element widens to string). as const is a const assertion that freezes a value to its narrowest, readonly, literal form — deeply. It's essential for building discriminant fields, tuple return types, and typed config/enum-like objects.

Detailed Answer

Without as const, an object literal's status: "loading" is inferred as string, breaking discriminated-union narrowing. With it, every property becomes readonly and every value its literal type. It also turns arrays into readonly tuples, which is exactly what custom hooks need to return so destructuring gives correct types per position (see Q10). A frequent pattern is deriving a union type from an object with typeof + keyof, giving you enum-like unions without TS enum (which has runtime cost and awkward semantics).

Code Example

// widening problem
const a = { status: "loading" };       // status: string
const b = { status: "loading" } as const; // status: "loading" (readonly)

// enum-like union without `enum`
const ROLES = ["admin", "editor", "viewer"] as const;
type Role = typeof ROLES[number];  // "admin" | "editor" | "viewer"

const THEME = { light: "#fff", dark: "#000" } as const;
type ThemeKey = keyof typeof THEME; // "light" | "dark"

Senior Engineer Perspective

Interviewers use this to see whether you understand widening — the reason a seemingly correct discriminated union silently fails to narrow. The advanced answer: prefer as const object maps over TypeScript enum because enums emit runtime code, don't tree-shake well, and their numeric variant allows unexpected value assignments. Deriving unions from as const arrays keeps a single source of truth for both runtime iteration and compile-time types.

SECTION 2 - TYPING REACT

Q7. How do you type component props and children? What is ReactNode?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

Define an interface/type for props and annotate the function's parameter directly — you rarely need React.FC anymore. For renderable children use React.ReactNode, which is the broadest "anything React can render" type (elements, strings, numbers, arrays, null, undefined, booleans). Use ReactElement only when you specifically require a single JSX element, and a function type when you use the render-props pattern.

Detailed Answer

The modern convention is to type props explicitly and return JSX, letting TypeScript infer the return type. React.FC fell out of favour because older versions implicitly added children to every component (even those that shouldn't have any), complicated generic components, and made the return type less flexible. In React 18 typings, FC no longer includes implicit children, so if you use it you must declare children yourself — at which point the explicit style is simpler.

TypeAccepts
ReactNodeAnything renderable (elements, strings, arrays, null…)
ReactElementA single JSX element only
JSX.ElementRoughly the same as ReactElement in practice
(x) => ReactNodeRender-prop / function-as-child

Code Example

interface CardProps {
  title: string;
  footer?: React.ReactNode;      // optional renderable
  children: React.ReactNode;     // declare children explicitly
}

function Card({ title, footer, children }: CardProps) {
  return (
    <section>
      <h2>{title}</h2>
      <div>{children}</div>
      {footer && <footer>{footer}</footer>}
    </section>
  );
}

// PropsWithChildren helper adds children for you
type BoxProps = React.PropsWithChildren<{ padding: number }>;

Senior Engineer Perspective

Expect "why not React.FC?" — the crisp answer is implicit children (pre-18), poor generic support, and enforced return type. Another probe: the difference between ReactNode and ReactElement; using ReactElement where you meant ReactNode rejects valid children like strings and arrays. For extending native elements, mention ComponentPropsWithoutRef<"button"> so your component transparently accepts all real DOM props.

Q8. How do you type useState, useRef, and useReducer?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

useState usually infers from the initial value; provide an explicit generic when the value can be more than the initial type (e.g. useState<User | null>(null)). useRef has two modes: a mutable value ref (useRef<number>(0) → { current: number }) and a DOM ref (useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null) → readonly-ish, may be null). useReducer is typed by annotating the state and action types, ideally with a discriminated union of actions.

Detailed Answer

The useState gotcha is useState(null) or useState([]) — inference gives null or never[], which then rejects real values. Supply the generic. For useRef, if you initialise a DOM ref with null and pass it to a JSX ref attribute, use useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null); the resulting current is HTMLInputElement | null, forcing a null check because the element isn't attached until after render. For a mutable instance variable that you write to, initialise with a real value so current is non-nullable and writable. For useReducer, model actions as a discriminated union so the reducer's switch narrows the payload per action type.

Code Example

// useState — explicit generic when initial value is narrower
const [user, setUser] = useState<User | null>(null);
const [items, setItems] = useState<Item[]>([]);

// useRef — DOM ref (nullable) vs mutable value ref
const inputRef = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null);
const renderCount = useRef<number>(0); // mutable, current: number
useEffect(() => { inputRef.current?.focus(); }, []);

// useReducer — discriminated union of actions
type State = { count: number };
type Action =
  | { type: "inc"; by: number }
  | { type: "reset" };

function reducer(state: State, action: Action): State {
  switch (action.type) {
    case "inc":   return { count: state.count + action.by };
    case "reset": return { count: 0 };
  }
}
const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, { count: 0 });

Senior Engineer Perspective

The useRef two-modes distinction separates seniors from juniors: passing null as the initial value makes current read-only for DOM refs but nullable, whereas a non-null initial value yields MutableRefObject. Interviewers may ask why current is nullable for DOM refs — because the ref is populated after commit, so you must guard with ?.. For reducers, the discriminated-union action type is the "correct" answer; a loose { type: string; payload?: any } throws away all safety.

Q9. How do you type event handlers in React?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Use React's synthetic event generics, parameterised by the element that fires them: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>, React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>, React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>, React.KeyboardEvent, and so on. If you write the handler inline in JSX, TypeScript infers the event type automatically — you only annotate when the handler is defined separately.

Detailed Answer

The element generic determines the type of e.target / e.currentTarget, so e.currentTarget.value is typed as string for an input. A frequent point of confusion: e.target is typed as the generic EventTarget-ish element for the whole event, while e.currentTarget is precisely the element the handler is attached to — prefer currentTarget for reliable typing. For a prop that is an event handler, you can type it as React.ChangeEventHandler<HTMLInputElement> instead of writing the function signature by hand.

Code Example

function SearchForm() {
  // inline handlers: event type is inferred, no annotation needed
  return (
    <form onSubmit={(e) => e.preventDefault()}>
      <input onChange={(e) => console.log(e.currentTarget.value)} />
    </form>
  );
}

// separate handler: annotate explicitly
const handleChange = (e: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>) => {
  console.log(e.currentTarget.value);
};

const handleClick: React.MouseEventHandler<HTMLButtonElement> = (e) => {
  e.preventDefault();
};

Senior Engineer Perspective

The target vs currentTarget distinction is the classic gotcha — currentTarget is strongly typed to your element, target is whatever was actually clicked (could be a child). Mentioning the ...Handler alias types (ChangeEventHandler, MouseEventHandler) shows fluency. Also note these are React synthetic events, not native DOM events — using MouseEvent from lib.dom instead of React.MouseEvent is a subtle mismatch interviewers watch for.

Q10. How do you type a custom hook, especially one returning a tuple?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Type the arguments and let the return be inferred where possible. For hooks that return a tuple (like useState), either annotate the return type explicitly or use as const — otherwise TypeScript widens the tuple to an array union ((T | Setter)[]), which breaks positional destructuring. For object-returning hooks, inference is usually fine.

Detailed Answer

If you return [value, setValue], TS infers Array<value | setValue>, so consumers destructuring by position get a union type on each slot. Two fixes: annotate the function's return type as a tuple, or append as const to the returned array (which also makes it readonly). Explicit annotation is generally clearer for a public hook. Prefer generics when the hook is reusable across value types (e.g. a useToggle vs a useLocalStorage<T>).

Code Example

// Generic hook with an explicit tuple return type
function useToggle(
  initial = false
): [boolean, () => void] {
  const [on, setOn] = useState(initial);
  const toggle = useCallback(() => setOn((o) => !o), []);
  return [on, toggle];              // typed as [boolean, () => void]
}

// Generic + as const alternative
function useLocalStorage<T>(key: string, initial: T) {
  const [value, setValue] = useState<T>(initial);
  // ... sync effect ...
  return [value, setValue] as const; // readonly [T, Dispatch<SetStateAction<T>>]
}

const [name, setName] = useToggle(); // correctly typed by position

Senior Engineer Perspective

The tuple-widening problem is the whole point of this question. Saying "I add as const or an explicit tuple annotation so destructuring keeps per-position types" nails it. A deeper follow-up: prefer returning an object from hooks with more than two values, because tuples rely on positional memory and readability degrades fast — tuples are best when consumers frequently rename (like useState). Show you choose the shape deliberately.

Q11. How do you type React Context correctly?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Create the context with an explicit generic, then guard consumption so components never receive the default. The clean pattern is to default the context to undefined (typed Ctx | undefined) and expose a custom useX() hook that throws if the value is missing — this removes null checks from every consumer and enforces that the provider wraps the tree.

Detailed Answer

The naive approach passes a fake default object to createContext just to satisfy types, which silently hides the bug of consuming outside a provider. The robust pattern initialises with undefined and narrows inside a custom hook that throws a helpful error. Consumers then get a non-nullable, fully typed value with zero boilerplate. Also remember to memoise the provider's value so unrelated re-renders don't invalidate every consumer.

Code Example

interface AuthContextValue {
  user: User | null;
  login: (email: string) => Promise<void>;
  logout: () => void;
}

const AuthContext = createContext<AuthContextValue | undefined>(undefined);

export function AuthProvider({ children }: React.PropsWithChildren) {
  const [user, setUser] = useState<User | null>(null);
  const value = useMemo<AuthContextValue>(
    () => ({ user, login: async () => {}, logout: () => {} }),
    [user]
  );
  return <AuthContext.Provider value={value}>{children}</AuthContext.Provider>;
}

// custom hook removes the undefined from consumers
export function useAuth(): AuthContextValue {
  const ctx = useContext(AuthContext);
  if (!ctx) throw new Error("useAuth must be used within <AuthProvider>");
  return ctx;
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

Interviewers want the "throwing custom hook" pattern; supplying a fake default object is the anti-pattern because it defers a missing-provider bug to runtime confusion instead of a clear error. Bonus points for mentioning useMemo on the provider value (a real performance footgun) and for noting that a large context often should be split into state and dispatch contexts so components that only dispatch don't re-render on state changes.

SECTION 3 - ADVANCED TYPES

Q12. What are generics and what problem do they solve?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Generics are type parameters — placeholders that let a function, type, or component work over many types while preserving the relationship between input and output. They give you reuse without losing type information the way any would. A generic identity<T>(x: T): T guarantees the return type equals the argument type.

Detailed Answer

The alternative to generics is either duplicating a function per type or using any and losing safety. Generics preserve the link: whatever T is at the call site flows through. You can constrain a parameter with extends (e.g. <T extends { id: number }>) to require certain members, and provide defaults (<T = string>). TypeScript usually infers the type argument from usage, so callers rarely write it explicitly. Generics power almost every reusable abstraction: data-fetching hooks, form utilities, table components, and the utility types in Q13.

Code Example

// preserves the input/output relationship
function first<T>(arr: T[]): T | undefined {
  return arr[0];
}
const n = first([1, 2, 3]);      // number | undefined
const s = first(["a", "b"]);     // string  | undefined

// constrained generic
function getId<T extends { id: number }>(entity: T): number {
  return entity.id;
}

// generic with a default
interface ApiResponse<T = unknown> {
  data: T;
  status: number;
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

The tell of a mature answer is "generics let me stay type-safe across many types without any, and constraints let me require the minimum shape I need". Interviewers may push on over-genericising: adding type parameters that are used only once adds cognitive load with no benefit — a generic parameter should appear at least twice (input and output) to earn its place. Knowing when not to reach for generics is as senior as knowing how.

Q13. Explain the common utility types: Partial, Pick, Omit, Record, Required, Readonly.

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

These are built-in generic type transformers. Partial<T> makes all properties optional; Required<T> makes them all required; Readonly<T> makes them read-only; Pick<T, K> selects a subset of keys; Omit<T, K> removes keys; Record<K, V> builds an object type with keys K and values V. They let you derive types from a single source instead of hand-copying shapes.

Detailed Answer

UtilityEffectTypical use
Partial<T>All props optionalUpdate payloads, defaults merging
Required<T>All props requiredAfter validation / normalisation
Readonly<T>All props readonlyImmutable props / state
Pick<T, K>Keep only keys KNarrow props for a subcomponent
Omit<T, K>Remove keys KStrip id before create; extend DOM props
Record<K, V>Object of K→VLookup maps, dictionaries

Deriving types keeps them in sync: define User once and express "create input" as Omit<User, "id" | "createdAt">. When the base type changes, the derived types update automatically.

Code Example

interface User {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  email: string;
  createdAt: Date;
}

type CreateUser = Omit<User, "id" | "createdAt">;     // { name; email }
type UserPreview = Pick<User, "id" | "name">;         // { id; name }
type UserPatch = Partial<User>;                       // all optional
type FrozenUser = Readonly<User>;                     // all readonly
type UsersById = Record<string, User>;               // dictionary

// Omit is the idiomatic way to override a native prop's type
type InputProps = Omit<React.ComponentProps<"input">, "onChange"> & {
  onChange: (value: string) => void;
};

Senior Engineer Perspective

Interviewers check whether you derive or duplicate. The senior habit is "single source of truth" — a create-DTO is Omit of the entity, a patch is Partial. A subtle trap: Omit is not distributive over unions and doesn't preserve discriminated-union narrowing well, so on unions prefer Exclude/custom mapped types. Also know these are just mapped types under the hood — being able to reimplement Partial (Q14) proves real understanding.

Q14. What are keyof, mapped types, and conditional types?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: Medium

Short Answer

keyof T produces a union of T's property names. A mapped type iterates over those keys to build a new type ({ [K in keyof T]: ... }) — this is how Partial/Readonly are implemented. A conditional type is a type-level ternary (T extends U ? X : Y) that picks a type based on a relationship, and infer lets you extract a piece of a type inside the condition.

Detailed Answer

Together these are the engine behind the utility types. Combining keyof with indexed access (T[K]) lets you write a fully type-safe property getter. Mapped-type modifiers ? and readonly (and their removal via -? / -readonly) implement Partial/Required/Readonly. Conditional types with infer underpin ReturnType, Parameters, and Awaited, and distribute over unions when the checked type is a naked type parameter.

Code Example

interface User { id: string; name: string }

// keyof + indexed access -> type-safe getter
function getProp<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K] {
  return obj[key];
}
getProp({ id: "1", name: "Ada" }, "name"); // string, "age" is rejected

// mapped type: reimplementing Partial
type MyPartial<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] };

// conditional type + infer: extract a function's return type
type MyReturn<F> = F extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : never;
type R = MyReturn<() => User>; // User

Senior Engineer Perspective

Being able to reimplement Partial or ReturnType from scratch is the demarcation line for "knows TypeScript deeply" versus "uses TypeScript". Interviewers rarely need this daily, but asking it filters candidates. The pragmatic caveat to voice: heavy conditional/mapped type gymnastics hurt compile times and readability — use them for genuinely reusable library-grade utilities, not everyday app code where a plain type is clearer.

Q15. How do you write a generic (reusable) component?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: Medium

Short Answer

Declare a type parameter on the component function and use it in the props. TypeScript infers the concrete type from the props passed at the JSX call site, so a <List> knows its item type from the items array. This gives fully typed renderItem callbacks and key extractors without any.

Detailed Answer

Write the component as a generic function: function List<T>(props: ListProps<T>). Inference flows from the items: T[] prop into renderItem: (item: T) => ReactNode. Two caveats: (1) arrow-function components with generics need a trailing comma in .tsx (<T,>) to disambiguate from JSX, so a function declaration is cleaner; (2) generic components don't compose with React.FC, which is another reason the plain-function style won. This pattern powers reusable tables, selects, comboboxes and data lists.

Code Example

interface ListProps<T> {
  items: T[];
  keyOf: (item: T) => string | number;
  renderItem: (item: T) => React.ReactNode;
}

function List<T>({ items, keyOf, renderItem }: ListProps<T>) {
  return (
    <ul>
      {items.map((item) => (
        <li key={keyOf(item)}>{renderItem(item)}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

// T inferred as User — renderItem's param is fully typed
<List
  items={users}
  keyOf={(u) => u.id}
  renderItem={(u) => <span>{u.name}</span>}
/>;

Senior Engineer Perspective

The .tsx generic-arrow ambiguity (<T,> trailing comma) is a favourite "have you actually done this" check. Explain that inference from the items prop is what makes the callbacks type-safe — that's the payoff. A follow-up may ask how to constrain T (e.g. T extends { id: string }) so you can drop the keyOf prop; showing you can trade flexibility for ergonomics demonstrates design judgement.

Q16. How do you type a component that uses forwardRef?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: Medium

Short Answer

forwardRef takes two type parameters: the ref (element) type first, then the props type. So forwardRef<HTMLInputElement, InputProps>. Inside, the ref argument is typed as ForwardedRef<HTMLInputElement>. In React 19 this is simpler — ref can be a normal prop, and forwardRef is being phased out.

Detailed Answer

Note the parameter order is reversed from intuition: element type first, props second. This trips people up constantly. To expose an imperative API rather than the raw DOM node, combine forwardRef with useImperativeHandle and type the ref as your custom handle interface. As of React 19, function components can accept ref directly in their props (typed as Ref<T>), so new code often skips forwardRef entirely — worth mentioning to show you track the current API.

Code Example

interface InputProps {
  label: string;
  value: string;
  onChange: (v: string) => void;
}

// <ElementType, PropsType> — element FIRST
const TextField = forwardRef<HTMLInputElement, InputProps>(
  ({ label, value, onChange }, ref) => (
    <label>
      {label}
      <input
        ref={ref}
        value={value}
        onChange={(e) => onChange(e.currentTarget.value)}
      />
    </label>
  )
);
TextField.displayName = "TextField";

// React 19 style: ref as a normal prop, no forwardRef
function TextField19({ ref, label }: InputProps & { ref?: React.Ref<HTMLInputElement> }) {
  return <input ref={ref} aria-label={label} />;
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

The reversed generic order (element before props) is the single most-missed detail here — stating it unprompted is a strong signal. Interviewers may ask how to expose a controlled API instead of the DOM node: the answer is useImperativeHandle with a typed handle interface. And mentioning that React 19 makes forwardRef largely unnecessary shows you're current rather than parroting older tutorials.

SECTION 4 - CONFIG & PRACTICE

Q17. How do you type a fetch / API layer safely?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Never trust the network: fetch().json() returns any (effectively unsafe). Wrap it so the raw result is unknown, then validate at runtime with a schema (Zod/Valibot) and infer the TypeScript type from that single schema. A generic request<T> helper centralises error handling and typing so call sites are clean and safe.

Detailed Answer

A plain generic like request<User>(url) only asserts the shape — it lies if the server returns something different. The robust layer parses the response through a runtime schema so the compile-time type and the actual data can't drift; the inferred type comes from the schema via z.infer. This catches API contract changes at the boundary with a clear error instead of an undefined-property crash three components deep. Pair this with TanStack Query, whose useQuery infers its data type from the query function's return type.

Code Example

import { z } from "zod";

const UserSchema = z.object({
  id: z.string(),
  name: z.string(),
  email: z.string().email(),
});
type User = z.infer<typeof UserSchema>; // single source of truth

async function getUser(id: string): Promise<User> {
  const res = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`);
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
  const json: unknown = await res.json();   // untrusted
  return UserSchema.parse(json);             // validated + typed
}

// TanStack Query infers `data: User` from getUser's return type
// const { data } = useQuery({ queryKey: ["user", id], queryFn: () => getUser(id) });

Senior Engineer Perspective

The line interviewers listen for: "a generic fetch<T> is a type assertion, not a guarantee — it trusts data it never checked." Elevating to runtime validation with an inferred type shows you understand the gap between compile-time and runtime. Follow-ups often go to error typing (model errors as a discriminated result rather than throwing), and to keeping DTOs vs domain models separate so backend shape changes don't leak through the whole UI.

Q18. What are declaration files, and what tsconfig / strict-mode settings matter most?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: Medium

Short Answer

Declaration files (.d.ts) describe the types of JavaScript that has none — third-party libs (via @types/*), globals, and non-code imports (CSS modules, SVGs). For config, the single most important flag is "strict": true, which turns on strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny, and friends. Add "jsx": "react-jsx" for the modern automatic runtime and "isolatedModules" for bundler compatibility.

Detailed Answer

.d.ts files contain only type information, no runtime code. You use declare module to type untyped packages or asset imports, and declare global to augment Window or add global types. Most libraries ship their own types or have community @types packages.

SettingWhy it matters
strict: trueEnables all strict checks — the baseline for real safety
strictNullChecksSeparates null/undefined from other types — catches the top JS bug
noImplicitAnyForces annotations instead of silent any
noUncheckedIndexedAccessAdds undefined to index access — catches out-of-bounds reads
jsx: "react-jsx"Automatic JSX runtime — no more import React
isolatedModulesRequired by Vite/esbuild/swc single-file transpilers

Code Example

// global.d.ts — type non-code imports and globals
declare module "*.svg" {
  const src: string;
  export default src;
}

declare module "*.module.css" {
  const classes: { readonly [key: string]: string };
  export default classes;
}

declare global {
  interface Window {
    dataLayer: unknown[];
  }
}
export {}; // make this file a module

// tsconfig.json (essentials)
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "strict": true,
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,
    "jsx": "react-jsx",
    "module": "ESNext",
    "moduleResolution": "Bundler",
    "isolatedModules": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true
  }
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

The must-say answer is "strict: true, non-negotiable" — a codebase with strict off is only cosmetically typed. Bonus depth: noUncheckedIndexedAccess is off even under strict and is the flag that catches arr[i] possibly being undefined — mentioning it signals you've fought real bugs. Explain that .d.ts for asset imports is what makes import logo from "./logo.svg" type-check under a bundler, and that skipLibCheck trades full lib validation for much faster builds.

Q19. What are the most common TypeScript-with-React mistakes?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

The recurring offenders: leaning on any (or casual as casts) instead of narrowing; forgetting the useState generic for null/empty initial values; typing API responses without runtime validation; using loose action types in reducers; misusing ReactElement vs ReactNode; and defining unstable object/array props inline that break memoisation.

Detailed Answer

  • as as a hammer: a type assertion silences the compiler without proving anything. Prefer narrowing or validation; reserve as for cases you genuinely know better than TS (and even then, as const or a guard is usually cleaner).
  • Widening surprises: forgetting as const on discriminant literals so unions won't narrow (Q5/Q6).
  • useState inference: useState(null) or useState([]) infers null/never[] and rejects real data.
  • Untyped events: using DOM MouseEvent instead of React.MouseEvent, or reaching for target instead of currentTarget.
  • Non-null assertion (!) abuse: ref.current!.focus() hides real null cases; guard with ?. instead.
  • Ignoring exhaustiveness: not using the never default trick, so new union members slip through unhandled.

Code Example

// BAD: assertion lies to the compiler
const user = JSON.parse(raw) as User;   // no runtime check
element!.focus();                        // hides null case

// GOOD: narrow / validate / guard
const user = UserSchema.parse(JSON.parse(raw));
element?.focus();

// BAD: inference collapses to never[]
const [items, setItems] = useState([]);        // never[]
// GOOD
const [items2, setItems2] = useState<Item[]>([]);

Senior Engineer Perspective

This question doubles as a values check: interviewers want to see that you treat any and as as smells, not tools. The strongest answer connects each mistake to the runtime bug it eventually causes — e.g. "casting the API response means a backend rename becomes an undefined is not a function crash in production instead of a caught validation error." Mentioning ESLint rules (no-explicit-any, no-non-null-assertion) shows you enforce these standards across a team, not just personally.

05 - REACT FUNDAMENTALS

Target Audience: Frontend / React Engineer (3–6 Years) Goal: Not just answer questions, but survive follow-up grilling from experienced interviewers.

TOP HIGHEST-ROI QUESTIONS IN THIS CHAPTER

  1. What is React and what does "declarative UI" actually mean?
  2. What is JSX and what does it compile to?
  3. Function components vs class components — why did functions win?
  4. Props vs state — what is the real difference?
  5. What is one-way data flow and why does React enforce it?
  6. What does "lifting state up" mean and when do you do it?
  7. Controlled vs uncontrolled inputs.
  8. Why do lists need keys, and why are index keys dangerous?
  9. Conditional rendering patterns in JSX.
  10. What are Fragments and why do they exist?
  11. The children prop and component composition.
  12. How does event handling work — what is a synthetic event?
  13. How do you pass data from child to parent?
  14. Why must you update state immutably?
  15. When and why do React components re-render?
  16. What is StrictMode and why do things run twice in dev?
  17. How is component lifecycle expressed with hooks vs class methods?
  18. What are refs and portals, and when do you reach for them?

SECTION 1 - JSX & COMPONENTS

Q1. What is React, and what does "declarative UI" actually mean?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces out of composable components. It is declarative: you describe what the UI should look like for a given state, and React figures out the DOM operations needed to get there. You never manually append, remove, or mutate DOM nodes — you change state, and React reconciles the output.

Detailed Answer

The core mental model is a pure function: UI = f(state). Your component returns a description of the UI (a tree of elements) as a function of its current props and state. When state changes, React re-runs that function, produces a new element tree, diffs it against the previous one (reconciliation), and applies the minimal set of DOM mutations.

Declarative vs Imperative

In an imperative world (vanilla DOM, jQuery) you write the steps: "find the node, read its text, if the count changed update it, toggle this class." Every branch of state is a manual instruction, and keeping the DOM in sync with data is the source of most bugs.

In a declarative world you write the destination: "when count is N, the label reads N." React owns the transition from the old picture to the new one. This removes an entire class of "the screen says one thing but the data says another" bugs because there is a single source of truth (state) and one place that renders it.

Why it matters

  • Predictability — the UI is a deterministic projection of state.
  • Composability — components nest like functions call functions.
  • The Virtual DOM — React batches and minimizes real DOM writes, which are the expensive part.

Code Example

// Imperative (vanilla) — you describe every step
const btn = document.querySelector("#like");
let liked = false;
btn.addEventListener("click", () => {
  liked = !liked;
  btn.textContent = liked ? "Liked" : "Like"; // manual sync
  btn.classList.toggle("active", liked);
});

// Declarative (React) — you describe the result for a given state
function LikeButton() {
  const [liked, setLiked] = React.useState(false);
  return (
    <button
      className={liked ? "active" : ""}
      onClick={() => setLiked(!liked)}
    >
      {liked ? "Liked" : "Like"}
    </button>
  );
}

Project Example

On a dashboard I built, a filter panel controlled a table of results. Declaratively, the table simply rendered rows.filter(matchesFilters). Adding a new filter meant adding one predicate — I never touched the DOM, wrote no "clear old rows / append new rows" code, and there was no way for the table to drift out of sync with the filter chips.

Senior Engineer Perspective

Interviewers use this to check whether you actually understand the paradigm or just memorized "Virtual DOM = fast." The honest nuance: the Virtual DOM is not inherently faster than hand-optimized imperative DOM code — a skilled engineer can beat React on a single widget. React's win is maintainability at scale: it makes correct UI the default and keeps a large app's state and view coherent. If you claim "React is fast because of the Virtual DOM," expect a follow-up like "faster than what?" — and the correct answer is "faster and safer than the imperative code most teams would otherwise write, by minimizing and batching DOM writes."

Q2. What is JSX, and what does it compile to?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

JSX is a syntax extension that looks like HTML but is really sugar for function calls. A build step (Babel, SWC, esbuild, TypeScript) compiles each JSX element into a call — historically React.createElement(...), and since React 17 into the automatic JSX runtime (jsx / jsxs from react/jsx-runtime). Those calls return plain JavaScript objects called React elements. The browser never sees JSX.

Detailed Answer

JSX is not HTML and it is not a template language — it is expressions. Anything in { } is arbitrary JavaScript. Because it compiles to function calls, JSX obeys JavaScript rules: components must be capitalized (lowercase compiles to a string tag like "div", capitalized to a variable reference), attributes are camelCased (className, onClick), and a component must return a single root (an element, a Fragment, or an array).

The two compile targets

  • Classic runtime (pre-17): each element becomes React.createElement(type, props, ...children). This is why you had to import React in every file even if you didn't reference it — the compiled code did.
  • Automatic runtime (17+): the compiler injects imports from react/jsx-runtime and emits _jsx(type, props) / _jsxs(...) for multiple children. You no longer need import React just to use JSX.

A React element is a lightweight, immutable description — roughly { type, key, props }. It is not a DOM node and not a component instance; it is a plain object React later reconciles into DOM.

Code Example

// What you write
const el = (
  <button className="primary" onClick={handleClick}>
    Hello {name}
  </button>
);

// Classic runtime (React.createElement)
const el = React.createElement(
  "button",
  { className: "primary", onClick: handleClick },
  "Hello ",
  name
);

// Automatic runtime (React 17+), roughly:
import { jsx as _jsx } from "react/jsx-runtime";
const el = _jsx("button", {
  className: "primary",
  onClick: handleClick,
  children: ["Hello ", name],
});

// The element is just an object:
// { type: "button", key: null, props: { className, onClick, children } }

Project Example

Understanding that JSX is "just function calls returning objects" paid off when I built a config-driven form: instead of writing JSX by hand, I mapped a JSON schema to an array of elements and rendered them. Knowing elements are plain objects made it obvious that I could generate, filter, and compose them programmatically — something that feels impossible if you think JSX is magic HTML.

Senior Engineer Perspective

The trap here is candidates who say "JSX is HTML in JavaScript." It isn't — it's expressions that compile to calls. A strong follow-up: "Why must component names be capitalized?" Answer: because JSX compiles the tag name literally; lowercase becomes the string "div" (a host element), while capitalized becomes a variable reference to your component. Another sharp follow-up: "Why doesn't <MyComp /> re-run when I only mutate a prop object in place?" — because elements are immutable snapshots; React compares by reference and value, not by watching your object.

Q3. Function components vs class components — why did functions win?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Both produce UI, but function components + hooks (React 16.8+) became the standard because they let you reuse stateful logic without wrapper hell, avoid the this-binding footguns of classes, and colocate related logic instead of scattering it across lifecycle methods. New React features (concurrent rendering, most modern APIs) are built for functions. Classes still work but are legacy for new code.

Detailed Answer

A class component extends React.Component, holds state in this.state, and reacts to lifecycle via methods like componentDidMount. A function component is just a function that returns JSX and uses hooks (useState, useEffect, …) for state and side effects.

ConcernClassFunction + Hooks
Statethis.state / setStateuseState / useReducer
Side effectsSplit across componentDidMount, componentDidUpdate, componentWillUnmountUnified in useEffect
this bindingManual (constructor or arrow methods)No this at all
Logic reuseHOCs / render props (nesting hell)Custom hooks (flat, composable)
Concurrent featuresLimitedFirst-class

The killer reason functions won is stateful logic reuse. In the class era, sharing "subscribe to window resize" logic meant HOCs or render props, which produced deeply nested "wrapper hell" and made the tree hard to read. A custom hook packages that same logic into a plain function you call — flat, testable, and composable.

The second reason is that lifecycle methods split related code (a subscription set up in componentDidMount and torn down in componentWillUnmount) and merged unrelated code (two features both living in componentDidUpdate). Effects group by concern instead.

Code Example

// Class
class Counter extends React.Component {
  state = { count: 0 };
  increment = () => this.setState(s => ({ count: s.count + 1 }));
  componentDidMount() { document.title = `Count ${this.state.count}`; }
  componentDidUpdate() { document.title = `Count ${this.state.count}`; }
  render() {
    return <button onClick={this.increment}>{this.state.count}</button>;
  }
}

// Function + hooks — same behaviour, less ceremony, effect colocated
function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = React.useState(0);
  React.useEffect(() => {
    document.title = `Count ${count}`;
  }, [count]);
  return <button onClick={() => setCount(c => c + 1)}>{count}</button>;
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

Don't say "functions are faster" — they aren't meaningfully faster; the win is ergonomics and logic reuse. Know the two things classes can still technically do that hooks can't natively: error boundaries require a class (componentDidCatch / getDerivedStateFromError), and there is no hook equivalent yet. Also be ready for "isn't useEffect just componentDidMount?" — no: effects run after paint, can run multiple times, and their dependency array + cleanup semantics don't map one-to-one to lifecycle methods. Conflating the two is the classic junior mistake.

Q4. What are Fragments and why do they exist?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

A component must return a single root node, but you often don't want an extra wrapper <div> in the DOM. A Fragment lets you group children without adding any node. Use <>...</> shorthand, or <React.Fragment> when you need a key (e.g. in a list).

Detailed Answer

Wrapper divs cause real problems: they break CSS layouts that depend on direct parent-child relationships (flexbox, grid, tables), they pollute the DOM, and they can break semantics (you can't wrap <td> elements in a <div> inside a <tr>). Fragments solve this by grouping siblings with zero DOM footprint.

The shorthand <></> cannot take attributes. When you render a list of grouped elements and need a key, you must use the explicit <React.Fragment key={id}> form.

Code Example

// No wrapper div in the output
function Columns() {
  return (
    <>
      <td>Name</td>
      <td>Email</td>
    </>
  );
}

// Keyed fragment in a list — shorthand can't hold a key
function Definitions({ items }) {
  return (
    <dl>
      {items.map((item) => (
        <React.Fragment key={item.id}>
          <dt>{item.term}</dt>
          <dd>{item.desc}</dd>
        </React.Fragment>
      ))}
    </dl>
  );
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

Interviewers like the table example because it exposes whether you understand that "div soup" isn't just ugly — it breaks valid HTML and CSS. A good follow-up answer: mention that unnecessary wrapper divs also make styling and accessibility harder (extra layers screen readers must traverse) and can subtly change flex/grid behaviour. Knowing that the shorthand can't take a key is a small detail that signals real hands-on experience.

Q5. Explain the children prop and component composition.

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Whatever you nest between a component's opening and closing tags is passed to it as props.children. This enables composition — building flexible, reusable "container" components (cards, modals, layouts) that don't need to know what they wrap. React's answer to "inheritance vs composition" is: strongly prefer composition, and children is the primary tool.

Detailed Answer

A generic Card shouldn't hardcode its contents. By rendering {children}, it becomes a shell any caller can fill. You can also accept multiple "slots" by passing elements as named props (e.g. header, footer) — sometimes called the slots pattern.

Composition beats inheritance in React because components are functions, not class hierarchies. Instead of a FancyButton extends Button chain, you compose: a specialized component renders a generic one and passes props/children through. This keeps components loosely coupled and avoids brittle hierarchies.

Code Example

// Container that doesn't care what it wraps
function Card({ title, children }) {
  return (
    <section className="card">
      <h3>{title}</h3>
      <div className="card-body">{children}</div>
    </section>
  );
}

// Composition via children + a "slot" prop
function Dialog({ footer, children }) {
  return (
    <div className="dialog">
      <div className="content">{children}</div>
      <div className="actions">{footer}</div>
    </div>
  );
}

// Usage
<Card title="Profile">
  <Avatar user={user} />
  <p>{user.bio}</p>
</Card>

Senior Engineer Perspective

A frequent follow-up: "How would you avoid prop drilling deep composition?" — answer with Context for cross-cutting values, but note that passing components as children is itself a powerful way to sidestep drilling: the parent that has the data renders the child directly and hands the tree down. This is also the basis of the "children as a performance boundary" trick — a child passed via children doesn't re-render when the parent's own state changes, because its element was created by the grandparent. Mentioning that shows depth.

SECTION 2 - PROPS & STATE

Q6. Props vs state — what is the real difference?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

Props are inputs passed into a component by its parent; they are read-only from the component's perspective. State is data a component owns and manages internally over time. Props flow down and are immutable to the receiver; state is local, mutable via a setter, and triggers re-renders when it changes.

Detailed Answer

PropsState
Owned byParentThe component itself
Mutable?No (read-only to receiver)Yes, via setter (useState)
PurposeConfigure / pass data downTrack changing internal data
Triggers re-renderWhen parent passes new valuesWhen you call the setter

A useful test: "Can this value be computed from props or other state?" If yes, it should not be state (derive it during render instead). "Does it change over the component's life due to user interaction or async data?" If yes, it's state. "Is it given by a parent?" Then it's a prop.

Treat props as immutable — never assign to props.x. If a component needs to change a value it received, it should either lift that decision to the owner (call a callback prop) or copy the initial value into its own state.

Code Example

// `label` and `onClick` are PROPS (from parent, read-only here)
// `count` is STATE (owned here, changes over time)
function Counter({ label }) {
  const [count, setCount] = React.useState(0);

  // Derived value — NOT state, computed each render
  const isEven = count % 2 === 0;

  return (
    <button onClick={() => setCount(c => c + 1)}>
      {label}: {count} ({isEven ? "even" : "odd"})
    </button>
  );
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

The single most common junior mistake this question exposes is redundant state — copying a prop into state and then wondering why it "doesn't update" when the prop changes (because useState's initial value is only read on the first render). Say clearly: derive whenever possible, and only mirror a prop into state when you deliberately want to "fork" it (e.g. an editable form initialized from a server value). Interviewers probe "what would you never make state?" — answer: anything derivable, because duplicated sources of truth drift apart.

Q7. What is one-way data flow, and why does React enforce it?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Data in React flows in a single direction: down from parent to child via props. A child cannot reach up and mutate its parent's data directly; instead the parent passes callbacks down, and the child calls them to request a change. This unidirectional flow makes state changes predictable and traceable.

Detailed Answer

State lives in one place (the owner), and that owner passes the current value down as props and passes handlers down for changes. When a child triggers a handler, the owner updates its state, which re-renders and pushes fresh props down. The loop is: state → props → view → event → callback → new state.

Compare this to two-way binding (older Angular, Knockout) where a view field and a model auto-sync in both directions. Two-way binding is convenient for small forms but makes it hard to answer "who changed this value and when?" in a large app. One-way flow trades a little verbosity for a clear, debuggable audit trail — there is always exactly one owner of any piece of state.

Code Example

// Parent owns the state; child receives value + a way to request change
function Parent() {
  const [name, setName] = React.useState("");
  return <NameInput value={name} onChange={setName} />;
}

function NameInput({ value, onChange }) {
  // Child never mutates parent directly — it calls the callback
  return (
    <input
      value={value}
      onChange={(e) => onChange(e.target.value)}
    />
  );
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

Expect "but isn't a controlled input two-way binding?" The sharp answer: it looks two-way but is implemented as two one-way flows — value flows down, change events flow up as function calls; React never silently syncs anything. That distinction is the whole point. Interviewers also like to ask what breaks one-way flow: mutating props, mutating state objects in place, or lifting shared state too late. A senior engineer frames one-way flow as the property that makes time-travel debugging and predictable renders possible.

Q8. What does "lifting state up" mean, and when do you do it?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

When two or more components need to share or stay in sync with the same data, you move that state up to their closest common ancestor and pass it back down as props. The ancestor becomes the single source of truth; the children become controlled by it.

Detailed Answer

Suppose two sibling components need the same value — say a temperature entered in Celsius should reflect in a Fahrenheit field. If each holds its own state, they drift. The fix: lift the temperature into their parent, which passes value and onChange to both. Now there is one owner and both views are always consistent.

The heuristic: state should live at the lowest common ancestor of all components that read or write it — no higher (which causes needless re-renders and prop drilling), no lower (which causes duplication and drift). If lifting produces excessive prop drilling across many layers, that's the signal to reach for Context or a state library — but lifting is always the first move.

Code Example

// State lifted to the parent so both children stay in sync
function TemperatureCalculator() {
  const [celsius, setCelsius] = React.useState(20);
  const fahrenheit = celsius * 9 / 5 + 32;

  return (
    <>
      <TempInput scale="C" value={celsius}
        onChange={setCelsius} />
      <TempInput scale="F" value={fahrenheit}
        onChange={(f) => setCelsius((f - 32) * 5 / 9)} />
    </>
  );
}

function TempInput({ scale, value, onChange }) {
  return (
    <label>
      {scale}: <input value={value}
        onChange={(e) => onChange(Number(e.target.value))} />
    </label>
  );
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

The follow-up is almost always "and when does lifting become a problem?" — when the common ancestor is many levels up and you drill props through components that don't care about them. That's the cue for Context (for low-frequency, cross-cutting state like theme/auth) or a dedicated store (Redux Toolkit, Zustand) for complex, frequently-updated shared state. A senior answer sequences the tools: derive → lift → Context → store, escalating only when the previous tool hurts.

Q9. Why must you update state immutably instead of mutating it?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

React decides whether to re-render (and whether memoized children changed) by comparing references with Object.is. If you mutate an object or array in place, the reference doesn't change, so React may skip the re-render and the UI goes stale. You must produce a new object/array so the reference differs.

Detailed Answer

State updates in React are shallow-compared by reference. state.items.push(x) mutates the same array — same reference — and setItems(state.items) tells React "nothing changed." Even if a re-render does happen for another reason, React.memo, useMemo, and effect dependency arrays all rely on reference equality and will misbehave.

The rule: always create new containers. Use spread ([...arr, item], { ...obj, key: val }), array methods that return new arrays (map, filter, concat — not push/splice/sort in place), and the functional updater form setX(prev => ...) when the next value depends on the previous one.

For deeply nested state, manual spreading gets painful — that's where useReducer plus Immer (which lets you "mutate" a draft that produces an immutable result) shines.

Code Example

const [todos, setTodos] = React.useState([]);

// WRONG — mutates same array, same reference, React may skip render
function addWrong(text) {
  todos.push({ id: Date.now(), text });
  setTodos(todos); // same reference!
}

// RIGHT — new array, new reference
function addRight(text) {
  setTodos((prev) => [...prev, { id: Date.now(), text }]);
}

// RIGHT — updating one item immutably
function toggle(id) {
  setTodos((prev) =>
    prev.map((t) => (t.id === id ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t))
  );
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

This is a top filter question. The strongest answer connects it to Object.is reference comparison and names the concrete failure modes: skipped re-renders, stale React.memo, and effects that don't fire because their dependency reference didn't change. A common follow-up: "why does the functional updater setX(prev => ...) matter?" — because in batched updates or closures, x may be stale; reading prev guarantees you build on the latest committed value. If asked about deep updates, mention Immer rather than hand-rolling five levels of spread.

SECTION 3 - RENDERING & LISTS

Q10. When and why do React components re-render?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

A component re-renders when (1) its own state changes, (2) its parent re-renders, or (3) a Context it consumes changes value. "Re-render" means React calls the component function again to produce a new element tree; it does not necessarily mean DOM changes — reconciliation still diffs and only touches the DOM where output actually differs.

Detailed Answer

The crucial and counter-intuitive part: when a component re-renders, all of its children re-render by default — regardless of whether their props changed. React does not bail out automatically. It re-runs the whole subtree and relies on reconciliation to keep DOM edits minimal.

Re-rendering is usually cheap and not a problem; premature optimization here is a classic mistake. But when a subtree is expensive, you opt into skipping with:

  • React.memo(Component) — skips re-render if props are shallowly equal.
  • useMemo — memoizes an expensive computed value.
  • useCallback — stabilizes a function reference so memoized children don't see it as "new."

Note that props "changing" is judged by reference — which is exactly why immutable updates (Q9) and stable references matter for these optimizations to work.

Code Example

function Parent() {
  const [count, setCount] = React.useState(0);
  return (
    <>
      <button onClick={() => setCount(c => c + 1)}>{count}</button>
      {/* Re-renders every time Parent does, even though its
          props never change — unless wrapped in React.memo */}
      <ExpensiveChild />
    </>
  );
}

const ExpensiveChild = React.memo(function ExpensiveChild() {
  // now skipped when props are shallow-equal
  return <div>...</div>;
});

Senior Engineer Perspective

The mistake juniors make is believing "props changed → re-render, props same → no re-render." Reality: parent render → child renders regardless, unless memoized. Interviewers push on "so should you wrap everything in React.memo?" — no; the comparison itself costs, and most renders are cheap. Profile first. A senior also mentions a free win: passing an expensive subtree via children so it isn't re-created by the state-holding component. And they'll note that React 19's compiler aims to auto-memoize, reducing manual useMemo/useCallback.

Q11. Why do lists need keys, and why are index keys dangerous?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

Keys give each list item a stable identity so React's reconciler can tell which items were added, removed, or reordered — instead of re-rendering the whole list. Use a stable, unique ID from your data. Using the array index as a key is dangerous because the index changes when items are inserted, removed, or reordered, causing React to associate the wrong DOM/state with the wrong item.

Detailed Answer

During reconciliation React matches old and new children by key. With stable keys, inserting an item at the top adds one node and leaves the rest untouched. Without keys (or with index keys), React matches by position: inserting at the top makes every index shift, so React thinks every item changed and either re-renders everything or — worse — keeps stale internal state attached to the wrong item.

The classic bug: a list of inputs keyed by index. Type into the first input, then prepend a new item. Because the DOM nodes are matched by position, your typed text and focus "stick" to position 0 and now belong to the wrong logical item. The same corruption hits uncontrolled inputs, animations, and component state inside list items.

Index keys are only acceptable when the list is static, never reordered, and items are never inserted/removed in the middle — and even then a real ID is safer.

Code Example

// DANGEROUS — index key breaks on reorder/insert/delete
{items.map((item, i) => (
  <li key={i}>
    <input defaultValue={item.name} />
  </li>
))}

// CORRECT — stable identity from the data
{items.map((item) => (
  <li key={item.id}>
    <input defaultValue={item.name} />
  </li>
))}

Project Example

On a drag-and-drop task board I once used the index as a key and shipped a maddening bug: reordering cards would keep an edit-in-progress textarea's content on the card that used to be in that slot. Switching to the task's UUID as the key fixed it instantly — a textbook demonstration of why keys are about identity, not position.

Senior Engineer Perspective

This question sorts people who've read docs from people who've been burned. Nail the why: keys are React's mechanism for preserving component identity and state across renders, not just to "silence a warning." Follow-ups: "Why not Math.random() as a key?" — because it changes every render, so React remounts every item every time (destroying state and killing performance). "Where must the key go?" — on the outermost element returned by map, and it only needs to be unique among siblings, not globally.

Q12. What are the common conditional rendering patterns in JSX?

ROI: ★★★☆☆ Frequency: Medium

Short Answer

Since JSX is expressions, you render conditionally with plain JavaScript: the ternary cond ? a : b for either/or, the logical && for "render or nothing," early return null to render nothing, and variables or helper functions for complex branches. There's no special template syntax.

Detailed Answer

  • Ternary — when you need one of two outputs: {isLoading ? <Spinner/> : <List/>}.
  • Logical AND — when you render something or nothing: {error && <Error/>}. Watch the gotcha below.
  • Early return — if (!user) return null; keeps the main JSX clean.
  • Extracted variable / function — for 3+ branches, compute the element above the return, or use a small helper / lookup map keyed by status.

The && falsy trap: {count && <Badge/>} renders the literal 0 when count is 0, because 0 is falsy but is a valid React child. Guard with a real boolean: {count > 0 && <Badge/>} or {!!count && ...}.

Code Example

// Ternary
{isLoading ? <Spinner /> : <Results data={data} />}

// Logical AND — but beware falsy 0
{items.length > 0 && <Count n={items.length} />}   // safe
{items.length && <Count />}                          // BUG: renders 0

// Lookup map for many states — cleaner than nested ternaries
const views = {
  loading: <Spinner />,
  error: <ErrorPanel />,
  empty: <EmptyState />,
  ready: <List data={data} />,
};
return views[status];

Senior Engineer Perspective

The 0 rendering trap is a favorite gotcha — many candidates have hit "why is there a random 0 in my UI?" in production. Mention it unprompted; it signals experience. Also worth saying: deeply nested ternaries hurt readability, so prefer early returns or a status-to-view map for multi-state components (loading/error/empty/ready), which also documents every state explicitly.

SECTION 4 - EVENTS & FORMS BASICS

Q13. How does event handling work in React, and what is a synthetic event?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

You attach handlers with camelCase props (onClick, onChange) and pass a function reference. React wraps the native browser event in a cross-browser SyntheticEvent to give consistent behaviour across browsers. In React 17+, React attaches one listener at the root container (not the document) and uses delegation, rather than binding a listener to each DOM node.

Detailed Answer

A SyntheticEvent has the same interface as the native event (preventDefault, stopPropagation, target, etc.) but normalizes quirks across browsers. You always pass a function, not call it: onClick={handleClick}, not onClick={handleClick()} (the latter calls it during render). To pass arguments, wrap in an arrow: onClick={() => handleClick(id)}.

React uses event delegation: instead of one listener per element, it attaches a single listener at the app root and dispatches events through its own synthetic system. This is a performance and consistency win. (Pre-React 17 it delegated at document; React 17 moved it to the root container, which fixed issues with multiple React versions and nested apps.)

Historical note you may be asked about: React used to pool synthetic events (reuse the object and null its fields after the handler), so accessing the event asynchronously required e.persist(). Event pooling was removed in React 17, so this is no longer a concern — but interviewers still ask.

Code Example

function Form() {
  function handleSubmit(e) {
    e.preventDefault();          // synthetic event API
    console.log("submitted");
  }
  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
      {/* pass a reference, not a call */}
      <button onClick={() => console.log("clicked")}>Go</button>
    </form>
  );
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

Two follow-ups recur. First: "Is onClick the same as addEventListener?" — no; it's a synthetic wrapper dispatched via React's delegated root listener, so e.stopPropagation() stops React-tree propagation but a native listener on document may still fire. Second: "Does inline onClick={() => ...} hurt performance by creating a new function each render?" — usually negligible, but it can defeat React.memo on a child, which is when useCallback earns its place. Mentioning that event pooling was removed in 17 signals you keep current.

Q14. Controlled vs uncontrolled inputs — what's the difference?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

A controlled input has its value driven by React state (value={state} + onChange) — React is the single source of truth. An uncontrolled input keeps its own value in the DOM, and you read it when needed via a ref (defaultValue for the initial value). Controlled is the default recommendation; uncontrolled is handy for simple/large forms or file inputs.

Detailed Answer

ControlledUncontrolled
Source of truthReact stateThe DOM node
Read valueDirectly from stateVia a ref, on demand
Set initial valuevaluedefaultValue
Live validation / formattingEasy (you own every keystroke)Harder
Re-renders per keystrokeYesNo

Controlled inputs let you validate, format, disable, or transform on every keystroke because state updates on each change. The cost is a re-render per keystroke (rarely a problem). Uncontrolled inputs are lighter and useful for file inputs (<input type="file"> is always uncontrolled) or when integrating non-React code, but you give up live control.

A subtle gotcha: never switch an input from uncontrolled to controlled mid-life (e.g. value={maybeUndefined}). React warns loudly. Initialize controlled values to "", not undefined.

Code Example

// Controlled — React state is the source of truth
function Controlled() {
  const [email, setEmail] = React.useState("");
  return (
    <input
      value={email}
      onChange={(e) => setEmail(e.target.value)}
    />
  );
}

// Uncontrolled — DOM holds the value, read via ref
function Uncontrolled() {
  const inputRef = React.useRef(null);
  function submit() {
    console.log(inputRef.current.value);
  }
  return <input ref={inputRef} defaultValue="hi" />;
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

Interviewers want to hear you default to controlled but know when uncontrolled is pragmatic. Strong points to raise: file inputs are inherently uncontrolled; large forms with per-keystroke re-renders may favor uncontrolled + a library like React Hook Form (which uses refs/uncontrolled under the hood for performance, then reads on submit). The "undefined → controlled" warning is a great detail to volunteer — it shows you've debugged real forms.

Q15. How do you pass data from a child up to a parent?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

You can't pass data "up" directly — data only flows down. Instead the parent passes a callback function down as a prop, and the child calls it with the data. The parent receives the value in that callback and updates its own state. This is the inverse-flow pattern that keeps data flow one-directional.

Detailed Answer

The parent owns the state and defines a handler like handleSelect(item). It passes onSelect={handleSelect} to the child. When the user interacts, the child invokes props.onSelect(theData). The parent's handler runs, updates state, re-renders, and the new data flows back down as props. Nothing violates one-way flow — the child merely requests a change by calling a function the parent gave it.

This is the foundation of controlled inputs (Q7/Q14), form submission, selection lists, and virtually every interactive component. For deeply nested children where threading callbacks becomes tedious, Context or a reducer can centralize the handler.

Code Example

function ProductList({ products }) {
  const [selected, setSelected] = React.useState(null);
  return (
    <>
      {products.map((p) => (
        // parent hands down a callback
        <ProductRow key={p.id} product={p} onSelect={setSelected} />
      ))}
      <p>Selected: {selected?.name ?? "none"}</p>
    </>
  );
}
