SECTION 1 - CONTROLLED VS UNCONTROLLED

Q1. What is the difference between a controlled and an uncontrolled input, and when would you use each?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

A controlled input keeps its value in React state — you pass value and update it in onChange, so React is the single source of truth. An uncontrolled input keeps its value in the DOM itself; you read it on demand via a ref (or on submit). Controlled gives you instant, reactive access to every keystroke at the cost of a render per keystroke; uncontrolled is cheaper and closer to native HTML but harder to react to live.

Detailed Answer

The distinction is about who owns the value. In a controlled input the value flows down from state and every change flows back up through onChange — a classic unidirectional loop. Because the rendered value always equals state, you can validate, format, mask, disable a submit button, or mirror the value elsewhere in real time.

An uncontrolled input lets the browser hold the value. You give it an initial value with defaultValue and later pull the current value out of the DOM node. This is essentially how a plain HTML form works, and it is what libraries like React Hook Form lean on for performance.

When to reach for each

  • Controlled — when the UI must react to input live: enabling/disabling buttons, live character counts, input masking/formatting, conditional fields, or driving other components from the value.
  • Uncontrolled — simple forms where you only need values at submit time, large forms where per-keystroke re-renders hurt, file inputs (which are always uncontrolled), and when integrating with non-React code.

A key rule: an input must be consistently controlled or uncontrolled across its lifetime. Switching from value={undefined} to a defined value triggers React's warning: "A component is changing an uncontrolled input to be controlled." The fix is to always pass a defined value (e.g. value={name ?? ""}).

Code Example

// Controlled: React state is the source of truth
function ControlledName() {
  const [name, setName] = React.useState("");
  return (
    <input
      value={name}
      onChange={(e) => setName(e.target.value)}
    />
  );
}

// Uncontrolled: the DOM holds the value, read via ref
function UncontrolledName() {
  const inputRef = React.useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null);
  const handleSubmit = (e: React.FormEvent) => {
    e.preventDefault();
    console.log(inputRef.current?.value); // read on demand
  };
  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
      <input defaultValue="" ref={inputRef} />
      <button>Submit</button>
    </form>
  );
}

Project Example

On a checkout page, the credit-card field is controlled so we can apply a "#### #### #### ####" mask and show the card-network logo as the user types. The optional "delivery notes" textarea, by contrast, is uncontrolled — nobody needs to react to it live, so we just read ref.current.value at submit and avoid re-rendering the whole form on each keystroke.

Senior Engineer Perspective

Interviewers use this to see whether you understand the render cost, not just the API. Weak answers say "controlled is the React way, always use it." A senior answer acknowledges that controlled inputs re-render on every keystroke, that React Hook Form deliberately embraces the uncontrolled model to avoid this, and that file inputs cannot be controlled at all. The follow-up trap is the "controlled to uncontrolled" warning — be ready to explain that it comes from passing value={undefined} and is fixed by defaulting to an empty string.

Q2. What is the difference between defaultValue and value (and defaultChecked vs checked)?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

value makes an input controlled — React enforces it on every render. defaultValue only sets the initial value and then lets the DOM take over, making the input uncontrolled. The same pairing exists for checkboxes/radios: checked (controlled) vs defaultChecked (uncontrolled).

Detailed Answer

If you pass value without an onChange, React makes the field read-only and logs a warning, because the value can never change from state. If you pass both value and defaultValue, value wins and defaultValue is ignored. Use defaultValue only when you want the browser to manage the field after seeding it — the typical uncontrolled pattern.

A common real bug: developers want to prefill a form from server data but keep it controlled, and they set defaultValue={user.name}. Because the data arrives asynchronously, the initial render has an empty default, and when data loads the DOM value never updates. The correct controlled approach is value={name} with state seeded from the fetched data (via useEffect or React Hook Form's reset()).

Code Example

// WRONG: async data won't populate an uncontrolled field after mount
<input defaultValue={user?.name} />   // stays blank if user loads later

// RIGHT (controlled): seed state once data arrives
const [name, setName] = React.useState("");
React.useEffect(() => {
  if (user) setName(user.name);
}, [user]);
<input value={name} onChange={(e) => setName(e.target.value)} />

// Checkbox equivalents
<input type="checkbox" defaultChecked />              // uncontrolled
<input type="checkbox" checked={agreed}
       onChange={(e) => setAgreed(e.target.checked)} /> // controlled

Senior Engineer Perspective

The trap here is async prefill. Interviewers love to ask "you set defaultValue from a fetch and it's blank — why?" The answer: defaultValue is only read on the first render, so a value that arrives later is ignored. Mention that React Hook Form solves exactly this with reset(serverData) or the values prop, which resyncs the form when async data lands.

Q3. How do you handle many inputs with a single change handler?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Give each input a name that matches a key in a state object, then use one handler that reads e.target.name and e.target.value and updates the object with a functional setState. This scales to any number of fields without writing a handler per input.

Detailed Answer

Storing all fields in a single object is idiomatic and keeps handlers DRY. Use the functional updater form (prev => ...) so batched updates never read a stale snapshot, and read type so checkboxes contribute a boolean rather than the literal string "on".

Beware nested objects: a shallow spread only copies the top level, so nested fields need a nested spread or a helper like immer. For anything beyond a handful of fields with real validation, prefer a form library — hand-rolling this quickly becomes a maintenance burden.

Code Example

function ProfileForm() {
  const [form, setForm] = React.useState({
    firstName: "",
    email: "",
    subscribe: false,
  });

  const handleChange = (e: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>) => {
    const { name, value, type, checked } = e.target;
    setForm((prev) => ({
      ...prev,
      [name]: type === "checkbox" ? checked : value,
    }));
  };

  return (
    <form>
      <input name="firstName" value={form.firstName} onChange={handleChange} />
      <input name="email" value={form.email} onChange={handleChange} />
      <input name="subscribe" type="checkbox"
             checked={form.subscribe} onChange={handleChange} />
    </form>
  );
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

The computed-key pattern [name]: value is the crux — many candidates hardcode a setter per field. Follow-ups probe edge cases: checkboxes (use checked, not value), multi-selects (read selectedOptions), and number inputs (e.target.value is always a string — coerce it). Mentioning that every keystroke re-renders the whole form here is a good segue into performance and why RHF exists.

SECTION 2 - PERFORMANCE OF CONTROLLED FORMS

Q4. Why do controlled forms re-render on every keystroke, and how do you mitigate it?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

Because each keystroke calls setState, and a state change re-renders the component that owns the state — plus its children unless memoized. For small forms this is invisible; for large forms or expensive children it causes jank. Mitigate by isolating state, memoizing children, moving to uncontrolled inputs, or using React Hook Form, which subscribes to fields instead of re-rendering the whole tree.

Detailed Answer

The re-render itself is usually cheap — React diffing a few inputs is fast. The problem is when the form component also renders heavy children (a rich text editor, a big list, a chart) that re-run their render on every character. Diagnose with the React DevTools Profiler before optimizing.

Mitigation ladder (cheapest first)

  • Isolate state — push each input's state down into its own small component so only that field re-renders (state colocation).
  • Memoize expensive siblings — wrap heavy children in React.memo so they skip renders when their props are unchanged.
  • Go uncontrolled — read values via refs at submit; zero re-renders while typing.
  • Use React Hook Form — it registers inputs as uncontrolled and only re-renders components that subscribe to a given field.
  • Debounce derived work — keep the input controlled but debounce the expensive side effect (search, validation), not the keystroke itself.

Code Example

// State colocation: only SearchBox re-renders on each keystroke,
// not the expensive <HugeResultsList /> sibling.
function Page() {
  return (
    <>
      <SearchBox />
      <HugeResultsList />   {/* unaffected by typing in SearchBox */}
    </>
  );
}

function SearchBox() {
  const [q, setQ] = React.useState("");
  return <input value={q} onChange={(e) => setQ(e.target.value)} />;
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

Junior answers jump straight to "memoize everything." A senior first says "measure it — most forms don't need this." Then they distinguish the render (cheap) from expensive children (the real cost) and explain state colocation as the primary lever. Bonus points for noting that React 19's compiler auto-memoizes many of these cases, reducing the need for manual memo/useCallback, and that RHF's whole selling point is sidestepping this problem via uncontrolled registration.

SECTION 3 - FORM LIBRARIES

Q5. Why is React Hook Form so popular, and how does register work?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

React Hook Form (RHF) is popular because it keeps inputs uncontrolled — it registers each field with a ref and reads values from the DOM — so typing doesn't re-render the form. register(name) returns the ref, name, onChange, and onBlur props you spread onto an input, wiring it into the form with almost no boilerplate.

Detailed Answer

RHF wins on three axes: performance (uncontrolled inputs, subscription-based re-renders), ergonomics (minimal boilerplate, built-in validation, first-class TypeScript inference), and bundle size (small, zero dependencies). You call useForm() once to get register, handleSubmit, formState, reset, watch, setValue, and control.

register("email", rules) attaches a ref to the input and tracks it internally. On submit, handleSubmit collects values from the registered refs, runs validation, and calls your callback with typed data only if validation passes. Because reads come from the DOM, RHF avoids the per-keystroke render churn that plagues large controlled forms.

The trade-off: native inputs work by spreading register, but custom/third-party components that don't forward a ref must be wired through Controller or useController (Q6). Also, watch() does subscribe to changes and will re-render — use it deliberately.

Code Example

import { useForm } from "react-hook-form";

type FormValues = { email: string; password: string };

function LoginForm() {
  const {
    register,
    handleSubmit,
    formState: { errors, isSubmitting },
  } = useForm<FormValues>();

  const onSubmit = async (data: FormValues) => {
    await api.login(data); // called only if validation passes
  };

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit(onSubmit)}>
      <input
        {...register("email", {
          required: "Email is required",
          pattern: { value: /^\S+@\S+$/, message: "Invalid email" },
        })}
      />
      {errors.email && <span role="alert">{errors.email.message}</span>}

      <input type="password" {...register("password", { required: true })} />

      <button disabled={isSubmitting}>Log in</button>
    </form>
  );
}

Project Example

We migrated a 40-field onboarding form from hand-rolled useState to RHF. The old version re-rendered the entire step on every keystroke and stuttered on low-end devices; after the migration, typing caused zero form re-renders, validation was declarative, and we deleted roughly 300 lines of change-handler boilerplate.

Senior Engineer Perspective

Interviewers want to hear "uncontrolled by default" — that single phrase signals you understand why RHF is fast, not just that it is. Follow-ups: how does RHF handle a component that hides its ref? (Controller). Does watch() hurt performance? (Yes — it subscribes; prefer useWatch scoped to a subtree). How do you prefill from the server? (reset(data) or the values prop, not defaultValues after mount).

Q6. What is the difference between useForm, Controller, and useController?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

useForm is the top-level hook that creates the form instance. Controller is a render-prop wrapper you use to connect controlled third-party components (MUI, Ant Design, react-select) that don't expose a ref for register. useController is the hook version of Controller for building your own reusable controlled field components.

Detailed Answer

register works only when you can spread its props (including a ref) directly onto a native input. Many UI-library components are controlled and expect value/onChange instead — they don't forward a DOM ref. That's where Controller comes in: it bridges RHF's uncontrolled core to a controlled component by giving you a field object (value, onChange, onBlur, ref, name) to hand to the component.

useController is the same bridge as a hook, ideal when you're authoring a design-system input wrapper (e.g. <TextField>) so consumers can just drop it into any RHF form. Use Controller/useController only when necessary — every controlled field re-renders on change, so keep native inputs on plain register.

Code Example

import { useForm, Controller } from "react-hook-form";
import Select from "react-select";

function TagPicker() {
  const { control, handleSubmit } = useForm<{ tags: Option[] }>();

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit(console.log)}>
      <Controller
        name="tags"
        control={control}
        rules={{ required: "Pick at least one tag" }}
        render={({ field, fieldState }) => (
          <>
            <Select {...field} isMulti options={options} />
            {fieldState.error && <span>{fieldState.error.message}</span>}
          </>
        )}
      />
    </form>
  );
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

The tell here is knowing why Controller exists: register needs a forwarded ref, and most controlled UI components don't give you one. If a candidate wraps every field in Controller, that's a smell — it re-introduces the per-render cost RHF avoids. Senior answer: native inputs via register, controlled third-party components via Controller/useController, and prefer building one reusable useController-based wrapper over scattering render props everywhere.

Q7. How does Formik compare to React Hook Form?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Formik was the dominant form library before RHF. It is controlled by default — form state lives in Formik's React state, so every keystroke re-renders the form — which makes large forms slower. RHF is uncontrolled by default, smaller, and generally faster. For new projects most teams now choose RHF; Formik remains common in legacy codebases and is largely in maintenance mode.

Detailed Answer

AspectFormikReact Hook Form
ModelControlled (state in React)Uncontrolled (refs / DOM)
Re-renders on keystrokeWhole form re-rendersIsolated / minimal
Bundle sizeLargerSmaller, zero deps
ValidationYup (built-in support), customAny schema via resolver, built-in rules
API styleComponents / render props (<Field>, <Formik>)Hooks (useForm)
TypeScriptWorkableExcellent inference
MomentumMaintenance modeActively developed, de facto standard

Formik's component-driven API (<Formik>, <Field>, <ErrorMessage>) reads nicely for small forms and pairs cleanly with Yup. But its controlled architecture is the reason RHF overtook it: on a large form, Formik's per-keystroke re-render becomes the bottleneck exactly where you feel it most.

Senior Engineer Perspective

Don't trash Formik — that reads as trend-chasing. The mature take: "Formik is fine and I'd keep it in an existing app; for greenfield I default to RHF for its uncontrolled model, smaller bundle, and TS inference." Being able to name the concrete architectural difference (controlled vs uncontrolled) rather than vague "RHF is better" is what separates the answers.

SECTION 4 - VALIDATION

Q8. How do you do schema validation with Zod or Yup, and what is the resolver pattern?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

You define the form's shape and rules once as a schema (Zod or Yup), then plug it into the form library through a resolver — a small adapter that runs the schema and maps its errors into the library's error format. With Zod you also get a TypeScript type for free via z.infer, so the schema is the single source of truth for both runtime validation and static types.

Detailed Answer

Inline per-field rules (RHF's required, pattern) work but scatter validation logic and duplicate it against your types. A schema centralizes rules, supports cross-field constraints (e.g. "confirm password matches password"), and can be shared with the backend. RHF exposes this via @hookform/resolvers, which offers zodResolver, yupResolver, and adapters for Joi, Valibot, and others.

Zod vs Yup

  • Zod — TypeScript-first; the schema infers the type (z.infer<typeof schema>), so types and validation can never drift. Now the common default.
  • Yup — older, chainable API, deeply integrated with Formik historically; TypeScript support is decent but less seamless than Zod's inference.

The big payoff of Zod is that the schema drives the type. You write one signupSchema, derive type SignupForm = z.infer<typeof signupSchema>, and pass both into useForm — no manual interface to keep in sync.

Code Example

import { z } from "zod";
import { useForm } from "react-hook-form";
import { zodResolver } from "@hookform/resolvers/zod";

const signupSchema = z
  .object({
    email: z.string().email("Enter a valid email"),
    password: z.string().min(8, "At least 8 characters"),
    confirm: z.string(),
  })
  .refine((d) => d.password === d.confirm, {
    message: "Passwords must match",
    path: ["confirm"], // attach the error to the confirm field
  });

type SignupForm = z.infer<typeof signupSchema>;

function Signup() {
  const {
    register,
    handleSubmit,
    formState: { errors },
  } = useForm<SignupForm>({ resolver: zodResolver(signupSchema) });

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit((data) => api.signup(data))}>
      <input {...register("email")} />
      {errors.email && <span role="alert">{errors.email.message}</span>}
      <input type="password" {...register("password")} />
      <input type="password" {...register("confirm")} />
      {errors.confirm && <span role="alert">{errors.confirm.message}</span>}
      <button>Create account</button>
    </form>
  );
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

The phrase interviewers listen for is "single source of truth." A senior answer highlights that Zod's z.infer unifies runtime validation and static types, and that the same schema can be reused on the server (e.g. in a Next.js route handler) so client and server agree on validity. Follow-up: cross-field validation — show you know .refine() with a path to attach the error to the right field. Know what a resolver actually is: an adapter mapping schema errors to formState.errors.

Q9. How do you handle asynchronous validation, such as checking username availability?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Sync validation (format, length, required) runs instantly and locally. Async validation calls a server — e.g. "is this username taken?" — so it must be debounced, must handle out-of-order responses, and must show a pending state. In RHF you can return a Promise from a field's validate function, or run the check separately and set an error with setError.

Detailed Answer

Three problems define async validation quality:

  • Too many requests — validating on every keystroke hammers the server. Debounce (250–500ms) so you only check after the user pauses.
  • Race conditions — a slow response for "jo" can land after "john" and show the wrong result. Cancel stale requests (AbortController) or track a request id and ignore outdated ones. TanStack Query handles this for you if you validate through a query.
  • Feedback — show a spinner while checking and never block submit on an in-flight check without indicating it.

RHF supports a validate function that returns a Promise; it awaits the result and treats a returned string as the error message. For richer UX (debounce + spinner) many teams run the availability check as a separate debounced effect/query and call setError/clearErrors on the field.

Code Example

// Async field validation in React Hook Form
<input
  {...register("username", {
    required: "Username required",
    validate: async (value) => {
      const res = await fetch(`/api/username-available?u=${value}`);
      const { available } = await res.json();
      return available || "That username is taken";
    },
  })}
/>

// For debounce + race safety, prefer a query-based check:
const { data } = useQuery({
  queryKey: ["username", debouncedValue],
  queryFn: ({ signal }) => checkUsername(debouncedValue, signal), // aborts stale
  enabled: debouncedValue.length > 2,
});
// TanStack Query cancels superseded requests and caches results.

Senior Engineer Perspective

The differentiator is naming the race condition and its fix (AbortController / request id / a query cache), not just "debounce it." Interviewers also probe validation timing: async checks should typically fire on blur or after a debounce, not on every keystroke, and you should re-check server-side on submit because client validation is only UX — never trust it for correctness or security.

Q10. How do you debounce validation or expensive input-driven work?

ROI: ★★★☆☆ Frequency: Medium

Short Answer

Keep the input responsive (update state on every keystroke) but delay the expensive effect — validation, search, autosave — until the user pauses. Implement with a debounced value via useEffect + setTimeout cleanup, a reusable useDebouncedValue hook, or, in React 18+, useDeferredValue for render-deferral.

Detailed Answer

Debouncing separates "what the user sees" (instant) from "what the system does" (delayed). Never debounce the controlled value itself — that makes the input feel laggy. Instead debounce the derived value that feeds the effect.

Two modern tools: useDeferredValue lets React keep the input snappy while re-rendering an expensive dependent list at lower priority (no timer, concurrent-scheduling based). A classic timer-based debounce is still right for network calls, where you genuinely want to skip intermediate requests.

Code Example

function useDebouncedValue<T>(value: T, delay = 400): T {
  const [debounced, setDebounced] = React.useState(value);
  React.useEffect(() => {
    const id = setTimeout(() => setDebounced(value), delay);
    return () => clearTimeout(id); // cancel on the next keystroke
  }, [value, delay]);
  return debounced;
}

function Search() {
  const [q, setQ] = React.useState("");
  const debouncedQ = useDebouncedValue(q, 400);

  React.useEffect(() => {
    if (debouncedQ) runSearch(debouncedQ); // fires only after a pause
  }, [debouncedQ]);

  return <input value={q} onChange={(e) => setQ(e.target.value)} />;
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

The key insight is what you debounce: the side effect, not the input. Candidates who debounce the value make the field janky. Bonus depth: contrast timer-based debounce (best for network throttling) with useDeferredValue (best for keeping renders responsive), and note the cleanup function in useEffect is what actually cancels the pending timer.

Q11. How do you display validation errors accessibly?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Associate the error message with its input using aria-describedby, mark the invalid field with aria-invalid="true", and put the message in a live region (role="alert" or aria-live) so screen readers announce it. Never signal errors with color alone, and move focus to the first invalid field on submit.

Detailed Answer

A visually shown error is invisible to a screen-reader user unless it's programmatically linked. The pattern:

  • Every input has a real <label> tied by htmlFor/id.
  • The error element has an id; the input references it with aria-describedby.
  • aria-invalid={!!error} exposes the invalid state to assistive tech.
  • The error container uses role="alert" (assertive) or aria-live="polite" so it's announced when it appears.
  • On a failed submit, move focus to the first error (RHF's setFocus or the shouldFocusError option does this).

Also validate at the right time: showing errors on every keystroke before the user finishes typing is hostile. A good default is validate on blur / on submit, then re-validate on change once a field already has an error (RHF: mode: "onTouched" with reValidateMode: "onChange").

Code Example

<label htmlFor="email">Email</label>
<input
  id="email"
  aria-invalid={errors.email ? "true" : "false"}
  aria-describedby={errors.email ? "email-error" : undefined}
  {...register("email")}
/>
{errors.email && (
  <p id="email-error" role="alert">
    {errors.email.message}
  </p>
)}

Senior Engineer Perspective

Accessibility is an easy way to stand out — most candidates render {error && <span>...</span>} and stop. A senior answer names aria-invalid, aria-describedby, and a live region, and adds the UX nuance of validation timing (onBlur/onSubmit, not aggressive onChange) plus focusing the first invalid field on submit. Mention that color-only error signaling fails WCAG.

SECTION 5 - ADVANCED PATTERNS & SUBMIT UX

Q12. How do you build dynamic forms with field arrays (add/remove rows)?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Model the repeating section as an array in form state and render a row per item, each field namespaced by index (e.g. items.0.name). React Hook Form's useFieldArray gives you fields, append, remove, and move, and — crucially — a stable field.id to use as the React key so rows don't get mismatched on reorder.

Detailed Answer

Field arrays power invoices with line items, questionnaires, tag lists, and similar. The two hazards are (1) keys — never key rows by array index, because inserting/removing rows shifts indices and corrupts input state; use the library-provided stable id — and (2) validation, which the schema handles per element via z.array(itemSchema).

Hand-rolling this with useState is possible (setItems(prev => [...prev, blank])), but you must manage stable keys yourself. useFieldArray removes that footgun and integrates with RHF's validation and dirty-tracking.

Code Example

import { useForm, useFieldArray } from "react-hook-form";

function InvoiceForm() {
  const { register, control, handleSubmit } = useForm<{
    items: { name: string; qty: number }[];
  }>({ defaultValues: { items: [{ name: "", qty: 1 }] } });

  const { fields, append, remove } = useFieldArray({ control, name: "items" });

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit(console.log)}>
      {fields.map((field, index) => (
        <div key={field.id}>  {/* stable id, NOT index */}
          <input {...register(`items.${index}.name`)} />
          <input type="number" {...register(`items.${index}.qty`)} />
          <button type="button" onClick={() => remove(index)}>Remove</button>
        </div>
      ))}
      <button type="button" onClick={() => append({ name: "", qty: 1 })}>
        Add item
      </button>
    </form>
  );
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

The interviewer is checking whether you know the React key rule under mutation. Using the array index as key here is the classic bug — remove row 1 and the value from row 2 appears to "stick" on the wrong row. Say explicitly: use field.id. Follow-up depth: nested field arrays, and the fact that append/remove mutate form state without re-rendering unrelated fields.

Q13. How do you build a multi-step form wizard, and where should the state live?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Keep all form state in one place that outlives the individual steps — a single form instance or a shared store — and swap which step's fields are visible. Validate per step before advancing. Do not unmount a step and lose its data; either mount one form spanning all steps or persist each step's values into a parent/store as the user moves forward.

Detailed Answer

The core question is state ownership. Three common approaches:

  • Single RHF form across all steps — one useForm in a parent; each step renders a slice of the fields. State survives step changes automatically. Validate the current step's fields with trigger(["fieldA", "fieldB"]) before advancing.
  • Per-step form + lift on next — each step is its own form; on "Next" you validate and merge that step's values into parent state (or a context/Zustand store). Cleaner isolation, more plumbing.
  • Shared store (Zustand/context) — good when steps are far apart in the tree or you need to persist to localStorage for resume-later.

Persistence matters: wizards are long, so autosaving to localStorage or the server lets users resume. Also expose progress and allow going back without data loss — which is exactly why the state must live above the steps.

Code Example

function Wizard() {
  const methods = useForm<WizardData>({ defaultValues });
  const [step, setStep] = React.useState(0);

  const next = async () => {
    // validate only the current step's fields before advancing
    const fieldsByStep = [["name", "email"], ["address"], ["payment"]];
    const ok = await methods.trigger(fieldsByStep[step]);
    if (ok) setStep((s) => s + 1);
  };

  return (
    <FormProvider {...methods}>
      {step === 0 && <StepAccount />}
      {step === 1 && <StepAddress />}
      {step === 2 && <StepPayment />}
      {step > 0 && <button onClick={() => setStep((s) => s - 1)}>Back</button>}
      {step < 2
        ? <button onClick={next}>Next</button>
        : <button onClick={methods.handleSubmit(submitAll)}>Finish</button>}
    </FormProvider>
  );
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

"Where does the state live?" is the whole question. The junior mistake is a separate useState per step that gets wiped when the step unmounts. Senior answer: one form instance (or store) above the steps, per-step validation via trigger, and FormProvider/useFormContext so nested steps read the same form without prop drilling. Bonus: mention resume-later persistence and URL-synced step so refresh/back-button behave.

Q14. How do you handle file uploads in a React form?

ROI: ★★★☆☆ Frequency: Medium

Short Answer

File inputs are always uncontrolled — you cannot set a file input's value from React for security reasons, so you read e.target.files (or a ref) instead. Send the file with FormData and multipart/form-data, validate type/size on the client for UX, and always re-validate on the server. Track upload progress via XMLHttpRequest or a library, since fetch doesn't expose upload progress natively.

Detailed Answer

Key facts interviewers probe:

  • You can't do <input type="file" value={...}> — the browser blocks programmatic setting of the selected file, so file inputs are inherently uncontrolled. Read from files.
  • Use FormData and let the browser set the multipart/form-data boundary — do not manually set the Content-Type header.
  • Client-side checks (accepted extensions, max size, image dimensions via a preview) improve UX but are not security; the server must enforce limits.
  • For progress bars use XMLHttpRequest's upload.onprogress or a lib like axios; native fetch lacks upload progress.
  • Show a preview with URL.createObjectURL and revoke it on cleanup to avoid leaks.

In RHF, register the file input and read files in the submit handler, or validate size/type via a validate function.

Code Example

function AvatarUpload() {
  const { register, handleSubmit } = useForm<{ avatar: FileList }>();

  const onSubmit = async (data: { avatar: FileList }) => {
    const file = data.avatar[0];
    const body = new FormData();
    body.append("avatar", file);
    // Do NOT set Content-Type manually; the browser adds the boundary.
    await fetch("/api/upload", { method: "POST", body });
  };

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit(onSubmit)}>
      <input
        type="file"
        accept="image/*"
        {...register("avatar", {
          validate: (list) =>
            !list?.[0] || list[0].size <= 2_000_000 || "Max 2 MB",
        })}
      />
      <button>Upload</button>
    </form>
  );
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

The one-line tell: "file inputs can't be controlled." If a candidate tries to bind value to a file input, that's a red flag. Follow-ups drill into FormData and the Content-Type mistake, upload progress (fetch can't do it — XHR can), and object-URL cleanup. Senior candidates also mention large-file strategies: presigned S3 URLs / direct-to-storage uploads and chunked/resumable uploads instead of routing big files through the app server.

Q15. How do you handle submit UX — loading state, disabling, and optimistic updates?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Track a submitting flag (RHF gives you formState.isSubmitting), disable the submit button and show a spinner while the request is in flight to prevent double submits, and re-enable on completion. For snappy UX you can apply an optimistic update — reflect the change in the UI immediately and roll back if the request fails.

Detailed Answer

Robust submit handling covers several concerns:

  • Prevent double submission — disable the button (or guard on isSubmitting) so an impatient user can't fire two requests.
  • Feedback — spinner/label change ("Saving…"), and on failure surface a server error, ideally mapped back onto fields via setError for 422-style validation responses.
  • Success — reset the form (reset()), navigate, or show a toast. Reset also clears the dirty state.
  • Optimistic update — update local/cache state before the server confirms; on error, roll back. TanStack Query's onMutate/onError/onSettled, or React 19's useOptimistic, standardize this.

Only make writes optimistic when failure is rare and rollback is cheap and unsurprising (e.g. toggling a like). For a payment, wait for confirmation.

Code Example

const {
  register,
  handleSubmit,
  setError,
  formState: { isSubmitting },
} = useForm<FormValues>();

const onSubmit = async (data: FormValues) => {
  try {
    await api.save(data);          // isSubmitting is true while this awaits
  } catch (err) {
    // Map a 422 field error back onto the form
    setError("email", { message: "Email already in use" });
  }
};

<form onSubmit={handleSubmit(onSubmit)}>
  {/* fields... */}
  <button disabled={isSubmitting}>
    {isSubmitting ? "Saving…" : "Save"}
  </button>
</form>

Senior Engineer Perspective

Candidates often forget the double-submit guard entirely. Emphasize deriving the loading state from isSubmitting rather than a hand-rolled boolean that can desync. Follow-up: how do you show server-side validation errors? (setError, mapping a 422 payload to fields). And know when not to be optimistic — payments and irreversible actions should wait for the server.

Q16. What are React 19 form actions, useActionState, and useFormStatus?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

React 19 lets you pass a function to a <form action={...}>. The action receives the submitted FormData, can be async, and integrates with pending/error state. useActionState wraps an action to expose its return value, an isPending flag, and a bound action. useFormStatus lets a nested component (like a submit button) read the parent form's pending state without prop drilling. With Server Components, actions can be Server Actions that run on the server.

Detailed Answer

Form actions are React's built-in answer to the boilerplate of "manage isSubmitting, call the API, handle the result." You attach a function to a form's action; React calls it with the FormData on submit, manages pending state, and resets uncontrolled fields on success.

  • useActionState(fn, initialState) — returns [state, formAction, isPending]. state is whatever the action returns (great for validation errors or messages), formAction is what you pass to <form action>, and isPending replaces manual submitting flags.
  • useFormStatus() — must be called from a component rendered inside the form; returns { pending, data, method }. Perfect for a reusable <SubmitButton> that disables itself during submission without the parent passing props down.
  • Server Actions (Next.js / RSC) — an action marked "use server" runs on the server; the form works even before hydration (progressive enhancement).

These are additive, not a replacement for React Hook Form. RHF still shines for complex client-side validation, field arrays, and rich interactivity; form actions shine for progressively-enhanced, server-driven mutations with minimal client code.

Code Example

"use client";
import { useActionState } from "react";
import { useFormStatus } from "react-dom";

type State = { error?: string };

async function subscribe(_prev: State, formData: FormData): Promise<State> {
  const email = formData.get("email") as string;
  if (!email.includes("@")) return { error: "Invalid email" };
  await api.subscribe(email);
  return {};
}

function SubmitButton() {
  const { pending } = useFormStatus();           // reads parent form status
  return <button disabled={pending}>{pending ? "…" : "Subscribe"}</button>;
}

export function NewsletterForm() {
  const [state, formAction, isPending] = useActionState(subscribe, {});
  return (
    <form action={formAction}>
      <input name="email" />
      {state.error && <p role="alert">{state.error}</p>}
      <SubmitButton />
    </form>
  );
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

Being current here signals you track the ecosystem. Key nuances: useFormStatus only works in a child of the form (not the same component that renders the form) — a classic gotcha. useActionState was renamed from the experimental useFormState, and it lives in react while useFormStatus lives in react-dom. The mature framing: form actions don't replace RHF/Zod for heavy client forms — they excel at progressively-enhanced server mutations. Know when each fits.

12 - REACT ROUTER & NAVIGATION

Target Audience: Frontend / React Engineer (3–6 Years) Goal: Not just answer questions, but survive follow-up grilling from experienced interviewers.

TOP HIGHEST-ROI QUESTIONS IN THIS CHAPTER

  1. How does client-side routing differ from server-side routing in an SPA?
  2. How do you set up React Router v6+ (Routes/Route vs createBrowserRouter)?
  3. How do route params work, and how do you read them with useParams?
  4. What are nested routes and how does Outlet render children?
  5. What is an index route and when do you need one?
  6. What is the difference between Link, NavLink, and useNavigate?
  7. How do you perform programmatic navigation and redirects?
  8. How do you read and update query params with useSearchParams?
  9. How do you build a protected/guarded route with an auth redirect?
  10. What are layout routes and how do they reduce duplication?
  11. How do you lazy-load routes for code splitting?
  12. What are loaders and actions in the v6.4+ data router?
  13. How do errorElement and useRouteError handle route-level errors?
  14. How do you handle scroll restoration and 404s?
  15. How does React Router compare with Next.js file-based routing?

SECTION 1 - ROUTING BASICS

Q1. How does client-side routing differ from server-side routing in a single-page app?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

With server-side routing, every URL change triggers a full HTTP request and the server returns a brand-new HTML document. With client-side routing, JavaScript intercepts navigation, updates the URL via the History API (pushState), and swaps the rendered component tree without a full page reload. React Router is a client-side router: one HTML shell is loaded once, then routing happens in the browser.

Detailed Answer

A traditional multi-page app maps each URL to a document on the server. Clicking a link means: request → server renders HTML → browser tears down the current page and paints a new one. State is lost between navigations, and the network round-trip is visible as a flash/reload.

A single-page app loads one shell document plus a JS bundle. React Router registers a listener on the History API and on link clicks. When you navigate, it:

  • Prevents the browser's default full-page navigation.
  • Calls history.pushState to change the URL bar without a request.
  • Matches the new URL against your route config and renders the matching component.

The popstate event lets the router respond to the browser's Back/Forward buttons so navigation still feels native. This gives instant transitions and preserves in-memory state (e.g. a form, a cart), at the cost of a larger initial JS payload and the need for SEO/first-paint strategies like SSR.

BrowserRouter vs HashRouter

RouterURL formWhen to use
BrowserRouter/users/42Default. Needs server configured to serve index.html for all paths (SPA fallback).
HashRouter/#/users/42Static hosting with no server rewrite control; the part after # is never sent to the server.

Code Example

// The server MUST fall back to index.html for unknown paths,
// otherwise a hard refresh on /users/42 returns a 404.

// Example: Vite / Express SPA fallback
app.get("*", (req, res) => {
  res.sendFile(path.join(__dirname, "dist", "index.html"));
});

// vercel.json rewrite for an SPA
{
  "rewrites": [{ "source": "/(.*)", "destination": "/index.html" }]
}

Project Example

In a dashboard app, moving between /overview and /reports feels instant and keeps the sidebar mounted. The classic bug: it works in dev but a production refresh on a deep link 404s — because the static host wasn't configured with the SPA fallback rewrite.

Senior Engineer Perspective

The interviewer wants to hear the History API named explicitly and the SPA-fallback gotcha. A strong answer also notes the trade-offs client routing forces: SEO and first-contentful-paint suffer because the initial HTML is empty, which is exactly why frameworks like Next.js and Remix add SSR/streaming on top of a router. Mention that pushState vs replaceState controls whether an entry is added to the history stack — relevant for redirects.

Q2. How do you set up React Router v6+ — Routes/Route vs createBrowserRouter?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

There are two idioms. The classic JSX approach wraps the app in <BrowserRouter> and declares <Routes> with nested <Route> elements. The newer data router (v6.4+) uses createBrowserRouter with a route-object array and a <RouterProvider>, which unlocks loaders, actions, and errorElement. New apps should prefer the data router.

Detailed Answer

Both describe the same route tree; the difference is what capabilities you get. <Routes>/<Route> is purely declarative rendering. The data router lets React Router own data fetching and mutations before a component renders, which is why loaders/actions only exist there.

Feature<BrowserRouter> + <Routes>createBrowserRouter
Loaders / actionsNoYes
errorElement + useRouteErrorNoYes
Route config shapeJSX elementsPlain objects (or JSX via helper)
Best forSimple/legacy appsNew apps, data-driven routing

Code Example

// --- Classic JSX approach ---
import { BrowserRouter, Routes, Route } from "react-router-dom";

function App() {
  return (
    <BrowserRouter>
      <Routes>
        <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
        <Route path="/users/:id" element={<UserPage />} />
      </Routes>
    </BrowserRouter>
  );
}

// --- Data router (v6.4+, recommended) ---
import { createBrowserRouter, RouterProvider } from "react-router-dom";

const router = createBrowserRouter([
  { path: "/", element: <Home /> },
  {
    path: "/users/:id",
    element: <UserPage />,
    loader: async ({ params }) => fetchUser(params.id),
    errorElement: <RouteError />,
  },
]);

export default function App() {
  return <RouterProvider router={router} />;
}

Project Example

Migrating an admin panel from <Routes> to createBrowserRouter let us move per-page fetches into loaders, so the page component received ready data via useLoaderData and we deleted a pile of in-component useEffect + loading-flag boilerplate.

Senior Engineer Perspective

Interviewers probe whether you know why the data router exists, not just that it does. Key line: loaders/actions/errorElement are only available under createBrowserRouter/RouterProvider because the router needs to control the render lifecycle to fetch before rendering and to catch thrown responses. Note also that React Router 7 merges Remix, so the data router idiom is the future direction — a good detail to drop.

Q3. How do route params work, and how do you read them with useParams?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

A colon segment in a path (/users/:id) is a dynamic param. React Router matches any value in that position and exposes it via the useParams() hook as a string keyed by the param name. Params are always strings, so coerce numbers yourself.

Detailed Answer

You can have multiple params (/org/:orgId/users/:userId) and optional params in v6.4+ using a trailing ? (/files/:name?). A * segment is a "splat"/catch-all that captures the rest of the path, useful for nested file-tree style routes and 404s.

Because every param is a string, validate and convert. A common defect is passing a string id where an API or numeric comparison expects a number.

Code Example

import { useParams } from "react-router-dom";

// Route: <Route path="/users/:id" element={<UserPage />} />
function UserPage() {
  const { id } = useParams();          // id: string | undefined
  const userId = Number(id);
  if (Number.isNaN(userId)) return <NotFound />;
  // ...fetch by userId
}

// TypeScript: type the params
const { orgId, userId } = useParams<{ orgId: string; userId: string }>();

// Splat / catch-all
// <Route path="/docs/*" element={<Docs />} />
// useParams()["*"] holds the remaining path segment

Senior Engineer Perspective

The trap here is the "params are strings" gotcha and forgetting that useParams returns string | undefined in TypeScript even when the route guarantees the param — because the type can't know which route rendered the component. Seniors validate/parse and handle the malformed-id case rather than trusting the URL. Mention that changing only the param (e.g. /users/1 → /users/2) reuses the same component instance, so data-fetching effects must key on the param or you'll show stale data.

SECTION 2 - DYNAMIC & NESTED ROUTES

Q4. What are nested routes and how does Outlet render child routes?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

Nested routes let a parent route render shared UI while a child route fills a placeholder. The parent component renders <Outlet />, and React Router substitutes the matched child route's element there. This composes URLs and UI together: /dashboard renders the dashboard layout, /dashboard/settings renders that layout with the settings panel in the outlet.

Detailed Answer

Outlet is the nested-routing equivalent of children. The parent stays mounted across child navigations, so shared state (open sidebar, tab selection) persists. Child paths are relative — a child path="settings" under path="/dashboard" resolves to /dashboard/settings. Deeply nested trees can chain outlets at each level.

Code Example

import { Outlet } from "react-router-dom";

function DashboardLayout() {
  return (
    <div className="dashboard">
      <Sidebar />
      <main>
        <Outlet />   {/* child route renders here */}
      </main>
    </div>
  );
}

const router = createBrowserRouter([
  {
    path: "/dashboard",
    element: <DashboardLayout />,
    children: [
      { index: true, element: <Overview /> },       // /dashboard
      { path: "settings", element: <Settings /> },   // /dashboard/settings
      { path: "users/:id", element: <UserDetail /> }, // /dashboard/users/42
    ],
  },
]);

Project Example

A settings area with a persistent left-nav (Profile / Billing / Security) is a textbook nested-route case: one SettingsLayout with an <Outlet />, and each tab is a child route. The nav highlight and scroll position of the layout survive tab switches.

Senior Engineer Perspective

A frequent mistake is forgetting the <Outlet /> — the child route matches but nothing renders. Another is using absolute paths for children (leading slash), which breaks the nesting. Seniors emphasise that the parent persisting across child navigations is the whole point: it's how you avoid re-mounting expensive layout shells and losing state.

Q5. What is an index route and when do you need one?

ROI: ★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

An index route is the default child rendered into a parent's <Outlet /> when the URL matches the parent exactly with no further segment. You declare it with index: true (or <Route index />) instead of a path. It answers "what shows at /dashboard itself?"

Detailed Answer

Without an index route, visiting the parent path renders the layout with an empty outlet. The index route fills that gap. It has no path of its own — it shares the parent's URL. You cannot give an index route a path; that's a common syntax error.

Code Example

<Route path="/dashboard" element={<DashboardLayout />}>
  <Route index element={<Overview />} />        {/* /dashboard */}
  <Route path="reports" element={<Reports />} /> {/* /dashboard/reports */}
</Route>

Senior Engineer Perspective

Interviewers use this to check you understand outlet defaults. Contrast the index route with a redirect: some teams redirect /dashboard → /dashboard/overview using <Navigate> instead of an index route. Both work; the index route keeps the canonical URL clean, while the redirect makes the landing tab explicit in the URL.

SECTION 3 - NAVIGATION

Q6. What is the difference between Link, NavLink, and useNavigate?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

Link renders an accessible anchor that does client-side navigation on click. NavLink is a Link that knows whether it points to the active route, so you can style the current nav item. useNavigate returns an imperative function to navigate from code (after a submit, on a timer, in an effect).

Detailed Answer

Prefer Link/NavLink for anything a user clicks: they render a real <a href>, so middle-click/open-in-new-tab, right-click, and screen readers all work. useNavigate is for programmatic transitions where there's no natural anchor. Never fake navigation with an onClick on a div — you lose accessibility and SEO.

NavLink exposes an isActive (and isPending in the data router) flag through a render-prop-style className/style function.

Code Example

import { Link, NavLink, useNavigate } from "react-router-dom";

// Simple link
<Link to="/users/42">View user</Link>

// Active-aware nav item
<NavLink
  to="/reports"
  className={({ isActive }) => (isActive ? "tab tab--active" : "tab")}
>
  Reports
</NavLink>

// Programmatic navigation after an action
function LoginForm() {
  const navigate = useNavigate();
  async function onSubmit(data) {
    await login(data);
    navigate("/dashboard", { replace: true }); // no back-to-login
  }
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

The accessibility point separates seniors: Link renders a semantic anchor, so don't reinvent it with click handlers. Follow-up traps: navigate(-1) for back, and the { replace: true } option to avoid trapping users in a back-button loop after redirects (e.g. after login or a successful form submit). Mention that NavLink matches by prefix for nested paths unless you pass end, a classic "why is my Home tab always active?" bug.

Q7. How do you perform programmatic navigation and redirects?

ROI: ★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

In components, call the function from useNavigate(): navigate("/path"), navigate(-1) to go back, or navigate(to, { replace: true, state }). Declaratively you render <Navigate to="/login" replace />. In loaders/actions you throw or return redirect("/login"), which is the correct place for auth redirects in the data router.

Detailed Answer

  • useNavigate — imperative, for event handlers and effects.
  • <Navigate> — declarative, render it conditionally to redirect during render.
  • redirect() — for loaders/actions; returns a Response the router honours before rendering.

Use replace to overwrite the current history entry instead of pushing a new one — essential so the Back button doesn't return the user to a page they were redirected away from. You can pass state to carry data (e.g. the originally requested URL) without exposing it in the URL.

Code Example

// Declarative redirect during render
if (!user) return <Navigate to="/login" replace />;

// Imperative, carrying "where they wanted to go"
const navigate = useNavigate();
const location = useLocation();
navigate("/login", { replace: true, state: { from: location.pathname } });

// In a data-router loader/action (preferred for auth):
import { redirect } from "react-router-dom";
export async function loader() {
  const user = await getUser();
  if (!user) throw redirect("/login");
  return user;
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

The nuance interviewers hunt for: don't call navigate() directly in the render body — it must run in an effect or event handler, or you'll get warnings and re-render loops; for render-time redirects use <Navigate>. And in the data router, redirecting inside a loader beats redirecting inside the component because it happens before any render, avoiding a flash of protected content.

Q8. How do you read and update query params with useSearchParams?

ROI: ★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

useSearchParams() returns a [searchParams, setSearchParams] pair, analogous to useState but backed by the URL. searchParams is a read-only URLSearchParams object; setSearchParams updates the query string (and thus navigates). It's the right tool for filters, pagination, sort order, and tabs you want shareable and bookmarkable.

Detailed Answer

Because state lives in the URL, it survives refresh, is shareable, and participates in the back/forward history. Read with searchParams.get("q") (returns string | null). Write by passing an object or a URLSearchParams; pass { replace: true } for high-frequency updates (like a search-as-you-type box) so you don't flood the history stack.

Code Example

import { useSearchParams } from "react-router-dom";

function ProductList() {
  const [searchParams, setSearchParams] = useSearchParams();
  const page = Number(searchParams.get("page") ?? "1");
  const q = searchParams.get("q") ?? "";

  function onSearch(text) {
    // functional update preserves other params
    setSearchParams(prev => {
      prev.set("q", text);
      prev.set("page", "1");
      return prev;
    }, { replace: true });
  }

  return <input value={q} onChange={e => onSearch(e.target.value)} />;
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

Interviewers probe whether you keep filter state in the URL rather than local useState — URL state is the "single source of truth" that makes links shareable and back-button correct. Traps: values are always strings (coerce), and blindly replacing the whole search string wipes unrelated params — use the functional updater or spread existing entries. For rapid updates, debounce and use replace to keep history clean.

Q9. What does useLocation give you and when do you need it?

ROI: ★★★ Frequency: Medium

Short Answer

useLocation() returns the current location object: pathname, search, hash, state, and a unique key. It's how you react to URL changes (analytics page-views), read navigation state, or remember where a user came from before a redirect.

Detailed Answer

Common uses: firing a page-view analytics event in an effect keyed on location.pathname; reading location.state?.from to send a user back after login; and driving scroll restoration. The key is a stable id per history entry, handy for animations and per-page scroll memory.

Code Example

import { useLocation } from "react-router-dom";
import { useEffect } from "react";

function usePageViews() {
  const location = useLocation();
  useEffect(() => {
    analytics.track("page_view", { path: location.pathname + location.search });
  }, [location.pathname, location.search]);
}

// After login, return the user to where they were
const location = useLocation();
const from = location.state?.from ?? "/dashboard";
navigate(from, { replace: true });

Senior Engineer Perspective

The subtlety: depend on location.pathname/search, not the whole location object, when you only care about the URL — otherwise a new key on identical URLs can retrigger effects. Seniors also know location.state is ephemeral (it lives in the history entry, not the URL) so it survives back/forward but is gone on a fresh load — don't rely on it for anything critical.

SECTION 4 - DATA & GUARDS

Q10. How do you build a protected/guarded route with an auth redirect?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

Two patterns. In the classic router, wrap protected routes in a guard component that checks auth and either renders <Outlet /> or <Navigate to="/login" />. In the data router, do the check in a loader and throw redirect("/login") — this runs before render, avoiding a flash of protected content.

Detailed Answer

The guard-component pattern uses a layout route: the guard is the parent element and all protected pages are its children, so one check covers the whole subtree. Capture the requested URL in location so you can return the user there after login.

Remember client-side guards are a UX convenience, not security — the API must authorize every request independently. A savvy user can bypass client routing.

Code Example

// --- Guard component (classic) ---
function RequireAuth() {
  const { user } = useAuth();
  const location = useLocation();
  if (!user) {
    return <Navigate to="/login" replace state={{ from: location }} />;
  }
  return <Outlet />;
}

<Route element={<RequireAuth />}>
  <Route path="/dashboard" element={<Dashboard />} />
  <Route path="/settings" element={<Settings />} />
</Route>

// --- Loader guard (data router, preferred) ---
async function protectedLoader({ request }) {
  const user = await getUser();
  if (!user) {
    const url = new URL(request.url);
    throw redirect("/login?next=" + encodeURIComponent(url.pathname));
  }
  return user;
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

The line that lands: "client-side route guards are UX, not security — the server must still authorize." Follow-ups probe the flash-of-content problem (loader redirect solves it because it runs before render) and the redirect-back-after-login flow (store the intended URL in state or a ?next= param). Also mention handling the loading state while auth is being determined, so you don't bounce the user to /login before the session resolves.

Q11. What are loaders and actions in the v6.4+ data router?

ROI: ★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

A loader is a per-route async function that fetches data before the route renders; the component reads it with useLoaderData(). An action handles mutations (form submits) for that route and is invoked by <Form>/useSubmit. Together they move data fetching and mutation out of components and into the route layer, eliminating fetch-on-render waterfalls.

Detailed Answer

Because loaders run in parallel as soon as a navigation starts (not after a component mounts), you avoid the classic useEffect fetch waterfall and its loading-flag/race-condition boilerplate. React Router revalidates loaders automatically after an action succeeds, keeping the UI in sync with mutations. useNavigation() exposes the pending state for global spinners/optimistic UI.

Code Example

import { useLoaderData, Form, redirect } from "react-router-dom";

const router = createBrowserRouter([
  {
    path: "/users/:id",
    element: <UserPage />,
    loader: async ({ params }) => {
      const res = await fetch("/api/users/" + params.id);
      if (!res.ok) throw new Response("Not Found", { status: 404 });
      return res.json();
    },
    action: async ({ request, params }) => {
      const form = await request.formData();
      await updateUser(params.id, Object.fromEntries(form));
      return redirect("/users/" + params.id); // triggers revalidation
    },
  },
]);

function UserPage() {
  const user = useLoaderData();      // data is already here — no loading flag
  return (
    <Form method="post">
      <input name="name" defaultValue={user.name} />
      <button>Save</button>
    </Form>
  );
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

Interviewers want the "why": loaders kick off fetching at navigation time, so parallel routes load together and you avoid render-triggered waterfalls. Be ready to compare with TanStack Query — loaders are great for route-critical data and integrate with caching libraries (you can call the query client inside a loader). A thrown Response is caught by the nearest errorElement, which is how loaders surface 404s and failures cleanly.

Q12. How do errorElement and useRouteError handle route-level errors?

ROI: ★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

In the data router, if a loader/action throws or a component errors during render, React Router renders the nearest route's errorElement instead of the normal element. Inside it, useRouteError() returns the thrown value. This is a route-scoped error boundary that also handles thrown Response objects (e.g. 404/500).

Detailed Answer

Errors bubble to the closest ancestor route that defines an errorElement, so you can have a granular boundary per section and a catch-all at the root. Use isRouteErrorResponse(error) to distinguish a thrown HTTP-style Response (with status/statusText) from an unexpected JS Error, and render 404 vs generic-crash UI accordingly.

Code Example

import { useRouteError, isRouteErrorResponse } from "react-router-dom";

function RouteError() {
  const error = useRouteError();
  if (isRouteErrorResponse(error)) {
    if (error.status === 404) return <h1>Page not found</h1>;
    return <h1>{error.status} {error.statusText}</h1>;
  }
  return <h1>Something went wrong</h1>;
}

const router = createBrowserRouter([
  {
    path: "/",
    element: <Root />,
    errorElement: <RouteError />,   // catches errors from Root and its children
    children: [/* ... */],
  },
]);

Senior Engineer Perspective

The distinction interviewers want: errorElement replaces manual <ErrorBoundary> plumbing for route-level failures and, crucially, catches loader/action errors — which a regular React error boundary cannot, because they happen outside render. Put a root-level errorElement as a safety net and add finer boundaries where you want to keep the surrounding layout alive. Mention isRouteErrorResponse to branch on HTTP status.

SECTION 5 - ADVANCED

Q13. What are layout routes and how do they reduce duplication?

ROI: ★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

A layout route is a parent route with an element (rendering shared chrome + an <Outlet />) but often no path of its own — a "pathless" route. It groups children under a common layout or guard without adding a URL segment, so you define shared UI once.

Detailed Answer

Pathless layout routes are ideal for: an authenticated shell vs a public shell, a marketing layout vs an app layout, or wrapping a group of routes in one guard. Because the layout route contributes no path segment, /dashboard and /settings can share a layout without becoming /app/dashboard. You can nest multiple layout routes for compound chrome.

Code Example

const router = createBrowserRouter([
  {
    element: <AuthenticatedLayout />,   // pathless: no `path`
    loader: protectedLoader,             // one guard for the whole group
    children: [
      { path: "/dashboard", element: <Dashboard /> },
      { path: "/settings", element: <Settings /> },
    ],
  },
  {
    element: <PublicLayout />,
    children: [
      { path: "/login", element: <Login /> },
      { path: "/about", element: <About /> },
    ],
  },
]);

Senior Engineer Perspective

The insight interviewers reward: a layout route can be pathless, letting you share chrome and guards across sibling URLs without polluting the path. Combined with a loader on the layout route, it's the cleanest way to protect an entire section with one check. Contrast with just importing a Layout component into each page — the route approach keeps the layout mounted across child navigations and centralises the guard.

Q14. How do you lazy-load routes for code splitting?

ROI: ★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Split each route into its own bundle so the initial download is small. Classically you use React.lazy() + <Suspense> around the routed component. In the data router you use the route's lazy property, which can code-split the element, loader, and action together and doesn't require a Suspense wrapper.

Detailed Answer

Route-based splitting is the highest-impact place to code-split: users only download the JS for pages they visit. With React.lazy, wrap the lazy element in <Suspense fallback>. With the data-router lazy option, the module exports the route pieces and React Router loads them on demand while showing pending UI via useNavigation. Pair with Await/defer for streaming slow data.

Code Example

// --- React.lazy + Suspense ---
import { lazy, Suspense } from "react";
const Reports = lazy(() => import("./Reports"));

<Route
  path="/reports"
  element={
    <Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}>
      <Reports />
    </Suspense>
  }
/>

// --- Data-router lazy (splits element + loader together) ---
{
  path: "/reports",
  lazy: async () => {
    const { Reports, reportsLoader } = await import("./reports");
    return { element: <Reports />, loader: reportsLoader };
  },
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

Interviewers check that you split at the route boundary (best cost/benefit) and that you handle the loading fallback. Advanced follow-ups: prefetch the next likely bundle on link hover/focus to hide the network cost, and be careful not to over-split (too many tiny chunks add request overhead). Note the data-router lazy is superior for routes because it also splits the loader/action, not just the component.

Q15. How do you handle scroll restoration and 404s in React Router?

ROI: ★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

SPAs don't reset scroll on navigation the way the browser does for full page loads. Render <ScrollRestoration /> (data router) to restore/reset scroll per navigation. For 404s, add a catch-all route with path="*" that renders your NotFound component; in loaders, throw new Response(..., { status: 404 }) to hit the error UI.

Detailed Answer

ScrollRestoration restores position on back/forward and scrolls to top on new navigations; you can customise with getKey (e.g. key by pathname so filter changes don't reset scroll). Without the data router, a small useEffect-on-pathname that calls window.scrollTo(0,0) is the manual equivalent.

The catch-all path="*" must be the last/lowest-priority match. Use it for a friendly 404 page and analytics on broken links.

Code Example

import { ScrollRestoration } from "react-router-dom";

function Root() {
  return (
    <>
      <Outlet />
      <ScrollRestoration />  {/* render once at the top of the tree */}
    </>
  );
}

// 404 catch-all — keep it last
const router = createBrowserRouter([
  { path: "/", element: <Root />, children: [
    { index: true, element: <Home /> },
    { path: "*", element: <NotFound /> },   // matches anything unmatched
  ]},
]);

// Manual scroll reset without the data router
useEffect(() => { window.scrollTo(0, 0); }, [pathname]);

Senior Engineer Perspective

The gotcha seniors call out: scroll restoration is a real UX gap in SPAs because the browser's native restore doesn't fire without full loads. Know that ScrollRestoration's getKey lets you preserve scroll across param-only changes. For 404s, distinguish "no route matched" (path="*") from "route matched but the resource doesn't exist" (loader throws a 404 Response to the errorElement) — they're different failures with different UX.

Q16. How does React Router compare with Next.js file-based routing?

ROI: ★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

React Router uses an explicit, code-defined route config and is primarily client-side (a library you add to any React app). Next.js infers routes from the filesystem — files/folders in app/ (or pages/) become routes — and is a full framework with built-in SSR, RSC, and server data fetching. React Router = flexible library; Next.js = opinionated framework with routing baked in.

Detailed Answer

AspectReact Router (v6+)Next.js (App Router)
Route definitionExplicit config / JSXFile & folder conventions
RenderingClient-side (SSR via Remix/RR7 or framework)Server-first (RSC), SSR, SSG, streaming
Data loadingloaders / actions (v6.4+)Server Components, fetch, route handlers
Nested layouts<Outlet />layout.tsx per segment
NatureLibraryFramework

Conceptually they've converged: Next's layout.tsx + page.tsx mirror layout routes + index routes, and Next's Server Component data fetching parallels React Router's loaders. React Router 7 (which merges Remix) narrows the gap further by offering SSR and file-based conventions as an option.

Senior Engineer Perspective

Interviewers want a framework-vs-library framing, not tribalism. Pick React Router when you have an existing CSR SPA or need routing without adopting a whole framework; pick Next.js when you want SSR/RSC, SEO, and file conventions out of the box. The strongest answer notes the convergence — loaders ≈ server data fetching, <Outlet /> ≈ layout.tsx — and that React Router 7 blurs the line by absorbing Remix's server-side capabilities.

13 - NEXT.JS, SSR & SERVER COMPONENTS

Target Audience: Frontend / React Engineer (3–6 Years) Goal: Not just answer questions, but survive follow-up grilling from experienced interviewers.

SECTION 1 - RENDERING STRATEGIES

Q1. What is the difference between CSR, SSR, SSG, and ISR, and when do you use each?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

They differ in where and when the HTML is produced. CSR ships an empty shell and renders in the browser. SSR renders HTML on the server on every request. SSG renders HTML once at build time and serves the same static file to everyone. ISR is SSG plus background revalidation — pages are pre-built but regenerated periodically so content can update without a full redeploy.

Detailed Answer

The axis is the freshness/performance trade-off:

StrategyHTML builtFreshnessBest forCost
CSRIn browser at runtimeLive (client fetch)Private dashboards, highly interactive apps behind authPoor first paint & SEO; big JS bundle
SSRServer, every requestAlways fresh, per-request/per-userPersonalized or fast-changing pages (feed, cart, auth-aware)Server CPU per request; higher TTFB
SSGServer, at build timeFrozen until next buildMarketing, docs, blogs — content that rarely changesRebuild to update; slow builds for many pages
ISRBuild time + background re-genEventually fresh (after revalidate window)Large catalogs, product/blog pages that change occasionallyStale window; cache infra needed

In the Next.js App Router these are not separate APIs you toggle — they emerge from how you fetch. A page with no dynamic data and cached fetches is statically generated (SSG). Add revalidate and it becomes ISR. Read a dynamic input (cookies, headers, searchParams) or opt out of caching and the same page becomes SSR. CSR is what happens inside a "use client" component that fetches in the browser.

Code Example

// SSG (default): cached fetch, rendered at build time
export default async function Page() {
  const posts = await fetch("https://api.site.com/posts").then(r => r.json());
  return <List posts={posts} />;
}

// ISR: rebuild this page at most once every 60s (in the background)
export const revalidate = 60;

// SSR: force per-request rendering (no caching)
export const dynamic = "force-dynamic";
// ...or simply read a dynamic input, which flips the route to dynamic:
import { cookies } from "next/headers";
export default async function Page() {
  const session = (await cookies()).get("session"); // Next 15: cookies() is async
  // ...renders fresh on every request
}

Project Example

On an e-commerce site: the marketing home page is SSG (rebuilt on deploy), product detail pages are ISR with revalidate = 300 (price/stock refreshes every 5 minutes without redeploying), the checkout/cart is SSR (per-user, never cached), and the logged-in account settings panel is effectively CSR inside client components.

Senior Engineer Perspective

Interviewers want to hear that in the App Router you rarely "choose SSR vs SSG" explicitly — the rendering mode is derived from your data access. Naming the triggers that force a route dynamic (calling cookies()/headers(), reading searchParams, fetch(..., { cache: "no-store" }), or export const dynamic = "force-dynamic") is the strong signal. Also mention that ISR gives stale-while-revalidate semantics: the first request after the window still gets the old page while a fresh one regenerates in the background — so "revalidate: 60" is not a hard 60-second freshness guarantee.

Q2. What is hydration, and what causes a "hydration mismatch"?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

Hydration is the process where React takes the server-rendered static HTML and attaches event listeners and client-side state to it, making it interactive without re-creating the DOM. A hydration mismatch happens when the HTML React renders on the client during hydration doesn't match the HTML the server sent — React then warns and may discard/repaint that subtree, causing flicker or lost markup.

Detailed Answer

With SSR/SSG the browser paints the server HTML instantly (fast first paint), but the page isn't interactive yet. React downloads its JS, walks the same component tree, and "adopts" the existing DOM nodes — wiring up handlers and state instead of throwing the DOM away. For this to work, the client's first render must produce the same tree the server produced.

Common causes of a mismatch:

  • Using typeof window !== "undefined", Date.now(), Math.random(), or new Date().toLocaleString() during render — server and client compute different values.
  • Reading localStorage or browser-only APIs during the initial render.
  • Locale/timezone-dependent formatting that differs between server and client.
  • Invalid HTML nesting (e.g. a <div> inside a <p>) that the browser silently "fixes", changing the DOM out from under React.

The fix for legitimately client-only values is to render the server-safe version first and set the client-only value in an effect (after mount), or gate it behind a mounted flag.

Code Example

// BAD: server renders one time, client renders another -> mismatch
function Clock() {
  return <span>{new Date().toLocaleTimeString()}</span>;
}

// GOOD: render a stable placeholder on the server, fill in after mount
function Clock() {
  const [now, setNow] = useState<string | null>(null);
  useEffect(() => {
    setNow(new Date().toLocaleTimeString());
  }, []);
  return <span>{now ?? "--:--:--"}</span>; // same output on server & first client render
}

// Escape hatch for a single element you know differs (use sparingly):
<time suppressHydrationWarning>{new Date().toISOString()}</time>

Senior Engineer Perspective

The senior signal is explaining why React insists on matching: hydration reuses existing DOM nodes for speed, so a mismatch forces a client re-render and defeats the point of SSR. Name the usual culprits (time, randomness, window/localStorage, locale formatting) rather than reaching straight for suppressHydrationWarning — that flag silences the warning for one element but does not fix a real logic divergence. Bonus: mention that React 18/19 error messages now point at the offending element, and that third-party widgets or browser extensions injecting DOM can also trigger it.

Q3. What makes a route statically vs dynamically rendered in Next.js?

ROI: ★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

By default the App Router tries to render each route statically at build time. A route becomes dynamic (rendered per request) the moment it touches request-time data — cookies(), headers(), the searchParams prop, draftMode() — or you use an uncached fetch, or you explicitly set export const dynamic = "force-dynamic".

Detailed Answer

Next classifies each route during build. If nothing in the tree needs request context and all fetches are cacheable, the HTML is generated once and served from the CDN — that's static rendering (SSG/ISR). If any component in the route reads a dynamic function or an uncached data source, the whole route "opts into" dynamic rendering (SSR) and runs on every request.

Forces DYNAMIC (SSR)Keeps it STATIC (SSG/ISR)
cookies(), headers(), draftMode()No request-scoped reads
Reading the searchParams propParams known at build (generateStaticParams)
fetch(url, { cache: "no-store" })fetch(url) with default caching
export const dynamic = "force-dynamic"export const dynamic = "force-static"

You can inspect this: next build prints a legend marking each route as static (○), dynamic (ƒ), or ISR, which is the fastest way to confirm a page rendered the way you intended.

Code Example

// Pre-render specific dynamic segments at build time (stays STATIC)
export async function generateStaticParams() {
  const posts = await getAllPosts();
  return posts.map(p => ({ slug: p.slug }));
}

export default async function Post({ params }: { params: Promise<{ slug: string }> }) {
  const { slug } = await params;            // Next 15: params is a Promise
  const post = await getPost(slug);         // cached fetch -> still static
  return <Article post={post} />;
}

// Route-level knobs
export const dynamic = "auto";        // default; "force-dynamic" | "force-static" | "error"
export const revalidate = 3600;       // ISR window in seconds

Senior Engineer Perspective

The trap here is "one dynamic read poisons the whole route." Juniors accidentally read cookies() in a shared layout and wonder why every page went SSR. Seniors isolate request-time reads into the smallest component (or wrap them in <Suspense> so the static shell still streams) using Next 15's Partial Prerendering concept — a static shell with dynamic holes. Also worth naming: generateStaticParams is how you keep dynamic-segment routes (like /blog/[slug]) static, and combining it with revalidate gives you ISR.

Q4. What is the difference between the Edge runtime and the Node.js runtime?

ROI: ★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

The Node.js runtime is the full Node environment — all Node APIs, npm packages, and the filesystem — running in regional serverless functions. The Edge runtime is a lightweight environment based on Web APIs (like the browser/service workers), deployed to many locations close to users.
