When a fiber has no child, completeUnitOfWork runs: it "completes" the fiber (for host components, it creates/prepares the DOM instance and bubbles effect flags up), then moves to the sibling, or up to the parent if there is no sibling. This traversal visits every fiber without recursion.

Yielding

Between units, concurrent React consults the scheduler. The scheduler uses a deadline model — historically approximated with MessageChannel to schedule a macrotask (not requestIdleCallback, which proved too unreliable). If the deadline passes, shouldYield() returns true, the loop breaks, and control returns to the browser so it can paint and handle input. React resumes from the saved workInProgress fiber later.

Legacy/synchronous rendering uses the same loop but never yields (workLoopSync), which is why pre-concurrent React could block the thread.

Code Example

// Concurrent vs sync loops share performUnitOfWork; only yielding differs.
function workLoopSync() {
  while (workInProgress !== null) {
    workInProgress = performUnitOfWork(workInProgress); // never yields
  }
}

function workLoopConcurrent() {
  while (workInProgress !== null && !shouldYield()) {
    workInProgress = performUnitOfWork(workInProgress); // yields per time-slice
  }
  // if workInProgress !== null here, schedule a continuation and return
}

Project Example

Rendering a 10,000-row report client-side used to freeze the tab for a second. Marking the report update as a transition lets the concurrent work loop render it in ~5ms slices, yielding between slices so the browser keeps painting a loading indicator and responding to a Cancel click. The total work is the same; it is just chopped up so the main thread is never hostage.

Senior Engineer Perspective

Be precise: yielding happens only during the render phase. The commit phase always runs to completion synchronously — you cannot have a half-committed DOM. A sharp follow-up: "Does yielding make total render faster?" No, it makes the app more responsive by not monopolizing the thread; wall-clock render time may even be slightly longer due to scheduling overhead. That responsiveness-vs-throughput tradeoff is the whole point of concurrency.

Q9. How are hooks stored on a fiber, and why do the Rules of Hooks exist at this level?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Hooks are stored as a singly linked list on the fiber's memoizedState, appended in call order during render. React identifies which hook is which purely by call order, not by name. That is why hooks must be called unconditionally at the top level — conditional or looped calls would shift the order and make React read the wrong slot for the wrong hook.

Detailed Answer

The linked list

On the first render (mount), each hook call creates a hook object { memoizedState, queue, next } and links it after the previous one; the head is stored on fiber.memoizedState. On subsequent renders (update), React walks that same list in order, returning the next hook each time a hook is called. There is a cursor pointing at the "current hook." No keys, no names — position in the list is the identity.

Why the Rules of Hooks are not arbitrary

If you wrote if (cond) useState(), then on renders where cond is false the list has one fewer node. React's cursor would then hand the next hook the state that belonged to a different hook — e.g. your effect's closure ends up reading a piece of state, or a useState receives another hook's queue. The result is corrupted state and crashes. The lint rule eslint-plugin-react-hooks enforces the constraint statically because the runtime has no way to recover.

How React knows mount vs update

React swaps the internal "dispatcher" (a set of hook implementations) depending on whether the fiber is mounting or updating, so useState resolves to mountState or updateState accordingly. Calling a hook outside a component's render means no dispatcher is set, which is why you get "Invalid hook call."

Code Example

// The hooks list built during render — order IS the identity:
function Profile() {
  const [name, setName] = useState("");   // hook #0
  const [age, setAge]   = useState(0);    // hook #1
  useEffect(() => {}, [name]);            // hook #2
}
// fiber.memoizedState ->
//   { state: "", queue, next ->
//     { state: 0,  queue, next ->
//       { deps: [name], next: null } } }

// WHY THIS BREAKS:
function Bad({ show }) {
  if (show) useState("x"); // hook #0 exists only sometimes
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0); // slot shifts between renders!
}

Project Example

A teammate wrapped a useMemo in an early-return guard to "skip work when data was missing." Intermittently the component crashed with "rendered fewer hooks than expected." The linked-list model explains it exactly: the early return changed how many hooks ran between renders. The fix was to always call the hook and put the condition inside it.

Senior Engineer Perspective

Interviewers use this to test whether you understand hooks mechanically or just cargo-cult the rules. Strong signals: naming that identity is by index/order, that state lives on the fiber (so it survives re-renders but is wiped on unmount/remount or key change), and that custom hooks are just functions that borrow the calling component's hook list — which is why a custom hook must also obey the same ordering rules. A subtle point: two components using the same custom hook each get their own hooks on their own fibers; there is no shared state unless you add it via context or an external store.

SECTION 4 - SCHEDULING, CONCURRENCY & OPTIMIZATION

Q10. What is batching, and what changed with automatic batching in React 18?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

Batching means grouping multiple state updates into a single re-render for efficiency. Before React 18, batching happened only inside React event handlers; updates in promises, setTimeout, or native events each triggered a separate render. React 18's automatic batching extends batching to all contexts (as long as you use createRoot), so multiple setState calls anywhere collapse into one render.

Detailed Answer

Before React 18

React batched updates that occurred within its synthetic event handlers because it controlled the entry point. But an update inside a fetch().then() or setTimeout escaped that boundary, so two updates caused two renders — extra work and potential intermediate states.

React 18 automatic batching

With createRoot, React batches updates regardless of where they originate — event handlers, promises, timeouts, native handlers. It schedules the work and processes queued updates together in one render pass. This is generally a pure win: fewer renders, no visible intermediate states.

Opting out

If you genuinely need a synchronous, flushed update between two updates (rare — usually third-party DOM integration), flushSync forces React to commit immediately. Overusing it defeats batching and hurts performance.

ContextLegacy (ReactDOM.render)React 18 (createRoot)
React event handlerBatchedBatched
setTimeout / PromiseNOT batchedBatched
Native / addEventListenerNOT batchedBatched

Code Example

// React 18 with createRoot: ONE render, not two.
function handleClick() {
  setCount(c => c + 1);
  setFlag(f => !f);          // batched together => single re-render
}

// Also batched in React 18 (was TWO renders pre-18):
fetch("/api").then(() => {
  setCount(c => c + 1);
  setFlag(f => !f);          // still one render in v18
});

// Force a synchronous flush when you truly must:
import { flushSync } from "react-dom";
flushSync(() => setCount(c => c + 1)); // commits now
doDomMeasurementThatNeedsUpdatedDom();

Project Example

After upgrading a checkout flow to React 18, a bug where a loading spinner flashed twice disappeared — previously two updates inside a payment promise caused two renders and two intermediate paints. Automatic batching collapsed them into one, and the UI became visibly smoother with zero code changes.

Senior Engineer Perspective

The classic trap is the functional-updater question: "Why does setCount(count + 1); setCount(count + 1) only add 1?" Because both reads capture the same stale count from the render's closure; batching then applies both to the same base. Using the updater form setCount(c => c + 1) queues both against the latest value and adds 2. A senior also notes that automatic batching requires createRoot — an app still on legacy ReactDOM.render won't get it — and that flushSync is an escape hatch, not a habit.

Q11. What are lanes and priorities in concurrent React?

ROI: ★★★★ Frequency: Medium

Short Answer

Lanes are React's internal priority model, implemented as a 31-bit bitmask where each bit (or group of bits) is a "lane" representing a class of work — e.g. synchronous/discrete input, default, transition, and idle. Each update is assigned a lane based on its urgency; the scheduler renders the highest-priority pending lanes first and can interrupt lower-priority work when something more urgent arrives.

Detailed Answer

Why a bitmask

Lanes replaced the older "expiration time" model. A bitmask lets React represent a set of pending priorities on a fiber and combine/compare them with cheap bitwise operations. Multiple updates of different priorities can be batched or separated by lane. When React picks work, it selects the set of lanes to render and leaves lower-priority lanes for later passes.

Priority tiers (conceptual)

  • Discrete / sync: clicks, typing, key presses — must feel instant, highest priority.
  • Default: normal updates like data arriving from a fetch.
  • Transition: updates marked with startTransition/useTransition — non-urgent UI that can be interrupted.
  • Idle / offscreen: lowest, e.g. prerendering hidden content.

How the API maps to lanes

useTransition and startTransition mark updates as transition-lane work so a fast, urgent update (like the input value) can preempt an expensive transition render. useDeferredValue similarly schedules a lower-priority "deferred" copy of a value. You never touch lanes directly, but these hooks are the developer-facing surface of the lane model.

Code Example

function Search() {
  const [query, setQuery] = React.useState("");
  const [results, setResults] = React.useState([]);
  const [isPending, startTransition] = React.useTransition();

  function onChange(e) {
    setQuery(e.target.value);            // urgent lane: keeps input snappy
    startTransition(() => {               // transition lane: interruptible
      setResults(computeExpensiveList(e.target.value));
    });
  }

  return (
    <>
      <input value={query} onChange={onChange} />
      {isPending && <Spinner />}
      <List items={results} />
    </>
  );
}

Project Example

On a filter-as-you-type analytics view, the input froze whenever the chart recomputed. Wrapping the chart-data update in startTransition put it on the transition lane, so React kept the keystroke updates on the urgent lane and interrupted/restarted the chart render on each new character — the input stayed at 60fps while the chart caught up slightly behind.

Senior Engineer Perspective

You are not expected to recite the exact 31 lanes, but you should convey the model: priority as a bitmask, urgent updates preempting transitions, and the developer APIs (useTransition, useDeferredValue) that ride on it. A sharp follow-up: "How is a transition different from a debounce?" A debounce delays firing the update on a timer and still blocks once it fires; a transition fires immediately but renders at low priority and is interruptible, so the urgent UI never blocks. That distinction is a strong senior signal.

Q12. How is a state update actually scheduled, from setState to a painted screen?

ROI: ★★★★ Frequency: Medium

Short Answer

Calling a state setter creates an update object, enqueues it on the fiber's update queue with a lane, and calls scheduleUpdateOnFiber. React marks the path from that fiber to the root as having pending work, then asks the scheduler to run a render at the appropriate priority. The scheduler eventually invokes the work loop (render phase), then React commits, and the browser paints.

Detailed Answer

The lifecycle of one update:

  1. Dispatch: setState(x) (really the hook's dispatch) creates an update { lane, action, next } and appends it to the hook's circular update queue.
  2. Schedule: scheduleUpdateOnFiber assigns a lane and walks return pointers up to the FiberRoot, OR-ing the lane into each fiber's childLanes so React knows which paths have work.
  3. Ensure a render is scheduled: React asks the Scheduler package to run a callback at a priority matching the lane (sync work may run before paint via a microtask-like flush; transitions run via the concurrent scheduler).
  4. Render phase: the work loop builds the WIP tree, replaying the update queue to compute new state, and diffs to tag effects.
  5. Commit phase: React applies DOM mutations, flips root.current, runs layout effects, then passive effects after paint.

A key optimization: if, during render, the new state computed for a fiber is identical (via Object.is) and nothing else changed, React can bail out and skip re-rendering that subtree (see next question).

Code Example

// What a hook dispatch roughly does:
function dispatchSetState(fiber, queue, action) {
  const lane = requestUpdateLane(fiber);       // pick priority
  const update = { lane, action, next: null };
  enqueueUpdate(queue, update);                // append to circular queue
  scheduleUpdateOnFiber(fiber, lane);          // mark root, ask scheduler to render
}

// Eager bailout: if the new state equals the current, skip the render.
const current = queue.lastRenderedState;
const next = typeof action === "function" ? action(current) : action;
if (Object.is(next, current)) {
  // no scheduled render needed
}

Project Example

A component called setStatus("idle") on every websocket heartbeat even though status was already "idle." Profiling showed no re-renders — React's Object.is bailout at dispatch time recognized the value was unchanged and skipped scheduling entirely. Knowing this prevented a "premature optimization" PR to guard the call manually.

Senior Engineer Perspective

Interviewers probe whether you know updates are asynchronous and queued, not applied immediately. The updater form matters because updates are replayed against the base state in order during render. Another nuance: even after a dispatch-time bailout on the setter, if the component re-renders for another reason, React still runs the component function but can bail out of updating children. Distinguishing "the component function re-ran" from "the DOM was updated" is a mature distinction that avoids false conclusions when profiling.

Q13. How do bailouts and internal memoization avoid re-rendering?

ROI: ★★★★ Frequency: Medium

Short Answer

During beginWork, if a fiber's props and state are unchanged and it has no pending update in the current lanes, React bails out: it clones the existing children without re-rendering them (bailoutOnAlreadyFinishedWork). React.memo, useMemo, and useCallback help create the referential stability that lets these bailouts fire, so unrelated subtrees are skipped entirely.

Detailed Answer

The two levels of bailout

  • Whole-subtree bailout: if a fiber has no work in the current lanes and its props are referentially equal, React reuses its child fibers as-is and does not descend — the entire subtree is skipped.
  • Component-level bailout: even when a parent re-renders, a child wrapped in React.memo is skipped if its props are shallowly equal to last time. Without memo, a child re-renders whenever its parent does, regardless of prop equality.

Why referential stability matters

Bailouts compare props by identity (shallow). If a parent passes a new object/array/function literal every render, the child's props are "different" each time and the bailout can't fire. useMemo/useCallback preserve the same reference across renders so memoized children can bail out. This is why "just wrap everything in memo" often does nothing — the props keep changing identity upstream.

State bailout

If a useState/useReducer update produces a value Object.is-equal to the current, React bails out of that update. If it is the only pending update, the component won't even re-render.

Code Example

const Child = React.memo(function Child({ config, onSave }) {
  return <button onClick={onSave}>{config.label}</button>;
});

function Parent({ label }) {
  const [n, setN] = React.useState(0);

  // WITHOUT these, config/onSave are new refs each render => memo useless.
  const config = React.useMemo(() => ({ label }), [label]);
  const onSave = React.useCallback(() => save(), []);

  return (
    <>
      <button onClick={() => setN(n + 1)}>{n}</button>
      <Child config={config} onSave={onSave} />  {/* bails out on n change */}
    </>
  );
}

Project Example

A settings page re-rendered a heavy <PermissionMatrix> on every keystroke in an unrelated name field. The matrix was already React.memo-wrapped, but a columns array was rebuilt inline each render, defeating the bailout. Memoizing columns with useMemo restored the bailout and dropped the matrix's renders to zero for name edits.

Senior Engineer Perspective

The senior message: memoization is about enabling bailouts, and bailouts propagate — skipping a fiber skips its whole subtree, which is where the real savings come from. Two important caveats: (1) React.memo does a shallow prop compare, so a stable-reference-but-deeply-changed object still bails incorrectly — pass a custom comparator or restructure props; (2) the React 19 Compiler auto-memoizes, potentially removing the need for manual useMemo/useCallback — a forward-looking candidate mentions this as the direction of travel while still explaining the underlying mechanism.

Q14. How does Context propagation work internally, and why can it be a performance trap?

ROI: ★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

When a Context Provider's value changes (by Object.is), React does a special traversal from the provider down, finding every consumer of that context and marking it for an update — bypassing the normal bailout that would otherwise skip unchanged subtrees. So every consumer re-renders when the value's reference changes, even components that only use one field of the value. That's the trap: an unstable or coarse-grained value re-renders the whole consumer set.

Detailed Answer

Propagation mechanism

Context does not rely on prop drilling through the tree. Each consumer fiber records a dependency on the context object during render. When the provider commits a new value, React runs propagateContextChange: it walks the subtree and, for any fiber depending on that context, schedules an update and marks the path so the work loop reaches it — even if intermediate components would have bailed out. This is why a React.memo wrapper does not stop a context-driven re-render of a consumer.

The performance trap

  • Unstable value: <Ctx.Provider value={{ user, theme }}> creates a new object every render, so every consumer re-renders every time the provider renders, regardless of whether the data changed. Fix: memoize the value.
  • Over-broad context: putting many unrelated fields in one context means a change to any field re-renders all consumers. Fix: split into multiple contexts by change frequency.

Mitigations

Memoize the provider value; split contexts (e.g. separate ThemeContext and AuthContext); or use an external store (Zustand, Redux, or useSyncExternalStore) with selectors so components subscribe to slices and only re-render when their slice changes.

Code Example

// TRAP: new object each render => every consumer re-renders.
<AppContext.Provider value={{ user, theme, setTheme }}>

// BETTER: memoize so identity is stable across unrelated renders.
const value = React.useMemo(
  () => ({ user, theme, setTheme }),
  [user, theme, setTheme]
);
<AppContext.Provider value={value}>{children}</AppContext.Provider>

// BEST for high-churn state: split contexts by update frequency.
<AuthContext.Provider value={authValue}>
  <ThemeContext.Provider value={themeValue}>
    {children}
  </ThemeContext.Provider>
</AuthContext.Provider>

Project Example

An app kept the current user, feature flags, and a live "unread count" in one context object. Every websocket-driven unread-count tick re-rendered the entire authenticated app. Splitting the volatile count into its own context (and memoizing the rest) cut re-renders by ~95% — the count badge updated in isolation while the rest of the tree stayed put.

Senior Engineer Perspective

The interviewer is testing whether you know context is not a state manager and has no built-in selector granularity. Strong points to raise: context propagation deliberately bypasses memoization for consumers; the value comparison is Object.is on the whole value; and the standard senior fixes are memoizing the value, splitting contexts, or reaching for an external store with selectors when you need slice-level subscriptions. Mentioning useSyncExternalStore as the concurrency-safe way to subscribe to external stores (avoiding tearing) shows current, internals-level awareness.

16 - STYLING & CSS ARCHITECTURE

Target Audience: Frontend / React Engineer (3–6 Years) Goal: Not just answer questions, but survive follow-up grilling from experienced interviewers.

CSS questions are deceptively deep. Interviewers use them to check whether you actually understand the rendering model (specificity, the cascade, stacking contexts) or just paste utility classes until it looks right. This chapter covers the CSS fundamentals that come up in every frontend loop, the modern layout systems, the real trade-offs between styling approaches in React, and how to build a scalable, themeable design system.

  1. How does CSS specificity and the cascade decide which rule wins?

SECTION 1 - CSS CORE FOR INTERVIEWS

Q1. How does CSS specificity and the cascade decide which rule wins?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

When multiple rules target the same element, the winner is decided by (1) importance/origin, (2) specificity, then (3) source order. Specificity is a tuple counting inline styles, IDs, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, and elements/pseudo-elements — higher tuple wins; ties go to whichever rule appears last.

Detailed Answer

Specificity tuple (a, b, c, d)

  • a — inline style="" (1 or 0)
  • b — number of IDs
  • c — number of classes, attribute selectors, pseudo-classes
  • d — number of element/pseudo-element selectors

Compare left to right: #nav .item (0,1,1,0) beats .header .item a (0,0,2,1) because the ID component wins before classes are even considered. !important overrides normal declarations (and should be a last resort). The universal selector * and combinators (>, +, ~) add nothing to specificity.

The cascade order: (1) origin & importance (author !important > author normal > user-agent), (2) specificity, (3) order of appearance. Modern CSS adds layers (@layer) which sit above specificity within the same origin, letting you control precedence explicitly.

Code Example

<a class="link" id="cta">Buy</a>

a          { color: black; }   /* (0,0,0,1) */
.link      { color: blue; }    /* (0,0,1,0) wins over element */
#cta       { color: red; }     /* (0,1,0,0) wins over class -> RED */

Senior Engineer Perspective

The senior point is that high specificity is a smell — ID selectors and !important create escalation wars. Modern architectures (BEM, utility classes, CSS Modules) deliberately keep specificity flat (mostly single classes) so overriding is predictable. Mention @layer and the new :where() (which has zero specificity) as tools for taming it.

Q2. Explain the box model and box-sizing.

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Every element is a box: content, then padding, then border, then margin. With the default box-sizing: content-box, width sets only the content width, so padding and border are added on top. With box-sizing: border-box, width includes content + padding + border, which is far more intuitive.

Detailed Answer

With content-box, a 200px box with 20px padding and 2px border actually occupies 244px — the source of endless layout surprises. That's why almost every codebase sets: 

*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }

so width: 200px means the box is exactly 200px including padding/border. Margins are always outside the box and can collapse vertically between block siblings (the larger of the two adjacent margins is used, not the sum) — a frequent gotcha.

Senior Engineer Perspective

Margin collapsing is a favourite follow-up: it happens between vertical block margins, not horizontal, and is prevented by padding/border between them, or by a fl/ grid container (flex/grid items don't collapse). Knowing this signals real CSS depth.

Q3. What do the different CSS position values do?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

static (default, in normal flow), relative (offset from its normal spot, still occupies original space, becomes a positioning context), absolute (removed from flow, positioned relative to the nearest positioned ancestor), fixed (relative to the viewport), and sticky (relative until a scroll threshold, then fixed within its container).

Detailed Answer

ValueIn flow?Positioned relative toTypical use
staticYesn/aDefault
relativeYes (keeps space)Its own normal positionNudge + create anchor for absolute children
absoluteNoNearest ancestor with position != staticTooltips, dropdowns, badges
fixedNoViewportSticky headers, modals, FAB
stickyYes then pinnedScroll container + offsetSticky section headers

The key relationship: absolute looks up the ancestor chain for the first element that is not static. That's why you set position: relative on a parent to "contain" an absolutely-positioned child.

Senior Engineer Perspective

sticky silently fails if the parent has overflow: hidden/auto or no defined height — a very common real bug. And position (other than static) plus a z-index creates a stacking context (Q7). Connecting these shows you understand the interactions, not just the definitions.

Q4. Flexbox: explain main vs cross axis and give common recipes.

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

Flexbox lays items along a main axis (set by flex-direction) and aligns them on the perpendicular cross axis. justify-content distributes along the main axis; align-items aligns along the cross axis. It's ideal for one-dimensional layouts (a row or a column).

Detailed Answer

With flex-direction: row (default), main axis is horizontal, cross axis is vertical. Switch to column and they swap — which is why beginners get confused about why justify-content suddenly controls vertical spacing.

  • justify-content: flex-start / center / space-between / space-around / space-evenly (main axis)
  • align-items: stretch / center / flex-start / flex-end / baseline (cross axis)
  • flex: 1 = flex-grow:1; flex-shrink:1; flex-basis:0 — item grows to fill
  • gap: modern spacing between items (no more margin hacks)
  • flex-wrap: wrap: allow items to flow onto new lines

Code Example

/* Navbar: logo left, links right, vertically centered */
.nav { display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; gap: 16px; }

/* Perfect centering */
.center { display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; min-height: 100vh; }

/* Card that fills remaining space next to a fixed sidebar */
.layout { display: flex; }
.sidebar { flex: 0 0 240px; }   /* fixed */
.main    { flex: 1; }           /* grows */

Senior Engineer Perspective

Know that flex-basis beats width in flex containers, and that min-width: auto (the default) is why flex items refuse to shrink below their content — the fix for "my text overflows the flex item" is min-width: 0. That one gotcha comes up constantly in real work.

Q5. Grid vs Flexbox — when do you use each?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Flexbox is one-dimensional (content flows along a single axis and wraps); Grid is two-dimensional (you define rows and columns simultaneously). Use Flexbox for components (toolbars, button groups, nav) and Grid for page/section layouts (dashboards, card grids, complex templates).

Detailed Answer

Rule of thumb: Flexbox is content-out (items size themselves and distribute in the available space), Grid is layout-in (you define the structure and place items into it). They compose — a grid cell often contains a flex container.

Code Example

/* Responsive card grid — auto-fit is the killer feature */
.cards {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr));
  gap: 16px;
}

/* Named-area page layout */
.app {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 240px 1fr;
  grid-template-rows: 56px 1fr;
  grid-template-areas: "sidebar header" "sidebar main";
}
.header { grid-area: header; }

Senior Engineer Perspective

The repeat(auto-fit, minmax(...)) pattern gives you a responsive grid with zero media queries — mentioning it signals modern CSS fluency. Also note auto-fit vs auto-fill: auto-fit collapses empty tracks (items stretch), auto-fill keeps them (items stay their min size).

Q6. px vs em vs rem — which do you use and why?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

px is an absolute, fixed unit. em is relative to the current element's font-size (compounds through nesting). rem is relative to the root font-size (no compounding). Prefer rem for font sizes and spacing so the whole UI scales with the user's browser font setting; use px for things that should never scale (hairline borders).

Detailed Answer

Accessibility is the real reason this matters: users who set a larger default font in their browser get a UI that scales if you use rem, but a UI frozen at your hard-coded sizes if you use px everywhere. em is useful for things that should scale relative to their own text (padding inside a button that grows with the button's font-size), but its compounding — a 1.2em inside a 1.2em is 1.44em — makes it unpredictable for global sizing.

Modern responsive typography often uses clamp(): font-size: clamp(1rem, 2.5vw, 1.5rem) for fluid, bounded scaling.

Senior Engineer Perspective

Don't set html { font-size: 62.5% } (the old "1rem = 10px" hack) blindly — it can fight user zoom expectations. The strongest answer ties unit choice to accessibility and to a spacing scale expressed in rem tokens.

Q7. How does z-index really work? (stacking contexts)

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: Medium-High

Short Answer

z-index only works on positioned elements (and flex/grid items) and only orders elements within the same stacking context. A high z-index inside one stacking context can never poke above a sibling context — so "my modal with z-index 9999 is still behind the header" is almost always a stacking-context problem, not a number problem.

Detailed Answer

A new stacking context is created by, among others: the root element; position other than static + a z-index; opacity < 1; transform, filter, will-change; isolation: isolate. Once an element forms a stacking context, its children's z-indexes are only compared against each other — the whole subtree stacks as one unit relative to outside elements.

This is why a parent with transform or opacity can trap a child modal beneath other content. The fix is usually to render the modal via a React portal at the document root, escaping the trapping context entirely.

Senior Engineer Perspective

The senior move: instead of a z-index arms race, portal overlays to document.body and keep a small, documented z-index scale (e.g. dropdown 1000, sticky 1100, modal 1300, toast 1400). Mention isolation: isolate as a way to deliberately contain z-index within a component.

Q8. How do you center an element? (all the ways)

ROI: ★★★☆☆ Frequency: Medium

Short Answer

Modern default: Flexbox (display:flex; justify-content:center; align-items:center) or Grid (display:grid; place-items:center). For a block with known width, margin: 0 auto centers horizontally. Absolute centering uses top/left:50% + transform: translate(-50%,-50%).

Code Example

/* Grid — shortest */
.wrap { display: grid; place-items: center; min-height: 100vh; }

/* Absolute (when you can't touch the parent's display) */
.box {
  position: absolute;
  top: 50%; left: 50%;
  transform: translate(-50%, -50%);
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

This used to be a "gotcha" question in the float/table era; today it's a warm-up. Score points by naming place-items: center as the one-liner and mentioning that the transform trick works without knowing the element's dimensions, unlike negative-margin centering.

SECTION 2 - STYLING REACT

Q9. Compare the main styling approaches in React and their trade-offs.

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

The main families are: plain CSS / CSS Modules (scoped classes at build time), CSS-in-JS (styled-components/Emotion — styles co-located in JS, dynamic props, runtime cost), utility-first (Tailwind — compose atomic classes), and zero-runtime CSS-in-JS (vanilla-extract, Linaria, or PandaCSS — CSS-in-JS ergonomics extracted to static CSS at build time).

Detailed Answer

ApproachScopingDynamic stylesRuntime costNotes
Plain CSS / globalManual (BEM)Via class togglesNoneSimple, but easy to leak
CSS ModulesAutomatic (hashed)Class togglesNone (build-time)Great default, no runtime
CSS-in-JS (styled/Emotion)AutomaticExcellent (props)Runtime style injectionDX great; RSC/SSR friction
TailwindN/A (atomic)Conditional class stringsNone (JIT purges)Fast to ship, verbose markup
Zero-runtime (vanilla-extract, Panda)AutomaticVariants, staticNone (extracted)Best of both, more setup

The modern trend, especially with React Server Components, moves away from runtime CSS-in-JS (styled-components has friction in RSC because it needs client context) toward CSS Modules, Tailwind, or zero-runtime solutions that produce static CSS.

Senior Engineer Perspective

Don't declare one "best." Frame it by constraints: "For a Next.js App Router app I'd lean Tailwind or CSS Modules to avoid runtime CSS-in-JS in Server Components; for a heavily-themed design system I might pick vanilla-extract for typed tokens with zero runtime." That contextual reasoning is what they're testing.

Q10. How do you scope styles and avoid global CSS leaks?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Use a scoping mechanism so class names can't collide: CSS Modules (build-time hashed names like Button_root__x7f2), CSS-in-JS (auto-generated unique classes), or a naming convention like BEM in plain CSS. Avoid broad element selectors and deeply nested global rules.

Detailed Answer

Plain global CSS has one namespace, so .button defined in two files fights, and generic selectors (div > p) leak into places you never intended. The failure mode is a change in one component silently breaking another. Solutions in order of guarantee:

  • CSS Modules — import styles from './Button.module.css'; the bundler rewrites class names to be unique. Zero runtime, strongest default.
  • CSS-in-JS — styles are generated with unique hashes automatically.
  • BEM — block__element--modifier discipline in plain CSS; works but relies on humans.
  • Cascade layers / :where() — keep specificity low so overrides are predictable.

Code Example

/* Button.module.css */
.root { padding: 8px 16px; border-radius: 6px; }

// Button.tsx
import styles from './Button.module.css';
export function Button(props) {
  return <button className={styles.root} {...props} />;
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

Global CSS still has a legitimate place: resets, CSS custom properties (design tokens), typography base, and third-party overrides. The senior answer is "scope component styles, keep a small deliberate global layer for tokens and resets" — not "never use global."

SECTION 3 - RESPONSIVE & THEMING

Q11. What are CSS custom properties, and how do you build theming / dark mode with them?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

CSS custom properties (variables) are runtime values declared with --name and read with var(--name). They cascade and can be overridden per scope, which makes theming trivial: define color tokens on :root, override them under a [data-theme="dark"] selector, and every component that reads the tokens updates instantly — no JS re-render, no duplicate stylesheets.

Detailed Answer

Unlike Sass variables (compiled away at build), CSS custom properties are live in the browser: you can change them at runtime and they re-cascade. That's exactly what you want for theming. The pattern:

  1. Define semantic tokens on :root (--color-bg, --color-text, --color-accent).
  2. Override them in a dark scope.
  3. Components reference only tokens, never raw hex.
  4. Toggle the theme by setting an attribute/class on <html>; persist the choice in localStorage and respect prefers-color-scheme as the default.

Code Example

:root {
  --color-bg: #ffffff;
  --color-text: #111827;
  --color-accent: #2563eb;
}
:root[data-theme="dark"] {
  --color-bg: #0f172a;
  --color-text: #e2e8f0;
}
body { background: var(--color-bg); color: var(--color-text); }

// React: toggle + persist
const [theme, setTheme] = useState(
  () => localStorage.getItem('theme')
     ?? (matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)').matches ? 'dark' : 'light')
);
useEffect(() => {
  document.documentElement.dataset.theme = theme;
  localStorage.setItem('theme', theme);
}, [theme]);

Senior Engineer Perspective

Two senior points: (1) avoid the dark-mode "flash of wrong theme" on load by setting the attribute in an inline script before first paint (in Next.js, a small blocking script or next-themes). (2) Prefer semantic tokens (--color-bg) over literal ones (--gray-900) so themes can remap meaning, not just values.

Q12. Responsive design: media queries vs container queries?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: Medium-High

Short Answer

Media queries respond to the viewport (or device features); container queries respond to the size of a component's container. Container queries let a component adapt based on where it's placed, making it truly reusable — a card can switch to a horizontal layout whenever its container is wide enough, regardless of screen size.

Detailed Answer

Media queries are still the backbone of page-level responsiveness (breakpoints for phone/tablet/desktop) and for feature detection (prefers-color-scheme, prefers-reduced-motion, hover, pointer). Their limitation: a component only knows the viewport width, not how much room it actually has — the same card in a sidebar vs a wide main area can't adapt independently.

Container queries (now broadly supported) fix this: mark an element as a container with container-type, then query it with @container.

Code Example

/* Media query — viewport based */
@media (min-width: 768px) { .grid { grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; } }

/* Container query — component based */
.card-wrap { container-type: inline-size; }
@container (min-width: 400px) {
  .card { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 120px 1fr; }
}

/* Respect motion preferences */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { * { animation: none !important; } }

Senior Engineer Perspective

Adopting a mobile-first approach (base styles for small screens, min-width queries to layer on larger) keeps CSS cleaner. Mention prefers-reduced-motion unprompted — it signals accessibility awareness, which senior interviewers weight heavily.

Q13. How do you build and maintain a design system with tokens?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: Medium

Short Answer

Define design tokens — named, single-source-of-truth values for color, spacing, typography, radii, shadows, z-index — and express them once (CSS variables, a Tailwind theme config, or typed constants). Every component consumes tokens, never raw values. Layer semantic tokens (--color-danger) on top of primitive tokens (--red-600) so intent is decoupled from value.

Detailed Answer

A scalable system typically has three tiers of tokens: primitive (raw palette and scale: --blue-500, --space-4), semantic (meaning: --color-accent, --color-surface), and component (--button-bg). Themes and brands remap the semantic layer without touching components. Pair this with a spacing scale (e.g. 4px base: 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32) so spacing is consistent and not arbitrary.

Tools: Tailwind's theme config, Style Dictionary (to generate tokens for web/iOS/Android from one source), vanilla-extract for typed tokens, and Storybook to document and visually test components in isolation.

Senior Engineer Perspective

The differentiator is the semantic layer. Junior systems hard-code color: var(--blue-500) everywhere; when the brand changes you touch hundreds of files. With semantic tokens you change one mapping. Mention Storybook + visual regression testing (Chromatic) as how you keep a system from drifting.

Q14. What are the performance implications of the different styling approaches?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: Medium

Short Answer

Build-time solutions (CSS Modules, Tailwind, zero-runtime CSS-in-JS) ship static CSS with no runtime cost. Runtime CSS-in-JS (styled-components/Emotion) serializes and injects styles during render, adding JS work and potential re-render/serialization overhead, plus SSR complexity. For large apps, extracting critical CSS and avoiding runtime style generation matters for LCP and INP.

Detailed Answer

  • Runtime CSS-in-JS: styles computed per render; dynamic props re-generate classes; SSR needs to collect and inline styles to avoid a flash. Fine for most apps, but a measurable tax at scale and awkward in Server Components.
  • Tailwind: JIT generates only used classes and purges the rest; the resulting stylesheet is small and cacheable. Atomic classes also dedupe repeated declarations.
  • CSS Modules / zero-runtime: plain .css files, cached and parsed by the browser once, no JS involvement.

Cross-cutting wins regardless of approach: minimize unused CSS, split critical vs non-critical CSS, avoid huge global stylesheets, and let the browser cache CSS separately from JS.

Senior Engineer Perspective

The industry moved off runtime CSS-in-JS for new large projects partly for these reasons plus RSC compatibility (styled-components can't run in Server Components without a client boundary). Framing the shift accurately — "not that CSS-in-JS is bad, but the constraints changed with RSC" — reads as current and balanced.

Q15. Animations: CSS vs Framer Motion, and what's cheap to animate?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: Medium

Short Answer

Animate transform and opacity — they're handled by the compositor (GPU) and skip layout and paint, so they hit 60fps. Avoid animating width, height, top, left, or margin, which trigger layout on every frame. Use plain CSS transitions/keyframes for simple state changes; reach for Framer Motion (motion/react) for orchestrated, gesture-driven, layout, or enter/exit animations.

Detailed Answer

The browser's rendering pipeline is layout → paint → composite. Animating geometric properties forces layout + paint every frame (expensive); animating transform/opacity only re-composites (cheap). This is the single most important animation-performance rule.

CSS handles hover, focus, and simple transitions with zero JS. Framer Motion adds: spring physics, AnimatePresence for exit animations (which CSS can't do when a component unmounts), shared-layout/FLIP animations, drag gestures, and scroll-linked effects — all declaratively. The cost is bundle size and JS on the main thread, so use it where it earns its keep.

Code Example

/* Cheap CSS transition — composited */
.card { transition: transform .2s ease, opacity .2s ease; }
.card:hover { transform: translateY(-4px); }

// Framer Motion enter/exit
import { motion, AnimatePresence } from 'motion/react';
<AnimatePresence>
  {open && (
    <motion.div
      initial={{ opacity: 0, y: 8 }}
      animate={{ opacity: 1, y: 0 }}
      exit={{ opacity: 0, y: 8 }}
    />
  )}
</AnimatePresence>

Senior Engineer Perspective

Always gate animation behind prefers-reduced-motion for accessibility. And know will-change is a hint to promote an element to its own layer — useful sparingly, harmful if overused (memory, too many layers). Naming the composited-properties rule unprompted is the strongest signal here.

17 - TESTING (JEST & REACT TESTING LIBRARY)

Target Audience: Frontend / React Engineer (3–6 Years) Goal: Not just answer questions, but survive follow-up grilling from experienced interviewers.

TOP HIGHEST-ROI QUESTIONS IN THIS CHAPTER

  1. The testing pyramid vs the testing trophy — what should you actually test in a frontend?
  2. React Testing Library's core philosophy: test behavior, not implementation
  3. Jest basics — describe/it/expect, matchers, and setup/teardown
  4. Mocking with jest.fn, jest.mock, and mocking modules
  5. Mocking timers, dates, and fetch
  6. RTL queries — getBy vs queryBy vs findBy
  7. Why is getByRole preferred, and what is the recommended query priority?
  8. user-event vs fireEvent — which should you use and why?
  9. Testing async UI — findBy and waitFor
  10. Testing custom hooks with renderHook
  11. Testing components that depend on Context or a Redux store
  12. Snapshot testing — pros, cons, and when it earns its keep
  13. Mocking the network with MSW and why it beats mocking fetch
  14. Code coverage — what it does and does not tell you
  15. End-to-end testing with Cypress and Playwright — overview and when to use it
  16. Vitest vs Jest — what changed and how to choose today

SECTION 1 - TESTING PHILOSOPHY

Q1. What is the testing pyramid, how does the "testing trophy" differ, and what should you actually test in a frontend?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

The classic testing pyramid says: lots of fast unit tests at the bottom, fewer integration tests in the middle, very few slow E2E tests at the top. Kent C. Dodds' testing trophy reshapes this for modern frontend: a base of static analysis (TypeScript + ESLint), a small layer of unit tests, and the largest layer being integration tests — because they give the best confidence-per-effort — topped by a thin slice of E2E. The practical rule: "write tests that resemble how your software is used," so favor integration-style component tests over testing tiny implementation units in isolation.

Detailed Answer

The pyramid optimizes for speed and cost: unit tests are cheap and fast, E2E tests are expensive and brittle, so you write many of the former and few of the latter. It is still a useful mental model, but taken literally it pushes people to unit-test every function and mock everything around a component — which produces tests that pass while the app is broken.

The trophy reframes the goal as confidence, not test count. Its four tiers, bottom to top:

  • Static — TypeScript and ESLint catch a whole class of bugs (typos, wrong types, undefined access) before a test even runs. Nearly free.
  • Unit — pure functions, reducers, utilities, complex custom hooks. Fast and precise, but low on integration confidence.
  • Integration — render a component (or a small tree) and test it the way a user would, mocking only the true boundaries (usually the network). This is where the trophy says to spend most effort.
  • E2E — a real browser driving the real app (Cypress/Playwright). Highest confidence, slowest, most flaky; keep to critical happy paths.

What to actually test in a frontend: user-visible behavior — "when I type an email and click submit, I see a success message"; conditional rendering; form validation; error and loading states; and the wiring between components and data. What to avoid testing: internal state variable names, whether a specific hook was called, CSS classes, and third-party library internals.

Project Example

On a checkout flow we deleted a swathe of shallow unit tests that asserted "setState was called with X" and replaced them with a handful of integration tests: render the cart, mock the /api/checkout endpoint with MSW, click "Pay", and assert the confirmation screen appears. The suite got smaller, faster to reason about, and — critically — it started catching real regressions (a broken prop wiring) that the old mocked unit tests had happily ignored.

Senior Engineer Perspective

Interviewers use this to see whether you test for confidence or for a coverage number. A junior answer recites "many unit, few E2E." A senior answer names the trophy, explains why integration tests dominate in frontend (components are mostly glue, and users don't call your functions — they click buttons), and cites the guiding principle: "the more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they give you." Bonus: mention that static analysis is the cheapest tier and often skipped in this conversation.

Q2. What is React Testing Library's core philosophy — "test behavior, not implementation"?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

RTL's guiding principle is that tests should interact with a component the way a user does — find elements by their visible text and accessible roles, click and type on them, and assert on what appears — rather than reaching into internals like state, props, or instance methods. Tests coupled to behavior survive refactors; tests coupled to implementation break the moment you rename a state variable or restructure the component, even though nothing user-facing changed.

Detailed Answer

This is a deliberate reaction against Enzyme, the previous dominant tool, which exposed wrapper.state(), wrapper.instance(), and shallow() rendering. Those APIs let you assert on implementation details, so tests were tightly coupled to how a component worked. Refactoring class components to hooks, or splitting one component into two, would break hundreds of tests without any behavioral change — the definition of brittle.

RTL removes those escape hatches on purpose. It gives you a rendered DOM and query functions that mirror how users and assistive technology perceive the page. There is no .state(), no way to read a hook's value directly, no shallow rendering. If you cannot express your test in terms of what the user sees and does, that is usually a signal to test behavior at a different level.

Two clarifications interviewers like:

  • "Behavior" means observable output: rendered text, roles, values, what happens on interaction — not "did this function get called." (Callback props are a legitimate exception: verifying onSubmit fired with the right data is testing a contract, not an internal.)
  • This does not mean "never mock." You still mock the network boundary. The principle is about not asserting on a component's private wiring.

Code Example

// Implementation-focused (brittle) — Enzyme style
// expect(wrapper.state("count")).toBe(1);   // breaks if you rename state

// Behavior-focused (resilient) — RTL style
import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
import userEvent from "@testing-library/user-event";

test("increments the visible count", async () => {
  render(<Counter />);
  // Find by what the user sees, act like a user, assert on output.
  await userEvent.click(screen.getByRole("button", { name: /increment/i }));
  expect(screen.getByText("Count: 1")).toBeInTheDocument();
});

Senior Engineer Perspective

The phrase to land is "the test should not know how the component is built." Explain the payoff concretely: you can convert a class to a hook, memoize a child, or split a component, and a good RTL test stays green. Common trap: candidates who reach for container.querySelector('.my-class') everywhere — that reintroduces implementation coupling through CSS selectors. Mention that querying by role/label also nudges you toward accessible markup as a side benefit, and that testing a callback prop fired correctly is fine because it is part of the component's public contract.

SECTION 2 - UNIT TESTING WITH JEST

Q3. What are the Jest basics — describe/it/expect, matchers, and setup/teardown?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

describe groups related tests; it (alias test) defines a single test; expect(value) returns an assertion object you chain a matcher onto (toBe, toEqual, toContain, etc.). The lifecycle hooks — beforeEach, afterEach, beforeAll, afterAll — run setup and teardown so each test starts from a clean, predictable state.

Detailed Answer

A few matcher distinctions interviewers probe:

  • toBe vs toEqual — toBe uses Object.is (reference/primitive equality); toEqual does a deep recursive comparison. Use toBe for primitives and toEqual for objects/arrays. toStrictEqual is stricter still (checks undefined keys and types).
  • Async assertions — either await a promise then assert, or use await expect(promise).resolves.toBe(...) / .rejects.toThrow(...).
  • Negation — expect(x).not.toBe(y).
  • jest-dom matchers — @testing-library/jest-dom adds DOM-aware matchers like toBeInTheDocument(), toHaveTextContent(), toBeDisabled(), which read far better than manual node checks.

Setup/teardown scope matters: beforeEach/afterEach run around every test (good for resetting mocks and clearing state); beforeAll/afterAll run once for the whole describe block (good for expensive one-time setup like starting a mock server). Prefer beforeEach for isolation — shared mutable state that leaks between tests is the number-one cause of "passes alone, fails in the suite" flakiness.

Code Example

describe("cart totals", () => {
  let cart;

  beforeEach(() => {
    cart = createCart();            // fresh state per test
  });

  it("starts empty", () => {
    expect(cart.items).toEqual([]); // deep equality for arrays/objects
    expect(cart.total).toBe(0);     // primitive: reference equality
  });

  it("adds an item and sums the price", () => {
    cart.add({ id: 1, price: 9.99 });
    expect(cart.items).toContain(expect.objectContaining({ id: 1 }));
    expect(cart.total).toBeCloseTo(9.99); // avoid float === traps
  });

  it("rejects a negative quantity", () => {
    expect(() => cart.add({ id: 2, qty: -1 })).toThrow(/quantity/i);
  });
});

Senior Engineer Perspective

The classic gotcha is toBe vs toEqual on objects — using toBe on two equal-looking objects fails because they're different references. Also mention toBeCloseTo for floats (never toBe on 0.1 + 0.2). On lifecycle, a strong answer stresses test isolation: reset mocks in beforeEach (or set clearMocks: true in config) so one test's mock state can't bleed into the next. Knowing that test and it are aliases, and that test.each exists for table-driven tests, signals real familiarity.

Q4. How do you mock with jest.fn, jest.mock, and mock a module?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

jest.fn() creates a standalone mock function you can configure (mockReturnValue, mockResolvedValue) and assert on (toHaveBeenCalledWith). jest.mock('module') replaces an entire imported module with an auto-mock (or a factory you supply), so the code under test uses your fake instead of the real dependency. jest.spyOn(obj, 'method') wraps a real method so you can observe or override it while optionally keeping the original behavior.

Detailed Answer

Three tools for three jobs:

  • jest.fn() — a fake function. Pass it as a callback/prop and assert it was called: expect(onSave).toHaveBeenCalledWith({ id: 1 }). Configure its return with mockReturnValue / mockResolvedValue / mockImplementation.
  • jest.mock(path) — replaces a module. Jest hoists this call to the top of the file, above imports, which is why the factory can't reference outer variables that aren't prefixed with mock. Use it to stub an API client, an analytics SDK, or next/navigation.
  • jest.spyOn — best when you want to watch a real method and restore it later. Combine with mockRestore() in teardown.

Hygiene is the real topic. Mocks accumulate call history across tests. Use mockClear() (clears calls), mockReset() (clears calls + implementation), or mockRestore() (restores original, spies only). Setting clearMocks: true in the Jest config auto-clears between tests. Over-mocking is the deeper danger: if you mock everything, your test verifies your mocks, not your app.

Code Example

// 1) A plain mock function passed as a prop/callback
const onSubmit = jest.fn();
render(<Form onSubmit={onSubmit} />);
// ...interact...
expect(onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
expect(onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalledWith({ email: "a@b.com" });

// 2) Mock a whole module (factory is hoisted above imports)
jest.mock("../api/userClient", () => ({
  getUser: jest.fn().mockResolvedValue({ id: 1, name: "Ada" }),
}));
import { getUser } from "../api/userClient";

test("loads the user", async () => {
  const user = await getUser("1");
  expect(user.name).toBe("Ada");
  expect(getUser).toHaveBeenCalledWith("1");
});

// 3) Spy on a real method, then restore it
const spy = jest.spyOn(console, "error").mockImplementation(() => {});
// ...assert something logged an error...
spy.mockRestore();

Senior Engineer Perspective

Two facts separate strong candidates. First, the hoisting rule: jest.mock is moved above imports, so a factory referencing an out-of-scope variable throws unless the variable name starts with mock. Second, mock cleanup: know the difference between mockClear, mockReset, and mockRestore, and that leaking mock state causes order-dependent test failures. The senior meta-point: prefer mocking at the network boundary (MSW) over mocking your own modules, so you mock less and test more of the real integration.

Q5. How do you mock timers, dates, and fetch?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

For timers, call jest.useFakeTimers() and drive the clock forward with jest.advanceTimersByTime(ms) or jest.runAllTimers(), so debounce/throttle/setTimeout logic runs instantly and deterministically. For dates, fake timers can also freeze "now" (jest.setSystemTime(...)). For fetch, you can stub global.fetch = jest.fn() — but the better modern approach is to intercept at the network layer with MSW (see Q13).

Detailed Answer

Fake timers replace setTimeout, setInterval, and (in modern mode) Date. This is how you test a debounced search without waiting a real 400ms. Remember two things: always restore with jest.useRealTimers() in teardown, and when combining fake timers with user-event, pass userEvent.setup({ advanceTimers: jest.advanceTimersByTime }) so events and the fake clock stay in sync.

Freezing dates makes "expires tomorrow" or "created just now" tests deterministic. With modern fake timers: jest.useFakeTimers().setSystemTime(new Date("2026-07-11")). This prevents flaky tests that pass in the morning and fail at midnight.

Mocking fetch directly works but is fragile: you rebuild request/response shapes by hand, and every test re-stubs fetch.mockResolvedValueOnce(...). It couples the test to the fact that you use fetch (not axios), and it's easy to forget to assert the URL/method. MSW solves all of this by intercepting the actual network request, so your app code runs unchanged.

Code Example

// Fake timers for a debounced callback
test("debounce fires once after the delay", () => {
  jest.useFakeTimers();
  const fn = jest.fn();
  const debounced = debounce(fn, 300);

  debounced();
  debounced();
  jest.advanceTimersByTime(299);
  expect(fn).not.toHaveBeenCalled(); // still within the window
  jest.advanceTimersByTime(1);
  expect(fn).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);

  jest.useRealTimers();              // always restore
});

// Freeze "now" for deterministic date logic
jest.useFakeTimers().setSystemTime(new Date("2026-07-11T00:00:00Z"));
expect(isExpired("2026-07-10")).toBe(true);

// Quick-and-dirty fetch stub (prefer MSW instead)
global.fetch = jest.fn().mockResolvedValue({
  ok: true,
  json: async () => ({ id: 1, name: "Ada" }),
});

Senior Engineer Perspective

The trap with fake timers is deadlock: if you await something that only resolves after a timer, but never advance the clock, the test hangs. Mention the user-event + fake-timers coordination (advanceTimers option) because it bites people constantly. On dates, freezing the system time is the professional move over monkey-patching Date.now. And be ready to say why you'd reach for MSW over a hand-rolled fetch mock — the follow-up almost always goes there.

SECTION 3 - COMPONENT TESTING (RTL)

Q6. What is the difference between getBy, queryBy, and findBy queries?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

They differ on two axes: throwing behavior and async. getBy* returns the element or throws if it's missing (use when it should exist). queryBy* returns the element or null without throwing (the only correct way to assert something is absent). findBy* returns a Promise that retries until the element appears or times out (use for async/appearing elements). Each has an *AllBy variant for matching multiple elements.

Detailed Answer

QueryNo matchMatchAsync / retriesUse for
getByThrowsElementNoAssert element exists now
queryByReturns nullElementNoAssert element is absent
findByRejects (after timeout)Promise<Element>Yes (waitFor built in)Element appears after async work
getAllByThrowsElement[]NoMultiple elements exist
queryAllByReturns []Element[]NoZero-or-more, no throw
findAllByRejectsPromise<Element[]>YesMultiple appear async

The single most common mistake is using getBy to check that something is gone — getBy throws when there's no match, so the test errors instead of asserting cleanly. To assert absence you must use queryBy with .not.toBeInTheDocument(). Conversely, using queryBy where you expect an element is worse for debugging: you get a null-dereference error instead of RTL's helpful "unable to find an element" message with a DOM dump.

findBy is essentially getBy wrapped in waitFor, defaulting to a 1000ms timeout and polling as the DOM changes. It's the idiomatic way to wait for data to load.

Code Example

import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";

test("query selection", async () => {
  render(<Profile userId="1" />);

  // Present immediately -> getBy (throws if missing = clear failure)
  expect(screen.getByRole("heading", { name: /profile/i })).toBeVisible();

  // Absent -> queryBy (returns null, does NOT throw)
  expect(screen.queryByText(/error/i)).not.toBeInTheDocument();

  // Appears after async fetch -> findBy (awaits, retries)
  expect(await screen.findByText("Ada Lovelace")).toBeInTheDocument();
});

Senior Engineer Perspective

The decision tree an interviewer wants to hear: "Is it there now? getBy. Am I checking it's NOT there? queryBy. Will it appear after async work? findBy." The disqualifying answer is wrapping getBy in a try/catch to test absence. Bonus depth: findBy accepts a waitFor options object for custom timeout, and you should never mix getBy inside a manual waitFor when findBy already does that job more readably.

Q7. Why is getByRole preferred, and what is Testing Library's recommended query priority?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

getByRole is preferred because it queries the DOM the way assistive technology does — by accessibility role and accessible name — so a passing test is also evidence that the element is reachable by screen-reader users. Testing Library publishes a priority order: prefer queries everyone can use (role, label, placeholder, text), then semantic queries, and only fall back to getByTestId when nothing else works. The rule of thumb: query the way a user (sighted or not) finds the element, not by DOM structure or CSS.

Detailed Answer

The recommended priority, highest to lowest:

  1. Accessible to everyone
    • getByRole — the top choice; e.g. getByRole('button', { name: /submit/i }). Combines role + accessible name.
    • getByLabelText — the best choice for form fields (matches a real <label>).
    • getByPlaceholderText — a fallback when there's no label.
    • getByText — for non-interactive content (paragraphs, divs, spans).
    • getByDisplayValue — for the current value of a filled-in input.
  2. Semantic (HTML5/ARIA attributes) — getByAltText (images), getByTitle.
  3. Test IDs — getByTestId, an escape hatch for elements with no accessible role or stable text (e.g. a purely visual wrapper).

Why role wins: it forces accessible markup (a real <button>, an <h1>, a labeled input) and it's resilient — text can change with copy edits, but the role of "the submit button" is stable. Roles come from semantic HTML for free (<button> = button, <a href> = link, <input type="checkbox"> = checkbox) or from explicit ARIA. The { name } option matches the accessible name, computed from label, aria-label, or text content.

getByTestId should be rare. It couples the test to a data-testid attribute that has no user meaning — fine as a last resort, but if you find yourself reaching for it constantly, your markup probably lacks semantics.

Code Example

// Preferred: role + accessible name
screen.getByRole("button", { name: /save changes/i });
screen.getByRole("textbox", { name: /email/i });   // input with a label
screen.getByRole("heading", { level: 1, name: /dashboard/i });

// Great for forms: match the visible label
screen.getByLabelText(/password/i);

// Non-interactive content
screen.getByText(/welcome back/i);

// Last resort only — no role or stable text available
screen.getByTestId("chart-canvas");

// Helpful during authoring: prints all available roles for the DOM
// screen.logTestingPlaygroundURL();  or  logRoles(container);

Senior Engineer Perspective

Say the priority list and the reason: "querying by role tests accessibility for free." A strong candidate notes that overusing getByTestId is a smell that signals non-semantic markup, and that the name option maps to the ARIA accessible-name computation. Practical tip worth mentioning: screen.getByRole('...') with a wrong name prints every available role, and Testing Library's "Testing Playground" helps pick the right query — showing you actually author tests, not just recite theory.

Q8. What is the difference between user-event and fireEvent, and which should you use?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

fireEvent dispatches a single raw DOM event (e.g. one change event). user-event simulates a full user interaction: typing a character fires keydown, keypress, input, and keyup, respects disabled elements, moves focus, and so on. Prefer @testing-library/user-event — it's higher fidelity and catches bugs fireEvent misses. In v14+ it's async, so you await its methods after calling userEvent.setup().

Detailed Answer

fireEvent.change(input, { target: { value: 'abc' } }) sets the value and fires one event in one shot. But a real user typing "abc" produces a stream of key and input events per character, and many components rely on that (masking, per-keystroke validation, onKeyDown handlers). user-event's type() reproduces that sequence, so it exercises the component the way production does.

Other realism user-event adds:

  • Won't "click" or "type" into a disabled element (fireEvent will happily fire the event anyway).
  • click fires pointerdown/mousedown/focus/mouseup/click, and moves focus like a browser.
  • Rich helpers: tab(), keyboard(), selectOptions(), upload(), clear(), hover().

The v14 API change: you call const user = userEvent.setup() once (ideally before render), then await user.click(...). The methods return Promises, so forgetting await produces "not wrapped in act(...)" warnings or flaky assertions. fireEvent is still fine for events with no user-interaction equivalent (e.g. scroll, mouseOver on a non-interactive element, or firing a synthetic event a library dispatches).

Code Example

import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
import userEvent from "@testing-library/user-event";

test("filling and submitting a form", async () => {
  const user = userEvent.setup();      // v14+: set up once
  const onSubmit = jest.fn();
  render(<LoginForm onSubmit={onSubmit} />);

  await user.type(screen.getByLabelText(/email/i), "a@b.com"); // per-keystroke events
  await user.type(screen.getByLabelText(/password/i), "secret1");
  await user.click(screen.getByRole("button", { name: /log in/i }));

  expect(onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalledWith({ email: "a@b.com", password: "secret1" });
});

// fireEvent still fits low-level / non-interaction events:
// fireEvent.scroll(window, { target: { scrollY: 500 } });

Senior Engineer Perspective

The headline: "user-event simulates a real user; fireEvent dispatches one raw event — default to user-event." Show you know the v14 async migration (setup() + await), because that's a frequent source of act() warnings and flaky suites. A concrete example of the difference wins points: fireEvent can "click" a disabled button and mask a bug, whereas user-event refuses, matching real browser behavior. Note that fireEvent is still the right tool when there's no user gesture equivalent.

Q9. How do you test asynchronous UI with findBy and waitFor?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

Use findBy* to wait for an element to appear after async work (it polls until found or times out). Use waitFor(callback) to wait for an arbitrary assertion or condition to become true — for example, that a mock was called or an element disappeared (waitForElementToBeRemoved is the purpose-built version). Prefer findBy for the common "data loads and renders" case; reach for waitFor only when there's no element to query for directly.

Detailed Answer

Async UI is where most flaky tests are born. The golden rule: never use fixed setTimeout to wait — always wait for a condition. RTL's async utilities poll the DOM using a MutationObserver and resolve as soon as the condition is met (default timeout ~1000ms).

  • findByText('Ada') — the idiomatic "wait for loaded content." Equivalent to waitFor(() => getByText('Ada')) but more readable.
  • waitFor(() => expect(mock).toHaveBeenCalled()) — for non-DOM conditions. Keep the callback tiny and side-effect-free; it may run many times. Don't put multiple unrelated assertions or state changes inside it.
  • waitForElementToBeRemoved(() => screen.queryByText(/loading/i)) — the correct way to assert a spinner/toast disappeared.

Common failure modes to name: (1) forgetting to await the async query, causing the test to finish before the assertion runs; (2) "not wrapped in act()" warnings from state updates that happen after the test body ends — usually fixed by awaiting a findBy so RTL flushes the update; (3) using getBy immediately after render for data that hasn't arrived yet, which throws.

Code Example

test("shows a spinner, then the loaded user", async () => {
  render(<UserCard id="1" />);

  // Loading state is synchronous
  expect(screen.getByText(/loading/i)).toBeInTheDocument();

  // Wait for the fetched content to appear
  expect(await screen.findByRole("heading", { name: /ada lovelace/i }))
    .toBeInTheDocument();

  // And for the spinner to go away
  await waitForElementToBeRemoved(() => screen.queryByText(/loading/i));
});

test("waitFor for a non-DOM condition", async () => {
  const onLoad = jest.fn();
  render(<Widget onLoad={onLoad} />);
  await waitFor(() => expect(onLoad).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1)); // keep it minimal
});

Senior Engineer Perspective

The strongest signal is "wait for a condition, never a fixed delay." Interviewers probe the findBy vs waitFor choice: use findBy when you're waiting for an element (it's cleaner), waitFor when you're waiting for a non-DOM fact. Warn against the anti-pattern of a bloated waitFor callback with side effects or several assertions — since it re-runs, side effects fire repeatedly and a late assertion masks which condition actually failed. Connecting act() warnings to un-awaited async updates shows real debugging experience.

Q10. How do you test a custom hook with renderHook?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Hooks can only run inside a component, so use renderHook from @testing-library/react (it moved there from the old react-hooks-testing-library). It renders a tiny host component that calls your hook and exposes the latest return value on result.current. To trigger updates, call the hook's functions inside act(...); to test dependency changes, use the rerender and initialProps options; and wrap in a provider via the wrapper option when the hook needs Context.

Detailed Answer

renderHook(callback) returns { result, rerender, unmount }. result.current always reflects the hook's most recent return, so after an action you read the updated value there. Any call that causes a state update must be wrapped in act() so React flushes it before you assert (async updates use await act(...) or a waitFor on result.current).

Two important nuances:

  • Props/dependencies — pass initialProps and re-run with rerender(newProps) to test how the hook responds to changing inputs (e.g. a useDebounce(value) when value changes).
  • Context — supply a wrapper component so hooks that call useContext (custom store hooks, useQuery needing a QueryClientProvider) have their provider.

A caveat worth voicing: don't over-test trivial hooks in isolation. If a hook is only meaningful inside a component, an integration test of that component often gives more confidence. Reserve renderHook for genuinely reusable, logic-heavy hooks (a state machine, a debounce, a pagination controller).

Code Example

import { renderHook, act, waitFor } from "@testing-library/react";

test("useCounter increments", () => {
  const { result } = renderHook(() => useCounter(5));

  expect(result.current.count).toBe(5);
  act(() => result.current.increment());   // state update must be in act()
  expect(result.current.count).toBe(6);
});

test("useDebounce reacts to prop changes", () => {
  const { result, rerender } = renderHook(
    ({ value }) => useDebounce(value, 300),
    { initialProps: { value: "a" } }
  );
  rerender({ value: "ab" });               // simulate a new input
  // ...advance fake timers, then assert result.current...
});

// Hook that needs a provider
const wrapper = ({ children }) => (
  <QueryClientProvider client={queryClient}>{children}</QueryClientProvider>
);
const { result } = renderHook(() => useUser("1"), { wrapper });
await waitFor(() => expect(result.current.isSuccess).toBe(true));

Senior Engineer Perspective

Know that renderHook now ships in @testing-library/react (the standalone hooks library is deprecated) — naming the wrong package dates you. The act() requirement around state-changing calls is the most common gotcha. And the mature caveat scores points: testing a hook in isolation is right for reusable logic, but for a hook that's inseparable from one component, an integration test better reflects real usage — a direct application of the "test the way it's used" principle.

Q11. How do you test a component that depends on Context or a Redux store?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Wrap the component in its required providers at render time. The clean, reusable approach is a custom render function that wraps children in all your app providers (Redux <Provider>, theme, router, query client) and re-exports everything from RTL. For Redux, create a real store per test with a known preloaded state rather than mocking the store — that tests the actual reducer/selector wiring. Pass different context values or preloaded state to exercise different scenarios.

Detailed Answer

Context: render the component inside the matching <Context.Provider value={...}>. Passing an explicit value lets you drive the component into any state (e.g. an "authenticated" vs "logged out" auth context) without touching internals.

Redux: the recommended pattern (from the Redux docs) is a custom render that builds a fresh store with configureStore({ reducer, preloadedState }) and wraps children in <Provider store={store}>. Prefer this over mocking useSelector/useDispatch: a real store means your selectors, reducers, and connected component all run, so the test verifies real behavior. You can dispatch actions before or during the test and assert on the resulting UI. Only mock the store if you specifically need to isolate a purely presentational connected component.

A single test-utils module that re-exports a custom render keeps every test terse — you render(<Cart />, { preloadedState }) and get all providers for free. This is one of the highest-leverage patterns in a real test suite.

Code Example

// test-utils.tsx — a custom render with all app providers
import { render } from "@testing-library/react";
import { Provider } from "react-redux";
import { configureStore } from "@reduxjs/toolkit";
import rootReducer from "../store/rootReducer";

export function renderWithProviders(
  ui,
  { preloadedState, store = configureStore({ reducer: rootReducer, preloadedState }) } = {}
) {
  const Wrapper = ({ children }) => <Provider store={store}>{children}</Provider>;
  return { store, ...render(ui, { wrapper: Wrapper }) };
}
export * from "@testing-library/react";  // re-export screen, etc.

// A test using a real store with preloaded state
import { renderWithProviders, screen } from "../test-utils";

test("shows items from the store", () => {
  renderWithProviders(<Cart />, {
    preloadedState: { cart: { items: [{ id: 1, name: "Book" }] } },
  });
  expect(screen.getByText("Book")).toBeInTheDocument();
});

// A plain Context provider wrap
render(
  <AuthContext.Provider value={{ user: { name: "Ada" }, isAuthed: true }}>
    <Navbar />
  </AuthContext.Provider>
);

Senior Engineer Perspective

The key insight is "use a real store, mock the network — not the store." Building a fresh configureStore with preloadedState per test keeps tests isolated and exercises real reducers/selectors, which is far more valuable than stubbing useSelector. The custom-render / test-utils pattern signals you've maintained a real suite. Follow-up traps: needing a fresh store per test to avoid cross-test leakage, and wrapping in a router (MemoryRouter) or QueryClientProvider when the component also depends on those.

Q12. What is snapshot testing — its pros, cons, and when does it earn its keep?

ROI: ★★★☆☆ Frequency: Medium

Short Answer

A snapshot test serializes a component's rendered output to a .snap file on the first run and, on later runs, fails if the output differs. Pros: cheap to write and catches unintended UI changes. Cons: large snapshots are unreadable, break constantly on legitimate changes, and developers "just press u" to update them without reviewing — so they rot into noise. They earn their keep for small, stable, serializable output (a formatted string, a design-system icon, an error object), not for big component trees.

Detailed Answer

Snapshots test "did the output change" rather than "is the output correct" — an important distinction. On the first run Jest writes the serialized tree; thereafter any diff is a failure you review and either fix or accept with jest --updateSnapshot (-u).

The failure mode is cultural: on a large component, any real change produces a huge diff, and because updating is one keystroke, teams reflexively accept snapshots without reading them. At that point the test provides zero protection — it rubber-stamps whatever the code currently does. Large snapshots also review poorly in PRs.

Better practices:

  • Prefer inline snapshots (toMatchInlineSnapshot()) for small output — the expected value lives in the test, so it's reviewable and diffs are local.
  • Keep them small and focused; snapshot a single formatted value, not an entire page.
  • For visual regressions, use image snapshots via Playwright/Chromatic/Percy, not DOM snapshots — they catch actual rendering changes DOM snapshots miss.
  • Assert explicit, meaningful expectations (getByRole + toHaveTextContent) for anything behavioral; reserve snapshots for stable structural output.

Code Example

// Whole-tree snapshot (use sparingly — brittle, review-hostile)
