import { render } from "@testing-library/react";
test("Button renders", () => {
  const { container } = render(<Button variant="primary">Save</Button>);
  expect(container).toMatchSnapshot();
});

// Better: inline snapshot for small, stable output
test("formats currency", () => {
  expect(formatCurrency(1999, "USD")).toMatchInlineSnapshot(`"$19.99"`);
});

Senior Engineer Perspective

The nuanced take interviewers reward: "snapshots test change, not correctness, and they only add value if people actually review the diffs." Call out the press u to update anti-pattern by name. Show range by distinguishing DOM snapshots (Jest) from visual/image snapshots (Chromatic/Percy/Playwright) — the latter catch CSS regressions the former can't. Recommending inline snapshots for small values and explicit assertions for behavior demonstrates you've felt the pain of a rotten snapshot suite.

SECTION 4 - INTEGRATION & E2E

Q13. What is MSW (Mock Service Worker), and why is it better than mocking fetch?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

MSW intercepts requests at the network layer — via a Service Worker in the browser and a request interceptor in Node for tests — and responds with handlers you define per endpoint. Because it operates below your app code, your components use their real data-fetching (fetch, axios, React Query) completely unchanged. That's the advantage over stubbing global.fetch: no rewiring the fetch shape, one set of handlers reused across tests, Storybook, and even local dev, and you test the real integration rather than a hand-built fake response.

Detailed Answer

Directly mocking fetch (or jest.mock-ing your API client) has real downsides:

  • You couple tests to the transport — swap fetch for axios and every mock breaks.
  • You reconstruct Response objects (ok, status, json()) by hand, easy to get subtly wrong.
  • Mocks live per test, so there's lots of duplication and drift.
  • You never exercise the actual request-building and response-parsing code, so bugs there go untested.

MSW inverts this. You declare handlers by URL and method (http.get('/api/user/:id', resolver)) that return real Response objects via the HttpResponse helper. In Jest you start a Node server in beforeAll, resetHandlers() in afterEach (so per-test overrides don't leak), and close() in afterAll. Individual tests override a handler with server.use(...) to simulate errors, empty states, or slow responses. The same handlers can back your Storybook stories and even a browser dev mode, so mocks stay consistent everywhere.

Note: MSW v2 moved to the http/graphql namespaces and the web-standard Response (HttpResponse), replacing v1's rest and (req, res, ctx) signature — worth knowing since lots of tutorials still show the old API.

Code Example

// handlers.ts
import { http, HttpResponse } from "msw";

export const handlers = [
  http.get("/api/user/:id", ({ params }) =>
    HttpResponse.json({ id: params.id, name: "Ada Lovelace" })
  ),
];

// server.ts (Node, for Jest)
import { setupServer } from "msw/node";
import { handlers } from "./handlers";
export const server = setupServer(...handlers);

// jest.setup.ts
beforeAll(() => server.listen());
afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers()); // undo per-test overrides
afterAll(() => server.close());

// a test that overrides one endpoint to simulate an error
import { http, HttpResponse } from "msw";
import { server } from "./server";

test("shows an error state on 500", async () => {
  server.use(
    http.get("/api/user/:id", () =>
      HttpResponse.json({ message: "boom" }, { status: 500 })
    )
  );
  render(<UserCard id="1" />);            // real fetch runs, MSW intercepts
  expect(await screen.findByText(/something went wrong/i)).toBeInTheDocument();
});

Senior Engineer Perspective

The one-liner: "MSW mocks the network, not your code, so components run their real fetching path." Emphasize the lifecycle discipline — listen/resetHandlers/close — and per-test server.use() overrides for error and edge cases, since forgetting resetHandlers is a classic source of leaking state. Bonus points for the reuse story (same handlers in tests, Storybook, and dev) and for knowing the v2 API (http + HttpResponse) versus the older v1 rest/ctx style.

Q14. What does code coverage tell you — and what does it not?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Coverage measures which lines/branches/functions/statements were executed while tests ran — Jest reports all four via Istanbul. It's a useful signal for finding untested code (0% coverage is a real gap). But it says nothing about whether your assertions are meaningful: you can hit 100% coverage with tests that assert nothing. High coverage means "the code ran," not "the code is correct." Chase confidence, not a coverage percentage.

Detailed Answer

The four metrics:

  • Statements — each statement executed.
  • Branches — each side of every if/ternary/&& taken. The most informative, because untested branches are where bugs hide.
  • Functions — each function called.
  • Lines — each line run (close to statements).

What it can't see: assertion quality. A test that renders a component and never checks anything will still mark all those lines "covered." Coverage also can't tell you about missing cases you never wrote a test for at all (it only measures code you have), nor about integration correctness, race conditions, accessibility, or visual bugs.

Chasing 100% is usually a net negative — the last 10-20% (error branches, defensive guards) is expensive and often tested with low-value tests written purely to move the number. A pragmatic policy: set a reasonable threshold (e.g. 70-80%) via coverageThreshold to catch regressions, exclude generated/config files, and read coverage as a map of gaps to investigate, not a scoreboard. Mutation testing (e.g. Stryker) actually measures assertion quality by changing code and checking whether tests fail — a better proxy for "do the tests catch bugs."

Code Example

// jest.config.js
module.exports = {
  collectCoverage: true,
  coverageReporters: ["text", "lcov"],
  collectCoverageFrom: [
    "src/**/*.{ts,tsx}",
    "!src/**/*.d.ts",
    "!src/**/*.stories.tsx",     // exclude noise from the denominator
  ],
  coverageThreshold: {
    global: { branches: 75, functions: 80, lines: 80, statements: 80 },
  },
};

// This test gives 100% coverage of add() but asserts NOTHING useful:
test("covers add", () => {
  add(2, 3);                     // executed -> "covered", but no expect()
});
// Coverage: 100%. Confidence: 0%.

Senior Engineer Perspective

The maxim to deliver: "coverage tells you what code ran, not whether it's correct." Give the killer example — a test with no expect still scores 100%. Argue against a blanket 100% mandate (diminishing returns, incentivizes low-value tests) while defending a sensible threshold to catch regressions. Naming branch coverage as the most useful metric, and mutation testing (Stryker) as the real measure of assertion strength, shows depth beyond the standard talking points.

Q15. What is end-to-end testing with Cypress and Playwright, and when should you use it?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

E2E tests drive a real browser against the running app (real or realistically-stubbed backend), clicking through complete user journeys — login, checkout, signup — exactly as a user would. Cypress and Playwright are the two dominant tools. They give the highest confidence but are the slowest and most flaky, so you reserve them for a handful of business-critical happy paths, not exhaustive coverage. Everything cheaper (unit, integration/RTL) should catch the rest.

Detailed Answer

E2E complements, not replaces, component tests. RTL renders a component in jsdom (a simulated DOM, no real browser, no real navigation); E2E launches Chromium/Firefox/WebKit and exercises routing, real network, cookies, redirects, and cross-page flows that jsdom can't. Use E2E to answer "can a user actually complete the core journey end to end," and to smoke-test after deploys.

AspectCypressPlaywright
OriginCypress.io, 2017Microsoft, 2020
BrowsersChromium, Firefox, WebKit(exp.)Chromium, Firefox, WebKit — first-class
Execution modelRuns in the browser event loopOut-of-process via CDP/drivers
ParallelismPaid dashboard / pluginsBuilt-in, free, fast
LanguagesJavaScript/TypeScriptTS/JS, Python, Java, .NET
WaitingAutomatic retry-abilityAuto-waiting + web-first assertions
MomentumMature, great DX/time-travel UIFast-growing, now often the default

Both auto-wait for elements (reducing flakiness versus manual sleeps), record videos/screenshots on failure, and support network stubbing. Playwright's built-in free parallelism, true multi-browser support, and multi-language bindings have made it the common new-project choice; Cypress remains beloved for its interactive time-travel debugger and developer experience. Keep the E2E suite small and stable — flaky E2E that everyone ignores is worse than none.

Code Example

// Playwright
import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

test("user can log in", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("/login");
  await page.getByLabel("Email").fill("a@b.com");
  await page.getByLabel("Password").fill("secret1");
  await page.getByRole("button", { name: /log in/i }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole("heading", { name: /dashboard/i })).toBeVisible();
});

// Cypress (equivalent flow)
it("user can log in", () => {
  cy.visit("/login");
  cy.findByLabelText("Email").type("a@b.com");
  cy.findByLabelText("Password").type("secret1");
  cy.findByRole("button", { name: /log in/i }).click();
  cy.findByRole("heading", { name: /dashboard/i }).should("be.visible");
});

Senior Engineer Perspective

Frame E2E by cost/confidence: highest confidence, highest cost and flakiness, so cover only critical journeys and let RTL handle breadth — a direct callback to the testing trophy from Q1. Note that both tools share Testing-Library-style queries (getByRole), so the accessible-query habit transfers. On tool choice, the current honest answer is "Playwright has become the default for new projects — free parallelism, true cross-browser, multi-language — while Cypress still wins on interactive DX." Mention that E2E should run against seeded/stubbed data for determinism, not a shared mutable environment.

Q16. Vitest vs Jest — what's the difference and how do you choose today?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Jest is the long-standing, battle-tested test runner ubiquitous in the React/CRA world. Vitest is a newer, Vite-native runner with a nearly Jest-compatible API (describe/it/expect, same matchers) that's dramatically faster in Vite projects because it shares Vite's transform pipeline and needs no Babel/ts-jest transpile step, plus first-class ESM and TypeScript support and instant HMR-style watch mode. The current guidance: if your app is built with Vite, use Vitest; if you're on Next.js/CRA/webpack with an established Jest setup, Jest is still perfectly fine.

Detailed Answer

The API overlap is deliberate — Vitest was designed as a near drop-in replacement, so most Jest tests run with minimal changes (RTL, jest-dom, and MSW all work with either). Key differences:

AspectJestVitest
Config / transformBabel or ts-jest; separate configReuses your vite.config & plugins
ESM supportHistorically awkward (needs flags)Native ESM first
Speed (Vite apps)Slower (extra transpile)Much faster; instant watch
Mocking APIjest.fn/mock/spyOnvi.fn/mock/spyOn (same shape)
GlobalsOn by defaultOpt-in (globals: true) or import
Ecosystem maturityLargest; most docs/pluginsNewer but growing fast

Practical migration notes: replace the jest namespace with vi (or enable a Jest-compat alias), and either set globals: true or import describe/it/expect from vitest. Both use jsdom/happy-dom for the DOM environment and pair with React Testing Library identically. Vitest's headline win is speed and zero-config alignment with a Vite toolchain — no maintaining a parallel Babel/ts-jest config that can drift from how the app actually builds.

Why Jest still holds ground: it's the default in Next.js and many enterprise codebases, has the deepest ecosystem and documentation, and there's little reason to migrate a large, working, webpack-based suite. The choice is mostly dictated by your build tool, not by one being "better."

Code Example

// Nearly identical test — only the mock namespace changes.

// Jest
import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
const onClick = jest.fn();
test("calls onClick", () => {
  render(<Button onClick={onClick}>Go</Button>);
  screen.getByRole("button").click();
  expect(onClick).toHaveBeenCalled();
});

// Vitest
import { describe, it, expect, vi } from "vitest";  // or globals: true
import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
const onClick = vi.fn();                            // vi instead of jest
it("calls onClick", () => {
  render(<Button onClick={onClick}>Go</Button>);
  screen.getByRole("button").click();
  expect(onClick).toHaveBeenCalled();
});

Senior Engineer Perspective

The mature framing is "choose by toolchain, not hype": Vitest for Vite projects (speed, native ESM/TS, shared config), Jest for established webpack/Next.js suites. Show you know the API is intentionally near-identical (vi mirrors jest), so migration is mechanical and RTL/MSW/jest-dom carry over. Interviewers like hearing that the testing approach — behavior over implementation, integration-first, MSW at the boundary — is identical regardless of runner; the runner is an implementation detail, and switching one doesn't change how you write good tests.

18 - ACCESSIBILITY (A11Y)

Target Audience: Frontend / React Engineer (3–6 Years) Goal: Not just answer questions, but survive follow-up grilling from experienced interviewers.

TOP HIGHEST-ROI QUESTIONS IN THIS CHAPTER

  1. Why does accessibility matter — legally, for UX, and for SEO?
  2. What are WCAG and the POUR principles, and what do the A/AA/AAA levels mean?
  3. Why should you reach for semantic HTML first, and why does it beat "div soup"?
  4. When should you use ARIA, and what is the first rule of ARIA?
  5. What are ARIA roles, states, and properties?
  6. How does an element get its accessible name (label / aria-label / aria-labelledby)?
  7. How do you build accessible forms with proper labels and error messaging?
  8. How do you handle keyboard navigation, tab order, and focus management?
  9. How do you trap focus in a modal and restore it when the modal closes?
  10. How do you manage focus on route change in a single-page app?
  11. What are skip links and why do they matter?
  12. What are the color-contrast requirements and how do you meet them?
  13. How do live regions (aria-live) announce dynamic updates to screen readers?
  14. How do you build accessible custom components (dropdown, modal, tabs) in React?
  15. How do you test accessibility — automated (axe, jest-axe, eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y) vs manual — and what are the common React a11y mistakes?

SECTION 1 - FOUNDATIONS

Q1. Why does accessibility matter — legally, for UX, and for SEO?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Accessibility (a11y) means people with disabilities can perceive, understand, and operate your app. It matters for three concrete reasons: legal — laws like the ADA, Section 508, the EU's EN 301 549 / European Accessibility Act, and the UK Equality Act expose companies to real lawsuits; UX — roughly 15–20% of people have a disability, and accessible design (keyboard support, clear focus, good contrast) helps everyone, including temporary and situational impairments; and SEO — the same semantic structure that screen readers rely on (headings, landmarks, alt text, labels) is exactly what search-engine crawlers parse.

Detailed Answer

Disability is broader than most engineers assume. It spans visual (blindness, low vision, color blindness), motor (can't use a mouse, relies on keyboard or switch devices), auditory (needs captions), and cognitive (needs clear language, predictable layouts). It's also often temporary (a broken arm) or situational (bright sunlight, a noisy train, holding a baby). Building for the permanent case improves the product for the whole spectrum.

On the legal side, high-profile cases (e.g. Domino's in the US) confirmed that websites and apps count as "places of public accommodation." Most demand letters cite WCAG 2.1 AA as the objective standard. Accessibility is therefore a compliance requirement, not a nice-to-have, for anything customer-facing.

On UX and SEO, accessible markup is machine-readable markup. A crawler and a screen reader both need to know "this is the main content, this is a navigation region, this image shows X, this button does Y." A well-structured accessible page tends to rank and convert better because it's genuinely easier to use.

Senior Engineer Perspective

Interviewers want to hear that a11y is a requirement, not a phase-two polish task, and that it's cheapest when designed in rather than retrofitted. The line that lands: "the same semantics that make a screen reader work make Google's crawler work — accessibility and SEO are the same investment." Bonus: mention the "curb-cut effect" — features built for disability (curb cuts, captions, keyboard support) end up benefiting everyone.

Q2. What are WCAG and the POUR principles, and what do the A/AA/AAA levels mean?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) is the W3C standard that defines what "accessible" means, organised under four principles remembered by the acronym POUR: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust. Each guideline has testable success criteria graded at three conformance levels: A (minimum), AA (the practical/legal target), and AAA (enhanced, rarely required site-wide).

Detailed Answer

The four POUR principles in plain terms:

  • Perceivable — users can perceive the content: text alternatives for images, captions for media, sufficient color contrast, content not conveyed by color alone.
  • Operable — users can operate the UI: everything works by keyboard, enough time to read/act, no seizure-inducing flashing, clear focus indicators and navigation.
  • Understandable — content and operation are predictable: readable language, consistent navigation, clear labels, helpful error identification and recovery.
  • Robust — content works across current and future user agents and assistive tech: valid markup, correct name/role/value for all UI components.
LevelMeaningTypical target
ABare minimum; blocking barriers removedNever sufficient alone
AAAddresses the biggest, most common barriersThe standard almost everyone must meet (laws, contracts)
AAAHighest bar (e.g. 7:1 contrast, sign language for video)Aspirational; not required across a whole site

Versions: WCAG 2.0 (2008), 2.1 (2018, added mobile/low-vision/cognitive criteria), 2.2 (2023, added focus-appearance and dragging alternatives). WCAG 3.0 is in draft. AA of 2.1/2.2 is the current practical benchmark.

Senior Engineer Perspective

You don't need to memorise every criterion, but you must be able to name POUR, know that AA is the target, and cite a couple of concrete AA criteria (4.5:1 text contrast, keyboard operability, visible focus, labels/instructions). Interviewers use this to separate people who've actually shipped compliant work from people who've only heard the buzzword. A good tell: knowing WCAG describes outcomes, while ARIA and semantic HTML are the techniques you use to satisfy them.

Q3. Why should you reach for semantic HTML first, and why does it beat "div soup"?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

Semantic HTML elements (<button>, <a>, <nav>, <main>, <label>, <h1>–<h6>) come with built-in role, keyboard behaviour, focus management, and states — for free. "Div soup" (<div onClick> everywhere) has none of that: a div is announced as nothing, isn't focusable, doesn't respond to Enter/Space, and forces you to reimplement everything the browser already gave you. Native first is faster, more robust, and less bug-prone.

Detailed Answer

Every native interactive element ships an entire accessibility contract. A real <button> is in the tab order, exposes the "button" role to screen readers, fires on both Enter and Space, shows a focus ring, and works with form submission. To make a <div> equivalent you'd have to add role="button", tabIndex={0}, a keydown handler for Enter and Space, and a focus style — and you'll still miss edge cases (right-click, high-contrast mode, forced-colors).

Semantic elements also give you landmarks (<header>, <nav>, <main>, <footer>, <aside>) that let screen-reader users jump directly to regions, and a heading outline (h1–h6) that acts like a table of contents. Div soup produces a flat, unnavigable page.

Code Example

// BAD: div soup — reinvents everything, still incomplete
<div className="btn" onClick={save}>Save</div>

// To make that div even roughly correct you must add ALL of this:
<div
  role="button"
  tabIndex={0}
  onClick={save}
  onKeyDown={(e) => {
    if (e.key === "Enter" || e.key === " ") { e.preventDefault(); save(); }
  }}
>
  Save
</div>

// GOOD: the native element gives role, focus, Enter/Space, and focus ring for free
<button type="button" onClick={save}>Save</button>

// Landmarks + headings give screen-reader users structure to navigate
<header>...</header>
<nav aria-label="Primary">...</nav>
<main>
  <h1>Dashboard</h1>
  <section><h2>Reports</h2>...</section>
</main>
<footer>...</footer>

Project Example

A common cleanup on a React codebase: replacing clickable <div> cards and icon "buttons" with real <button>/<a> elements. It usually deletes dozens of hand-rolled keydown handlers and tabIndex props, fixes a batch of axe violations at once, and makes the whole app keyboard-operable with far less code.

Senior Engineer Perspective

The one-liner interviewers want: "use the platform." The strongest signal is knowing exactly what you give up with a div — role, focusability, Enter/Space, focus ring — and that <a> is for navigation (has an href) while <button> is for actions. Watch for the trap of <a href="#"> or <a> with an onClick but no href used as a fake button — that's the same anti-pattern wearing a different tag.

SECTION 2 - SEMANTIC HTML & ARIA

Q4. When should you use ARIA, and what is the first rule of ARIA?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) is a set of attributes that add roles, states, and properties to markup so assistive tech can understand custom widgets. The first rule of ARIA is: don't use ARIA if a native HTML element or attribute already gives you the semantics and behaviour you need. ARIA changes only how something is announced — it adds no behaviour, no keyboard handling, no focus. Use it only for gaps native HTML can't fill.

Detailed Answer

The five rules of ARIA, condensed:

  • 1. Prefer native HTML; only use ARIA when no native element fits.
  • 2. Don't change native semantics unless you must (don't put role="heading" on a <button>).
  • 3. All interactive ARIA widgets must be keyboard-operable.
  • 4. Don't put role="presentation" or aria-hidden="true" on a focusable element — you'll create an element that's reachable but invisible to screen readers.
  • 5. Every interactive element needs an accessible name.

The crucial mental model: ARIA is a promise to the screen reader, not an implementation. Writing role="button" makes the element announced as a button but does not make Enter/Space work or make it focusable — you must add that yourself. This is why "no ARIA is better than bad ARIA": a wrong or unfulfilled promise actively misleads users.

Code Example

// WRONG: ARIA that duplicates native semantics (rule 1 violation)
<button role="button">Save</button>         // redundant
<input type="checkbox" role="checkbox" />    // redundant

// WRONG: role without the behaviour ARIA promises (rule 3 violation)
<div role="button">Save</div>
// announced as a button, but not focusable and Enter/Space do nothing

// RIGHT: use ARIA to fill a real gap native HTML can't express
<nav aria-label="Pagination">...</nav>          // distinguish multiple navs
<button aria-expanded={open} aria-controls="menu">Menu</button>
<ul id="menu" hidden={!open}>...</ul>

// RIGHT: hide decorative content from the accessibility tree
<span aria-hidden="true">🎉</span>

Senior Engineer Perspective

Say the first rule verbatim and then prove you understand why: ARIA adds semantics but zero behaviour, so misapplied ARIA is worse than none. Interviewers love the follow-up "what does role='button' on a div actually get you?" — the answer is "the announcement, but you still owe tabIndex, keyboard handlers, and focus styles." Mention that aria-hidden="true" on a focusable element is a classic footgun (rule 4).

Q5. What are ARIA roles, states, and properties?

ROI: ★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

ARIA describes UI to assistive tech in three parts. A role says what an element is (role="dialog", role="tablist"). States describe the current, changeable condition (aria-expanded, aria-checked, aria-disabled, aria-selected). Properties describe more static relationships and features (aria-label, aria-labelledby, aria-controls, aria-required). Together they form the "name, role, value" that WCAG 4.1.2 requires for every component.

Detailed Answer

The practical difference between a state and a property is how often it changes. States flip in response to user interaction and must be kept in sync in React — e.g. toggling aria-expanded when a disclosure opens. Properties tend to be set once and describe structure or naming.

CategoryExamplesNote
Roledialog, tab, tablist, tabpanel, alert, menu, switchSet once; defines the widget type
Statearia-expanded, aria-checked, aria-selected, aria-disabled, aria-pressed, aria-currentDynamic; update on interaction
Propertyaria-label, aria-labelledby, aria-describedby, aria-controls, aria-haspopup, aria-requiredMostly static; naming/relationships

In React, the key discipline is that ARIA state attributes are driven by your component state and re-render like any other prop — never let the DOM's ARIA and your state drift apart.

Code Example

function Disclosure({ title, children }) {
  const [open, setOpen] = React.useState(false);
  return (
    <>
      <button
        aria-expanded={open}          {/* STATE, synced to React state */}
        aria-controls="panel"         {/* PROPERTY, relationship */}
        onClick={() => setOpen(o => !o)}
      >
        {title}
      </button>
      <div id="panel" role="region" hidden={!open}>   {/* ROLE */}
        {children}
      </div>
    </>
  );
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

Frame it as "name, role, value" from WCAG 4.1.2 — that vocabulary signals depth. The senior insight is the React-specific one: ARIA states are just another piece of UI that must be derived from your state, so they belong in the render output, not set imperatively via a ref where they can desync. Note booleans are strings in the a11y tree but React lets you pass real booleans (aria-expanded={open}) — except quirks like aria-hidden which you often gate so it's absent rather than "false".

Q6. How does an element get its accessible name (label / aria-label / aria-labelledby)?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

The accessible name is the string a screen reader announces for an element (e.g. "Search, edit text" or "Close, button"). It's computed from a priority order: aria-labelledby wins, then aria-label, then a native association like a <label> tied to an input, then the element's own text content, and finally title. For form fields, prefer a real <label>; use aria-label only when there's no visible text (e.g. an icon-only button).

Detailed Answer

The accessible-name computation (simplified, highest priority first):

  1. aria-labelledby — references the id(s) of other elements; their text becomes the name. Best when a visible element already holds the label text.
  2. aria-label — a literal string you supply. Use for icon buttons and cases with no visible label. Downside: it's invisible, so it can drift from what's on screen and isn't translated by the page.
  3. Native labelling — a <label for="id"> (or wrapping label) for form controls, alt for images, <caption>/<legend>.
  4. Content — the element's own visible text (a <button>Save</button> is named "Save").

Two related but distinct concepts: the name (what it is) and the description (extra detail via aria-describedby, e.g. a hint or an error message). Don't stuff hints into the label — use a description.

Code Example

// Best for forms: visible, clickable, translatable native label
<label htmlFor="email">Email</label>
<input id="email" type="email" />

// Icon-only button: no visible text, so supply aria-label
<button aria-label="Close dialog">
  <XIcon aria-hidden="true" />   {/* hide the decorative icon */}
</button>

// aria-labelledby: reuse a visible heading as the name (great for dialogs)
<div role="dialog" aria-labelledby="dlg-title" aria-describedby="dlg-desc">
  <h2 id="dlg-title">Delete account</h2>
  <p id="dlg-desc">This action cannot be undone.</p>
</div>

// aria-labelledby can concatenate multiple ids in order
<span id="unit">Price in USD</span>
<input aria-labelledby="unit amount-label" />
<span id="amount-label">amount</span>

Senior Engineer Perspective

Interviewers probe the priority order and, critically, that aria-label is a last resort, not a default — a visible <label> helps sighted, cognitive, and voice-control users too (voice users say the visible label). Common bugs to name: placeholder-as-label (disappears on input, poor contrast, not a real name), and icon buttons with no name announced as just "button." Distinguish name vs description (aria-describedby) — a frequent follow-up.

Q7. How do you build accessible forms with proper labels and error messaging?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

Every control needs a programmatically associated <label>. Group related controls with <fieldset>/<legend>. Mark invalid fields with aria-invalid, link the error text with aria-describedby, indicate required with the native required attribute (and/or aria-required), and announce errors so screen-reader users hear them — either by moving focus to the first error or exposing the message in a live region. Don't rely on color alone to signal errors.

Detailed Answer

Accessible-form checklist:

  • Labels — visible <label htmlFor> for each input; never placeholder as the only label.
  • Grouping — radio groups and checkbox groups belong in a <fieldset> with a <legend> describing the group.
  • Required & format — use native required; describe format rules with aria-describedby hint text, not just placeholder.
  • Errors — set aria-invalid="true", connect the message via aria-describedby, and make the error text itself perceivable (icon + text, not color only).
  • Announcing — on submit, either focus the first invalid field (moves the SR there and reads its error) or render an error summary at the top in a live region / focus it.

In React with react-hook-form or Formik, wire aria-invalid and aria-describedby from the form state so they update on validation.

Code Example

function EmailField({ error }) {
  return (
    <div>
      <label htmlFor="email">Email</label>
      <input
        id="email"
        type="email"
        required
        aria-invalid={error ? true : undefined}
        aria-describedby={error ? "email-error email-hint" : "email-hint"}
      />
      <p id="email-hint">We'll never share your email.</p>
      {error && (
        <p id="email-error" role="alert">   {/* announced immediately */}
          {error}
        </p>
      )}
    </div>
  );
}

// Grouping radios correctly
<fieldset>
  <legend>Notification preference</legend>
  <label><input type="radio" name="notify" value="email" /> Email</label>
  <label><input type="radio" name="notify" value="sms" /> SMS</label>
</fieldset>

Senior Engineer Perspective

The senior differentiators: (1) errors must be announced, not just shown — role="alert" on the message or focusing the first bad field is the mechanism; (2) never signal validity with color alone (WCAG 1.4.1) — pair it with text/icons; (3) associate the error with the input via aria-describedby so it's read when focus lands there. A great detail: an error summary at the top that you focus on submit scales better than per-field focus for long forms, and it doubles as a set of skip-links to each error.

SECTION 3 - INTERACTION & KEYBOARD

Q8. How do you handle keyboard navigation, tab order, and focus management?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

Everything a mouse can do must be doable by keyboard (WCAG 2.1.1). Tab order should follow the DOM order — so structure your markup in reading order and avoid positive tabIndex. Use tabIndex={0} to make a custom control focusable, tabIndex={-1} to make an element focusable only programmatically (via .focus()), and never positive values, which hijack the natural order. Always keep a visible focus indicator.

Detailed Answer

Key rules:

  • Follow DOM order. The tab sequence is the DOM order of focusable elements. Reordering visually with CSS (flex/grid order, absolute positioning) can desync visual and tab order — a real trap.
  • tabIndex values: 0 = in natural order; -1 = focusable by script only (for roving focus, error fields, headings you jump to); positive numbers = an anti-pattern that overrides natural order and creates a maintenance nightmare.
  • Expected keys. Widgets follow the ARIA Authoring Practices: Enter/Space activate buttons, arrow keys move within composite widgets (menus, tabs, radios), Escape closes overlays.
  • Visible focus. Never do outline: none without an equally clear replacement. Use :focus-visible to show rings for keyboard users without cluttering mouse clicks.
  • Roving tabindex for composite widgets: only one item is tabIndex={0} at a time, the rest are -1, and arrow keys move the "0".

Code Example

/* Keep focus visible for keyboard users only */
button:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid #1f4e79;
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

// Roving tabindex: arrow keys move focus among toolbar buttons
function Toolbar({ items }) {
  const [active, setActive] = React.useState(0);
  const refs = React.useRef([]);

  function onKeyDown(e) {
    if (e.key === "ArrowRight") {
      const next = (active + 1) % items.length;
      setActive(next);
      refs.current[next].focus();
    }
    if (e.key === "ArrowLeft") {
      const prev = (active - 1 + items.length) % items.length;
      setActive(prev);
      refs.current[prev].focus();
    }
  }

  return (
    <div role="toolbar" onKeyDown={onKeyDown}>
      {items.map((label, i) => (
        <button
          key={label}
          ref={(el) => (refs.current[i] = el)}
          tabIndex={i === active ? 0 : -1}   {/* only one in tab order */}
        >
          {label}
        </button>
      ))}
    </div>
  );
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

Two lines that mark a senior: "tab order should equal DOM order — never use positive tabIndex," and "removing the outline without a replacement is a WCAG failure; use :focus-visible." Expect follow-ups on the visual-vs-DOM-order desync caused by CSS reordering, and on the roving-tabindex pattern for composite widgets (only one stop, arrows move within). Bonus: mention that you test by unplugging the mouse and driving the whole flow with Tab, Shift+Tab, arrows, Enter, Space, Escape.

Q9. How do you trap focus in a modal and restore it when the modal closes?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

When a modal opens: move focus into it (to the first focusable element or the dialog itself), trap Tab/Shift+Tab so focus can't escape to the page behind it, mark the rest of the page inert (aria-hidden or the inert attribute) so screen readers can't wander out, and close on Escape. When it closes: restore focus to the element that opened it (the trigger). The native <dialog> element with showModal() does most of this for you.

Detailed Answer

A correct accessible modal handles all of:

  • Role + name — role="dialog" (or alertdialog), aria-modal="true", and an accessible name via aria-labelledby.
  • Initial focus — send focus inside on open (first field, or the dialog container with tabIndex={-1}).
  • Focus trap — wrap Tab from the last focusable element back to the first and Shift+Tab from the first back to the last.
  • Background inert — the content behind must not be focusable or read; the inert attribute (or aria-hidden) on the app root achieves this.
  • Escape to close, and clicking the backdrop where appropriate.
  • Restore focus — remember document.activeElement before opening and .focus() it on close, or nothing has focus and the SR user is stranded.

In practice, use a battle-tested primitive — the native <dialog>, Radix UI Dialog, React Aria, or Headless UI — rather than reimplementing the trap, which is easy to get subtly wrong.

Code Example

function Modal({ open, onClose, labelledBy, children }) {
  const dialogRef = React.useRef(null);
  const lastFocused = React.useRef(null);

  React.useEffect(() => {
    if (!open) return;
    lastFocused.current = document.activeElement;   // remember trigger
    const dialog = dialogRef.current;
    dialog.focus();                                 // move focus in

    function onKeyDown(e) {
      if (e.key === "Escape") onClose();
      if (e.key !== "Tab") return;
      const focusable = dialog.querySelectorAll(
        'a[href], button:not([disabled]), input, textarea, select, [tabindex]:not([tabindex="-1"])'
      );
      const first = focusable[0];
      const last = focusable[focusable.length - 1];
      if (e.shiftKey && document.activeElement === first) {
        e.preventDefault(); last.focus();           // wrap to end
      } else if (!e.shiftKey && document.activeElement === last) {
        e.preventDefault(); first.focus();          // wrap to start
      }
    }
    dialog.addEventListener("keydown", onKeyDown);
    return () => {
      dialog.removeEventListener("keydown", onKeyDown);
      lastFocused.current?.focus();                 // restore focus on close
    };
  }, [open, onClose]);

  if (!open) return null;
  return (
    <div className="backdrop" onClick={onClose}>
      <div
        ref={dialogRef}
        role="dialog"
        aria-modal="true"
        aria-labelledby={labelledBy}
        tabIndex={-1}
        onClick={(e) => e.stopPropagation()}
      >
        {children}
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

The single most-forgotten step is restoring focus to the trigger on close — without it the keyboard/SR user is dumped at the top of the document. Interviewers also want aria-modal plus making the background inert (otherwise a screen reader can Tab or swipe into the hidden page). The mature answer: "I wouldn't hand-roll this in production — I'd use the native <dialog> or Radix/React Aria, which handle the trap, inert, and restore correctly." Knowing it well enough to explain the trap, but choosing a library, is the senior move.

Q10. How do you manage focus on route change in a single-page app?

ROI: ★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

In an MPA, a full page load resets focus to the top and the screen reader announces the new page. In an SPA, navigation only swaps components — focus stays put and nothing is announced, so keyboard/SR users don't realise the page changed. The fix: on each route change, move focus to a sensible target (usually the new page's <h1> or a focusable main container) and/or announce the new page title in a live region.

Detailed Answer

Two complementary techniques:

  • Focus management — after the route renders, call .focus() on the page's heading or main region. Give it tabIndex={-1} so it's programmatically focusable without entering the tab order. This mirrors the native "focus resets on load" behaviour and gives SR users the page heading.
  • Route announcer — an aria-live region that you update with the new page's title/name so a change is spoken even if you don't move focus. Frameworks like Next.js and Gatsby ship a route announcer; with React Router you add one yourself.

Also update document.title per route — assistive tech and browser history rely on it, and it's part of the announcement.

Code Example

import { useLocation } from "react-router-dom";

// Focus the page heading after each navigation
function useFocusOnRouteChange(headingRef) {
  const { pathname } = useLocation();
  React.useEffect(() => {
    headingRef.current?.focus();
  }, [pathname, headingRef]);
}

function Page({ title, children }) {
  const headingRef = React.useRef(null);
  useFocusOnRouteChange(headingRef);
  React.useEffect(() => { document.title = title + " — MyApp"; }, [title]);

  return (
    <main>
      <h1 ref={headingRef} tabIndex={-1}>{title}</h1>   {/* focusable target */}
      {children}
    </main>
  );
}

// Optional: a global route announcer (visually hidden live region)
function RouteAnnouncer({ message }) {
  return (
    <div
      aria-live="assertive"
      style={{ position: "absolute", width: 1, height: 1, overflow: "hidden",
               clip: "rect(0 0 0 0)", whiteSpace: "nowrap" }}
    >
      {message}
    </div>
  );
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

The core insight interviewers reward: "client-side routing breaks the browser's built-in focus reset and page announcement, so I have to recreate both." Focusing the <h1> (with tabIndex={-1}) is the standard pattern; a live-region route announcer is the belt-and-braces addition. Note Next.js App Router does this automatically, but a plain React Router SPA does not — a great "gotcha" to raise. Avoid tabIndex={0} on the heading, which would wrongly add it to the tab order.

Q11. What are skip links and why do they matter?

ROI: ★★★ Frequency: Medium

Short Answer

A skip link is a "Skip to main content" link that's the first focusable element on the page. It lets keyboard and screen-reader users jump past the repeated header/nav (which can be dozens of Tab stops) straight to the main content. It's commonly visually hidden until it receives focus, then appears. It satisfies WCAG 2.4.1 "Bypass Blocks."

Detailed Answer

Without a skip link, a keyboard user must tab through the entire masthead and navigation on every page before reaching content — exhausting on a site with a big nav. The skip link targets the main region's id; to make focus actually land there (not just scroll), the target should be focusable (tabIndex={-1}) or be a natural landmark like <main id="main">. It's typically hidden off-screen and revealed with :focus so it doesn't clutter the visual design but is available to keyboard users.

Landmarks (<main>, <nav>) provide a parallel bypass mechanism for screen-reader users (they can jump by region), so skip links most directly help sighted keyboard-only users.

Code Example

// First element inside <body>
<a className="skip-link" href="#main">Skip to main content</a>
...
<main id="main" tabIndex={-1}>
  <h1>Dashboard</h1>
</main>

/* Hidden until focused, then visible */
.skip-link {
  position: absolute;
  left: -9999px;
}
.skip-link:focus {
  left: 8px;
  top: 8px;
  background: #1f4e79;
  color: #fff;
  padding: 8px 12px;
  z-index: 1000;
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

The nuance seniors add: make the skip link's target focusable (tabIndex={-1} on <main>), because in some browsers jumping to an anchor scrolls the page but doesn't move keyboard focus — so the next Tab starts from the top again. Also: don't hide it with display:none (that removes it entirely) — position it off-screen so it's reachable and reveal on focus. It's WCAG 2.4.1, and it primarily serves keyboard-only users, complementing landmark navigation for SR users.

Q12. What are the color-contrast requirements and how do you meet them?

ROI: ★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

WCAG AA requires a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text (≥ 24px, or ≥ 18.66px bold) and for meaningful UI components / graphical objects and focus indicators. And you must never convey information by color alone (WCAG 1.4.1) — pair color with text, icons, or patterns. Check ratios with browser DevTools, the axe extension, or contrast checkers.

Detailed Answer

ContentWCAG AAWCAG AAA
Normal text4.5:17:1
Large text (≥24px / ≥18.66px bold)3:14.5:1
UI components & graphics (borders, icons, focus ring)3:1—

Two rules people conflate but shouldn't: contrast (1.4.3) is about legibility for low vision; use of color (1.4.1) is about not relying on hue alone — a red-only "error" state is invisible to a colorblind user, so add an icon or text. Placeholder text and disabled controls are frequent contrast failures. Also verify contrast holds in both light and dark themes.

Code Example

// BAD: status conveyed only by color
<span style={{ color: isError ? "red" : "green" }}>●</span>

// GOOD: color + icon + text (survives color blindness and grayscale)
<span className={isError ? "status status--error" : "status status--ok"}>
  {isError ? "✕ Failed" : "✓ Passed"}
</span>

/* Ensure the text itself meets 4.5:1 against its background.
   e.g. #595959 on #ffffff ≈ 7:1 (passes AA and AAA)
        #999999 on #ffffff ≈ 2.85:1 (FAILS AA) */

Senior Engineer Perspective

Have the numbers ready: 4.5:1 normal, 3:1 large text and UI/focus indicators. The distinction interviewers hunt for is contrast (1.4.3) vs color-alone (1.4.1) — they're separate criteria. Real-world traps to name: light-gray placeholder text, low-contrast disabled buttons that still need to be perceivable, brand colors that fail on white, and forgetting to re-check the dark theme. WCAG 2.2 also adds a focus-appearance requirement, so give focus rings real contrast and size.

SECTION 4 - TESTING & REACT

Q13. How do live regions (aria-live) announce dynamic updates to screen readers?

ROI: ★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

When content updates without a page reload (a toast, a search-results count, a form-submit result), a screen reader won't notice unless the region is a live region. Marking a container with aria-live="polite" (announce when idle) or aria-live="assertive" (interrupt immediately) makes the SR read out changes to that region. role="status" ≈ polite and role="alert" ≈ assertive are convenient shortcuts.

Detailed Answer

  • polite — waits until the user is idle; use for non-urgent updates (results loaded, "saved," a count changing).
  • assertive — interrupts whatever is being read; reserve for urgent messages (errors, session-expiry warnings). Overusing assertive is hostile.
  • The region must exist in the DOM before the text changes. Screen readers announce the diff when the region's contents mutate. If you mount the region and its text in the same render, some SRs miss it — render an empty live region up front and then populate it.
  • aria-atomic="true" makes the SR read the entire region on any change (useful for "3 results" → "5 results"); default reads only what changed.

In React, this "empty region exists, then text appears" pattern is the tricky part, because a conditional render mounts region + text together. Keep the region permanently mounted and toggle its text via state.

Code Example

// Permanently-mounted live region; only the text changes
function ToastRegion({ message }) {
  return (
    <div aria-live="polite" aria-atomic="true" className="sr-region">
      {message}   {/* update this via state to trigger an announcement */}
    </div>
  );
}

// Urgent, interrupting message
<div role="alert">{errorMessage}</div>   {/* assertive by default */}

// Non-urgent status, e.g. results count
<div role="status">{results.length} results found</div>

/* Visually-hidden but SR-available (do NOT use display:none) */
.sr-region {
  position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px;
  padding: 0; margin: -1px; overflow: hidden;
  clip: rect(0, 0, 0, 0); white-space: nowrap; border: 0;
}

Senior Engineer Perspective

The gotcha interviewers reward: the live region must be present in the DOM before it gets its text — a common React bug is conditionally rendering the whole region, which mounts container + message together and gets silently dropped. Also know polite vs assertive and that role="alert"/role="status" are the implicit-live shortcuts. And never hide a live region with display:none or visibility:hidden — those remove it from the a11y tree; use the visually-hidden clip pattern.

Q14. How do you build accessible custom components (dropdown, modal, tabs) in React?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Follow the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG) pattern for the specific widget — it specifies the exact roles, states, and keyboard interactions. Provide the roles (tablist/tab/tabpanel, menu/menuitem, dialog), sync states (aria-selected, aria-expanded), and wire the expected keys (arrows to move, Enter/Space to activate, Escape to close). For production, prefer a headless library (Radix UI, React Aria, Headless UI) that implements the APG correctly.

Detailed Answer

Each pattern has a defined keyboard contract:

WidgetRolesKeys
Tabstablist / tab / tabpanelLeft/Right (or Up/Down) move between tabs; Enter/Space or auto-activate; roving tabindex
Menu / dropdownbutton + menu / menuitemEnter/Space/Down to open; Up/Down to move; Esc to close; focus returns to trigger
Modal dialogdialog + aria-modalFocus trapped; Esc closes; focus restored on close
Combobox / selectcombobox + listbox / optionType to filter; arrows to move; Enter to select; aria-activedescendant

Common state wiring: the tab uses aria-selected and points at its panel via aria-controls; the panel points back with aria-labelledby. A menu button uses aria-haspopup and aria-expanded. Getting arrow-key handling and focus management right is where hand-rolled widgets usually fail — hence the strong recommendation to lean on a headless primitive.

Code Example

// Accessible Tabs following the APG (roving tabindex + arrow keys)
function Tabs({ tabs }) {
  const [active, setActive] = React.useState(0);
  const refs = React.useRef([]);

  function onKeyDown(e) {
    let next = active;
    if (e.key === "ArrowRight") next = (active + 1) % tabs.length;
    if (e.key === "ArrowLeft") next = (active - 1 + tabs.length) % tabs.length;
    if (next !== active) { setActive(next); refs.current[next].focus(); }
  }

  return (
    <div>
      <div role="tablist" aria-label="Settings" onKeyDown={onKeyDown}>
        {tabs.map((t, i) => (
          <button
            key={t.id}
            ref={(el) => (refs.current[i] = el)}
            role="tab"
            id={"tab-" + t.id}
            aria-selected={i === active}
            aria-controls={"panel-" + t.id}
            tabIndex={i === active ? 0 : -1}   {/* roving tabindex */}
            onClick={() => setActive(i)}
          >
            {t.label}
          </button>
        ))}
      </div>
      {tabs.map((t, i) => (
        <div
          key={t.id}
          role="tabpanel"
          id={"panel-" + t.id}
          aria-labelledby={"tab-" + t.id}
          hidden={i !== active}
        >
          {t.content}
        </div>
      ))}
    </div>
  );
}

// In production, prefer a headless lib that ships the full APG behaviour:
// import * as Tabs from "@radix-ui/react-tabs";

Senior Engineer Perspective

Name the APG explicitly — it's the spec for these keyboard contracts and signals you know where the answers live. The mature stance: "I understand the pattern well enough to build it, but in production I use Radix / React Aria / Headless UI because getting focus management and arrow keys exactly right across screen readers is genuinely hard and easy to regress." Interviewers probe the keyboard model (arrows within a widget, Tab between widgets — not Tab through every option), roving tabindex, and returning focus to the trigger on close.

Q15. How do you test accessibility — automated vs manual — and what are the common React a11y mistakes?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Use a layered approach. Automated tools catch the mechanical ~30–40%: lint with eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y as you code, run axe (browser extension) on pages, and add jest-axe / @axe-core/playwright in tests. But automation can't judge whether the experience is usable, so you must also do manual testing: keyboard-only navigation, and a real screen reader (VoiceOver, NVDA, or JAWS). Automated + manual together is the only reliable coverage.

Detailed Answer

Automated layers:

  • eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y — static analysis in the editor/CI; catches missing alt, labels without inputs, invalid ARIA, redundant roles, click handlers on non-interactive elements.
  • axe-core — the engine behind the axe DevTools extension; runs against rendered DOM and reports WCAG violations with fixes.
  • jest-axe — assert expect(await axe(container)).toHaveNoViolations() in unit tests; @axe-core/playwright/Cypress for E2E.

Manual layers (the part automation can't do):

  • Keyboard-only — unplug the mouse; Tab through everything, check visible focus, logical order, Escape closes overlays, no keyboard traps.
  • Screen reader — VoiceOver (macOS/iOS, Cmd+F5), NVDA (Windows, free), JAWS (Windows, enterprise). Verify names, roles, states, and that dynamic updates are announced.
  • Zoom/contrast — 200% zoom, dark mode, forced-colors/high-contrast.

Common React-specific mistakes:

MistakeFix
<div onClick> as a buttonUse <button>
Icon buttons with no accessible nameAdd aria-label; aria-hidden the icon
No focus management in modals / on route changeMove focus in, trap, restore; focus h1 on navigation
Conditionally rendering a live region with its textKeep region mounted, change only the text
Using array index as key for reordering listsStable ids — index keys confuse focus/SR state
outline: none with no replacementUse :focus-visible styles
Placeholder used as the only labelReal <label>
Auto-focusing / stealing focus unexpectedlyOnly move focus in response to user action

Code Example

// jest-axe: fail the test on any axe violation
import { render } from "@testing-library/react";
import { axe, toHaveNoViolations } from "jest-axe";
expect.extend(toHaveNoViolations);

test("Form has no a11y violations", async () => {
  const { container } = render(<SignupForm />);
  const results = await axe(container);
  expect(results).toHaveNoViolations();
});

// Testing Library nudges you toward accessible queries:
// query by role + accessible name, exactly how a screen reader finds it
screen.getByRole("button", { name: /save/i });
screen.getByRole("textbox", { name: /email/i });

// .eslintrc — lint a11y as you write
{ "extends": ["plugin:jsx-a11y/recommended"] }

Senior Engineer Perspective

The line that separates seniors: "automated tools catch only about a third of issues — they can tell you an image lacks alt text, not whether the alt text is meaningful, so they never replace keyboard and screen-reader testing." Show the layered pipeline (lint → jest-axe in CI → manual keyboard + SR pass). A strong extra: Testing Library's getByRole queries double as accessibility assertions — if you can't query a control by its role and name, neither can a screen reader. Then rattle off two or three of the common React mistakes above with their fixes.

19 - BROWSER & WEB PLATFORM FUNDAMENTALS

Target Audience: Frontend / React Engineer (3–6 Years) Goal: Not just answer questions, but survive follow-up grilling from experienced interviewers.

React sits on top of the browser, and interviewers want to know you understand the platform underneath the framework. These questions — how the browser turns bytes into pixels, how events propagate, how HTTP and CORS work, where to store data — separate engineers who use React from engineers who understand the web. This chapter covers the rendering pipeline, the DOM and event model, networking, and storage/caching.

TOP HIGHEST-ROI QUESTIONS IN THIS CHAPTER

  1. What happens when you type a URL and press Enter?
  2. Explain the critical rendering path.
  3. Reflow vs repaint — and how do you minimize them?
  4. What is the DOM, and how does it relate to the virtual DOM?
  5. Event bubbling, capturing, and delegation
  6. How does the browser event loop work?
  7. HTTP essentials: methods, status codes, HTTP/1.1 vs 2 vs 3
  8. What is CORS and how do you fix a CORS error?
  9. How does browser caching work (Cache-Control, ETag)?
  10. Cookies vs localStorage vs sessionStorage vs IndexedDB
  11. What are Service Workers and PWAs?
  12. What are Web Workers and when do you use them?
  13. IntersectionObserver and requestIdleCallback
  14. script: async vs defer

SECTION 1 - HOW THE BROWSER WORKS

Q1. What happens when you type a URL and press Enter?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

The browser resolves the domain via DNS to an IP, opens a TCP connection and negotiates TLS (for HTTPS), sends an HTTP request, receives the HTML response, then parses HTML into the DOM, fetches and applies CSS/JS/images, builds the render tree, lays it out, paints, and composites — while JavaScript can further mutate the page.

Detailed Answer

  1. URL parse — scheme, host, path. Check HSTS (force HTTPS).
  2. DNS resolution — domain → IP, using caches (browser, OS, resolver) before hitting a DNS server.
  3. TCP handshake — SYN / SYN-ACK / ACK (skipped/streamlined with HTTP/3 over QUIC/UDP).
  4. TLS handshake — for HTTPS, negotiate keys and verify the certificate.
  5. HTTP request — browser sends GET with headers (cookies, accept, user-agent).
  6. Server response — status + headers + HTML body (possibly served from a CDN edge).
  7. Parsing & rendering — HTML → DOM, CSS → CSSOM, JS executes (may block), render tree → layout → paint → composite.
  8. Subresources — images, fonts, scripts fetched (respecting caching and priorities).

Senior Engineer Perspective

Interviewers use this as an open-ended depth probe — you can go as deep as you like (DNS caching layers, TCP slow start, TLS 1.3 0-RTT, HTTP/2 multiplexing). Structure the answer in phases and offer to zoom into any. Tie it back to frontend: this is why we use CDNs, preconnect, and SSR — to shorten this chain to first paint.

Q2. Explain the critical rendering path.

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

The critical rendering path is the sequence the browser follows to turn HTML, CSS, and JS into pixels: parse HTML → DOM, parse CSS → CSSOM, combine into the render tree, compute layout (geometry), paint (pixels per layer), then composite layers to the screen. CSS is render-blocking and synchronous scripts are parser-blocking.

Detailed Answer

  • DOM — HTML parsed into a tree of nodes.
  • CSSOM — CSS parsed into a tree of style rules. CSS is render-blocking: the browser won't paint until it has the CSSOM, to avoid a flash of unstyled content.
  • Render tree — DOM + CSSOM merged, excluding non-visual nodes (display:none, <head>).
  • Layout (reflow) — compute each node's exact size and position.
  • Paint — fill in pixels (text, colors, borders, shadows) per layer.
  • Composite — assemble layers (some GPU-accelerated) into the final image.

To optimize: minimize and inline critical CSS, defer non-critical CSS/JS, use async/defer on scripts, and reduce the number of render-blocking resources so first paint happens sooner.

Senior Engineer Perspective

Connect this to Core Web Vitals: LCP is largely determined by how fast the critical path reaches the largest element. A synchronous <script> in the <head> stalls parsing; that's why bundlers inject scripts with defer and why SSR frameworks inline critical CSS.

Q3. Reflow vs repaint — and how do you minimize them?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: Medium-High

Short Answer

A reflow (layout) recomputes element geometry (positions/sizes) and is expensive because it can cascade to the whole document. A repaint redraws pixels without changing layout (e.g. color change) — cheaper. Changing transform/opacity can skip both and only re-composite.

Detailed Answer

Reflow is triggered by changing dimensions, position, adding/removing DOM nodes, or reading layout properties after a write (forced synchronous layout / "layout thrashing"). Repaint is triggered by visual-only changes (background, color, visibility). Compositing-only changes (transform, opacity) are the cheapest.

To minimize:

  • Batch DOM reads then writes; avoid interleaving (prevents forced reflow).
  • Animate transform/opacity, not width/top/margin.
  • Change classes instead of many inline style writes.
  • Take heavy DOM work off-screen (document fragment) then insert once.
  • Use content-visibility: auto to skip rendering off-screen content.

Senior Engineer Perspective

In React you rarely touch the DOM, but the same physics apply to what React's commit produces and to ref/animation code. Naming the read-then-write batching rule and the transform/opacity fast path is the senior signal.

SECTION 2 - DOM & EVENTS

Q4. What is the DOM, and how does it relate to the virtual DOM?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

The DOM (Document Object Model) is the browser's live, in-memory tree representation of the page that JavaScript can read and mutate. The virtual DOM is React's lightweight JS-object copy of what the UI should look like; React diffs the new virtual tree against the previous one and applies the minimal set of real DOM mutations.

Detailed Answer

Real DOM operations are relatively expensive (they can trigger layout/paint), and hand-writing minimal, correct mutations for a complex UI is error-prone. React's virtual DOM lets you describe the whole UI declaratively for a given state; React computes the difference and batches efficient updates. The virtual DOM is not "faster than the DOM" in a vacuum — it's a programming model that makes writing efficient, declarative updates practical and predictable.

Senior Engineer Perspective

Correct the common myth: the virtual DOM isn't magically fast; a hand-tuned direct DOM update can beat it. Its value is the declarative model plus batching. Note that newer frameworks (Svelte, Solid) skip the virtual DOM entirely by compiling to targeted updates — showing you understand the trade-off, not just the React talking point.

Q5. Explain event bubbling, capturing, and delegation.

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Events travel in three phases: capture (root → target), target, then bubble (target → root). By default handlers fire on the bubbling phase. Event delegation exploits bubbling by attaching one listener to a common ancestor and reading event.target, instead of one listener per child.

Detailed Answer

When you click a button inside a list, the event first descends from document to the button (capture), reaches the button (target), then bubbles back up. addEventListener(type, fn, true) listens in capture; the default (false) is bubble. stopPropagation() halts travel; preventDefault() cancels the default browser action (they're independent).

Delegation is the practical payoff: attach one listener to the <ul> and handle clicks for all current and future <li> children — fewer listeners, works for dynamically added items.

Code Example

// Event delegation: one listener for the whole list
list.addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  const li = e.target.closest('li');
  if (!li) return;
  select(li.dataset.id);
});

Senior Engineer Perspective

React's synthetic event system historically used delegation — it attached listeners at a root container (the document pre-17, the app root container in React 17+) rather than on each node, which is exactly this pattern. Knowing React's own delegation model and that e.stopPropagation() on a synthetic event doesn't necessarily stop native listeners is a strong follow-up answer.

Q6. How does the browser event loop work?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

JavaScript runs on a single thread with a call stack. Async callbacks are queued and run only when the stack is empty. There are two queues: microtasks (promises, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver) which drain completely after each task, and macrotasks (timers, I/O, events) which run one per loop iteration. Rendering happens between them.

Detailed Answer

Each loop iteration: run one macrotask → drain ALL microtasks → possibly render (rAF callbacks, style, layout, paint) → next macrotask. This ordering explains why a Promise callback runs before a setTimeout(…, 0) even if the timer was scheduled first.

Code Example

console.log('1');
setTimeout(() => console.log('2'), 0);   // macrotask
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('3')); // microtask
console.log('4');
// Output: 1, 4, 3, 2
// sync first, then all microtasks (3), then the macrotask (2)

Senior Engineer Perspective

The trap: a runaway microtask chain (a promise that keeps queueing more microtasks) can starve rendering and timers, because microtasks must fully drain before the loop moves on. Also tie in that requestAnimationFrame runs right before paint — the correct place for visual updates, unlike setTimeout.

SECTION 3 - NETWORKING

Q7. HTTP essentials: methods, status codes, and HTTP/1.1 vs 2 vs 3.

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Methods: GET (read), POST (create), PUT (replace), PATCH (partial update), DELETE. Status classes: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error. HTTP/2 adds multiplexing over one connection (no head-of-line blocking at the app layer) and header compression; HTTP/3 runs over QUIC/UDP, eliminating TCP head-of-line blocking and speeding connection setup.

Detailed Answer

CodeMeaning
200 / 201 / 204OK / Created / No Content
301 / 302 / 304Moved Permanently / Found / Not Modified (cache)
400 / 401 / 403 / 404Bad Request / Unauthorized / Forbidden / Not Found
422 / 429Unprocessable Entity / Too Many Requests
500 / 502 / 503 / 504Server Error / Bad Gateway / Unavailable / Gateway Timeout

GET should be safe and idempotent; PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not. HTTP/1.1 suffered from limited parallel connections and head-of-line blocking; HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection; HTTP/3 moves to QUIC so a lost packet on one stream doesn't stall the others.

Senior Engineer Perspective

Know the 401 vs 403 distinction (not authenticated vs authenticated-but-not-allowed) — it's asked constantly. And that HTTP/2 multiplexing reduced the value of old frontend hacks like domain sharding and sprite sheets. Mentioning that shows you connect protocol evolution to frontend practice.

Q8. What is CORS and how do you fix a CORS error?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser security mechanism that blocks JS from reading responses from a different origin unless the server explicitly opts in with Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers. You fix it on the server by sending the right CORS headers — not in the frontend, and not by disabling browser security.

Detailed Answer

The same-origin policy stops app.com's JS from reading api.other.com's responses (origin = scheme + host + port). CORS lets the server relax this. For "non-simple" requests (custom headers, methods like PUT/DELETE, JSON content-type), the browser first sends a preflight OPTIONS request; the server must answer with allowed origins, methods, and headers before the real request is sent.

Fixes (server-side):

  • Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.com (avoid * in production, especially with credentials).
  • Access-Control-Allow-Methods and Access-Control-Allow-Headers for preflight.
  • Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true if sending cookies (and you cannot use * for origin then).

In development, a dev proxy (Vite/Next rewrite) routes API calls through the same origin to sidestep CORS locally.

Code Example

// vite.config.js — dev proxy so the browser sees a same-origin request
export default {
  server: {
    proxy: { '/api': { target: 'https://api.other.com', changeOrigin: true } }
  }
};

Senior Engineer Perspective

The mistake juniors make is trying to "fix CORS in React" — you can't; it's enforced by the browser based on server headers. Say clearly: CORS is server-configured; the proxy is a dev convenience; and CORS is not authentication (Q relates to security chapter). That precision is exactly what's being tested.

SECTION 4 - STORAGE & CACHING

Q9. How does browser caching work (Cache-Control, ETag)?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: Medium-High

Short Answer

Servers control caching with response headers. Cache-Control sets freshness (max-age, no-cache, immutable). When a cached response goes stale, the browser revalidates using ETag/If-None-Match or Last-Modified/If-Modified-Since; if unchanged the server returns 304 Not Modified with no body, saving bandwidth.

Detailed Answer

  • Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable — cache for a year, never revalidate. Used for content-hashed assets (app.4f3a.js).
  • Cache-Control: no-cache — cache but always revalidate before use.
  • Cache-Control: no-store — never cache (sensitive data).
  • ETag — a fingerprint of the resource; the browser sends it back in If-None-Match, and the server replies 304 if it still matches.

The frontend build strategy that ties this together: hash filenames so assets can be cached forever (immutable), and serve index.html with no-cache so new deploys are picked up immediately (the fresh HTML references the new hashed asset URLs).

Senior Engineer Perspective

The "cache the hashed assets forever, never cache the HTML" strategy is the canonical SPA deploy pattern — stating it shows real production experience. Also distinguish the HTTP cache from the browser's disk/memory cache and from a Service Worker cache (Q11), which you control programmatically.

Q10. Cookies vs localStorage vs sessionStorage vs IndexedDB — when do you use each?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: High

Short Answer

Cookies: small (~4KB), sent with every request, ideal for auth session tokens (use HttpOnly+Secure+SameSite). localStorage: ~5–10MB, persistent, synchronous, same-origin, JS-accessible — for non-sensitive prefs. sessionStorage: same as localStorage but cleared when the tab closes. IndexedDB: large, async, structured/object storage for offline data and big caches.

Detailed Answer

CookieslocalStoragesessionStorageIndexedDB
Capacity~4KB~5–10MB~5MBHundreds of MB+
Sent to server?Yes (every request)NoNoNo
LifetimeConfigurable expiryUntil clearedTab sessionUntil cleared
APIstringsync stringsync stringasync, structured
JS accessible?No if HttpOnlyYesYesYes

Security note: because localStorage is readable by any JS on the page, it's vulnerable to XSS token theft — which is why auth tokens are best kept in HttpOnly cookies (see the Security chapter). localStorage is synchronous, so avoid large reads/writes on the main thread.

Senior Engineer Perspective

The token-storage debate (localStorage vs HttpOnly cookie) is the follow-up magnet: localStorage is exposed to XSS; cookies are exposed to CSRF but mitigated by SameSite. A balanced answer that names both threat models earns senior marks. For large offline datasets, IndexedDB (often via a wrapper like Dexie or idb) is the right tool, not localStorage.

Q11. What are Service Workers and PWAs?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: Medium

Short Answer

A Service Worker is a script that runs in the background, separate from the page, acting as a programmable network proxy: it can intercept fetch requests and serve responses from a cache, enabling offline support, custom caching strategies, background sync, and push notifications. A PWA (Progressive Web App) is a web app that uses a Service Worker plus a manifest to be installable and app-like.

Detailed Answer

The Service Worker sits between the app and the network. On fetch events you choose a strategy: cache-first (fast, for static assets), network-first (fresh data, fall back to cache offline), or stale-while-revalidate (serve cache instantly, update in background). It has its own lifecycle (install → activate → fetch) and cannot access the DOM. A PWA also needs a manifest.json (name, icons, theme, start URL) and HTTPS.

Code Example

// Simplified fetch handler: cache-first
self.addEventListener('fetch', (event) => {
  event.respondWith(
    caches.match(event.request).then(
      (cached) => cached || fetch(event.request)
    )
  );
});

Senior Engineer Perspective

Warn about the classic Service Worker footgun: a badly-scoped or overly-aggressive cache can "trap" users on a stale version after deploy. Mention versioned caches, skipWaiting/clients.claim, and that tools like Workbox (and Vite PWA plugin) encode safe strategies so you don't hand-roll it.

Q12. What are Web Workers and when do you use them?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: Medium

Short Answer

A Web Worker runs JavaScript on a background thread, separate from the main UI thread, so heavy computation doesn't block rendering or user interaction. They communicate with the main thread via postMessage and have no DOM access. Use them for CPU-intensive work: parsing large files, image/data processing, cryptography, heavy calculations.

Detailed Answer

JavaScript is single-threaded, so a long synchronous task freezes the whole UI (INP suffers, the page becomes unresponsive). A Web Worker offloads that work to another thread; you send input via postMessage and receive results via a message event. Data is copied (structured clone) unless you use Transferable objects or SharedArrayBuffer.

Code Example

// main.js
const worker = new Worker(new URL('./heavy.js', import.meta.url), { type: 'module' });
worker.postMessage(bigData);
worker.onmessage = (e) => setResult(e.data);

// heavy.js
onmessage = (e) => {
  const result = expensiveComputation(e.data); // off the main thread
  postMessage(result);
};

Senior Engineer Perspective

Distinguish the three worker types: Web Workers (compute), Service Workers (network proxy/offline), Worker threads (Node). In React, libraries like Comlink make worker messaging feel like async function calls. Mention that most apps don't need workers — reach for one only when the profiler shows main-thread-blocking computation.

Q13. What are IntersectionObserver and requestIdleCallback?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: Medium

Short Answer

IntersectionObserver asynchronously notifies you when an element enters or leaves the viewport (or a root) — the efficient way to do lazy loading, infinite scroll, and reveal-on-scroll without scroll-event thrashing. requestIdleCallback schedules low-priority work to run during the browser's idle periods, so it doesn't compete with rendering or input.

Detailed Answer

Before IntersectionObserver, "is this element visible?" meant listening to scroll and calling getBoundingClientRect() constantly — expensive and janky (forced reflow). IntersectionObserver does the visibility math off the main thread and fires a callback only on threshold crossings.

requestIdleCallback(cb, { timeout }) runs cb when the main thread is idle, giving you the remaining frame budget — good for analytics beacons, prefetching, or non-urgent work. It falls back to a setTimeout polyfill where unsupported.

Code Example

const io = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
  entries.forEach((entry) => {
    if (entry.isIntersecting) {
      loadImage(entry.target);
      io.unobserve(entry.target);
    }
  });
}, { rootMargin: '200px' }); // start loading 200px early
images.forEach((img) => io.observe(img));

Senior Engineer Perspective

IntersectionObserver is the backbone of most infinite-scroll and lazy-load implementations (and libraries like react-intersection-observer wrap it). Using rootMargin to preload just before entry is the detail that shows you've shipped it. Note native loading="lazy" handles the common image case with zero JS.

Q14. script: async vs defer — what's the difference?

ROI: ★★★★☆ Frequency: Medium

Short Answer

A plain <script> blocks HTML parsing while it downloads and executes. async downloads in parallel and executes as soon as it's ready (order not guaranteed, can still interrupt parsing). defer downloads in parallel but executes only after HTML parsing completes, in document order. For app bundles, defer (or a module script) is the right default.

Detailed Answer

AttributeBlocks parsing?Execution timingOrder preserved?
(none)YesImmediately on downloadYes
asyncNo (download), yes (exec)As soon as downloadedNo
deferNoAfter parsing, before DOMContentLoadedYes

Use async for independent scripts that don't depend on the DOM or each other (analytics). Use defer for app code and scripts that need the DOM and a predictable order. Note <script type="module"> is deferred by default.

Senior Engineer Perspective

This is why every bundler injects the main bundle with defer (or as a module) at the end of <head>/<body>: non-blocking download, DOM-ready execution, correct order. Mentioning that ES modules are deferred by default, and that a render-blocking script in <head> is a classic performance bug, closes the loop nicely.

20 - FRONTEND SECURITY

Target Audience: Frontend / React Engineer (3–6 Years) Goal: Not just answer questions, but survive follow-up grilling from experienced interviewers.

TOP HIGHEST-ROI QUESTIONS IN THIS CHAPTER

  1. What is XSS, and what is the difference between stored, reflected, and DOM-based XSS?
  2. How does React protect against XSS by default, and how does dangerouslySetInnerHTML reintroduce it?
  3. How do you safely render user-provided HTML (and why is DOMPurify the answer)?
  4. What is DOM-based XSS, and how do you validate/escape untrusted input on the client?
  5. Where should you store JWTs/access tokens — localStorage vs an httpOnly cookie?
  6. What is CSRF, why are cookie-based SPAs vulnerable, and how do tokens and SameSite cookies defend against it?
  7. How does OAuth2 / OIDC with PKCE work for a SPA, and why is the implicit flow dead?
  8. What is a Content Security Policy (CSP) and how does it mitigate XSS?
  9. What is clickjacking, and how do X-Frame-Options and frame-ancestors stop it?
  10. What are the key security response headers a frontend should ship?
  11. Is CORS a security mechanism — and why is it not a substitute for authorization?
  12. Why does HTTPS matter for a SPA, and what is mixed content?
  13. How do you avoid leaking secrets in a frontend bundle or environment variables?
  14. What are supply-chain risks in npm, and how do lockfiles and npm audit help?
  15. What is prototype pollution and how does it reach the frontend?
  16. What are open redirects and how do you sandbox untrusted iframes?

SECTION 1 - XSS

Q1. What is XSS, and what is the difference between stored, reflected, and DOM-based XSS?

ROI: ★★★★★ Frequency: Extremely High

Short Answer

Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) is an injection attack where an attacker gets their JavaScript to run in another user's browser, in the context of your origin. Once their script runs on your origin it can do anything the user can: read the DOM, steal tokens, make authenticated requests, and impersonate the user. The three classic types differ by where the malicious payload comes from: stored (persisted on the server and served to victims), reflected (bounced back off a request parameter), and DOM-based (never touches the server — the vulnerability is entirely in client-side JS).

Detailed Answer

Stored (persistent) XSS

The payload is saved in your data store — a comment, a profile bio, a support ticket — and later rendered to every user who views it. This is the most dangerous variant because it is self-propagating and hits many victims without them clicking anything special. A classic example is the old MySpace "Samy" worm.

Reflected XSS
